london-the-city-on-the-tidal-thames.context_blurb:
London grew up on the River Thames in southern England, where the river still rises and falls with the tides from the sea. It began as a Roman town, became the capital of medieval England and, in time, the hub of a worldwide empire. Again and again it has burned, been rebuilt and remade itself.

The Tower of London, the old stone fortress on the river's north bank, keeps a flock of ravens and keeps them very carefully. An old legend warns that if the ravens ever leave for good, the Tower will fall into ruin and the kingdom will fall with it. The Tower's own historians suspect the tale was invented in Victorian times, since the first record of ravens there dates only from 1883.

To make sure they stay, the Ravenmaster trims the flight feathers on one wing of each bird, about every three weeks, so a raven can hop and glide but is too lopsided to fly far.

For six centuries the Tower also kept a royal zoo, full of animals given to English kings. Around 1252 the King of Norway sent Henry III a polar bear, which was led to the Thames on a long rope so it could swim and catch its own fish. The menagerie closed in 1835, and its animals helped found London Zoo.

In September 1666, fire broke out in the bakery of Thomas Farriner, the king's baker. His shop stood on Pudding Lane, a narrow street named not for desserts but for the puddings, or animal guts, carted down it to the river. Driven by a dry east wind, the Great Fire burned for about four days. It consumed more than thirteen thousand houses, scores of churches and the medieval cathedral of St Paul, leaving perhaps 100,000 people without a home. Yet only around eight deaths were ever officially recorded, because the flames spread slowly enough for most people to flee, though some historians think poor victims went uncounted.

Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke raised a stone column, the Monument, to remember the fire. It is 202 feet high, and it stands exactly 202 feet from the spot on Pudding Lane where the fire started, a piece of hidden geometry. A spiral of 311 steps climbs inside.

Wren also built the new St Paul's. High in its dome runs the Whispering Gallery. A whisper there does not cross the open space; it clings to the smooth curved wall and creeps around it, so a friend on the far side hears every word.

In January 1863 the Metropolitan Railway opened beneath London's streets, the first underground railway anywhere in the world. Its tunnels were dug as trenches and roofed over, and since there were no electric trains yet, its steam engines carried special gear to swallow their own smoke.

Older London lies under it all. The Romans founded the city, which they called Londinium, around AD 47 to 50, and about AD 200 they ringed it with the London Wall, whose weathered stones still turn up among the glass towers of the City. The young town nearly died at once. Around AD 60 Boudica, warrior queen of the Iceni, rose in revolt and burned it to the ground. The fire was so fierce that it baked the earth red, and wherever archaeologists dig deep enough under the City they meet that layer of bright red burnt ash.

The tide that made London a port can also drown it. A storm surge from the North Sea is squeezed higher as it is funnelled up the narrowing estuary, and a deadly flood in 1953 showed the danger. Since 1982 the Thames Barrier at Woolwich has stood guard, its gates lying curved-side-down on the riverbed so ships pass over them. When a surge threatens, each gate turns on its pivots and swings up until it stands upright across the river, walling off the sea. The four biggest gates are each about 20 metres high.

luang-prabang.context_blurb:
Luang Prabang is a small old royal town high in the hills of northern Laos. It sits on a narrow tongue of land between two rivers, and its lanes are lined with gilded Buddhist temples with sweeping roofs and shuttered houses from French colonial times. Life in the town still moves to the rhythm of its monks.

At the tip of the peninsula the brown, silt-heavy Mekong and the clear blue-green Nam Khan join in a confluence, the spot where two rivers become one, and for a stretch below the point the two colours flow side by side before they mix.

Every dawn, a long line of barefoot, orange-robed monks files through the streets with their bowls, and kneeling townspeople give each one a handful of sticky rice, a daily offering called Tak Bat. The monks eat only what they are given, at breakfast and one midday meal, and nothing after.

The town was once called Muang Sua and later Xieng Thong before it took its present name. In 1359 a Khmer king gave a sacred gold Buddha, the Phra Bang, to Fa Ngum, founder of the kingdom of Lan Xang, the Million Elephants. In the Lao language luang means royal or great, so the town's name means the Royal Buddha Image, after that statue.

In the middle of town rises Mount Phousi, a wooded hill about 100 metres high, where pilgrims climb some 328 steps to a gilded stupa on the summit. From the top, at sunset, the rivers wrap around the temple roofs below.

The jewel of the town is Wat Xieng Thong, the royal temple King Setthathirath built in 1559, its tiered roofs sweeping almost to the ground. In 1887 raiders called the Black Flags attacked and set fire to most of the town. They spared Wat Xieng Thong on purpose, the story goes, because one of their commanders had trained there as a young monk and ordered it left alone.

On the deep red back wall of its main hall, thousands of tiny pieces of coloured mirror-glass form the Tree of Life, one of the best-loved images in all of Laos.

About 30 kilometres south, Kuang Si Falls tumbles down pale terraces into pools of unreal aquamarine. No dye or algae colours them. The stream runs over limestone and dissolves its calcium carbonate, and the fine mineral specks in the water scatter blue light, tinting the pools that dreamlike blue-green. The same mineral hardens again along the rims as travertine, slowly building the terraces higher.

machu-picchu.context_blurb:
Machu Picchu is a town of grey granite that the Inca built in the 1400s on a ridge high in the Andes of Peru, about 2,430 metres up in the cloud forest. Its temples, houses and green terraces cling to a thin rock saddle between two peaks, so often wrapped in mist that people call it the cloud city.

In the classic photograph, a steep sugarloaf summit towers just behind the ruins. That peak is Huayna Picchu, the sharp sister summit, climbed by a near-vertical stairway in the granite nicknamed the Stairs of Death. Many visitors assume the site is named for it, but it is not.

In Quechua, the Inca language, machu means old and pikchu means peak, so Machu Picchu simply means old peak, the name of the taller mountain at the other end of the ridge. Its neighbour Huayna Picchu is the young peak.

Some 450 metres below, the Urubamba River swings around the ridge on three sides in a tight hairpin, almost a natural moat.

Romantic tales once called it the work of a vanished race. In fact it was a royal country estate, a mountain retreat built around 1450 for the Inca emperor Pachacuti and lived in for only about 80 years.

In 1911 the American explorer Hiram Bingham announced that he had found a lost city. A local farmer, Melchor Arteaga, had guided him up. At the ruins Bingham found Quechua families, the Richartes and the Alvarezes, already farming the old terraces, and a Richarte boy led him the last stretch. A local man had even scratched his name on a wall in 1902, years before Bingham came.

The site survived nearly whole because the Spanish conquerors never discovered it: hidden on its remote ridge, it was never looted, never burned and never torn apart for church stone, as Cusco was.

The Inca came in along their royal road. Hikers on the Inca Trail still crest the Inti Punku, the Sun Gate, a stone doorway on the old road where the whole estate bursts into view between its two peaks.

The green terraces grew maize and potatoes, but their deeper work is to hold the mountainside in place: stone walls backed by layers of gravel and soil brace the steep, rain-soaked slope against landslides.

The ground here shakes often, and the builders shaped even the openings for it. Every door, window and niche is a trapezoid, wider at the bottom than at the top and leaning slightly inward, which lowers the wall's centre of gravity so it flexes instead of cracking.

At the highest sacred point stands the Intihuatana, the hitching post of the sun, a pillar carved from the bedrock whose faces line up with the sun's yearly path. Inca priests held that it could tie the sun to its course at the solstice. Similar stones elsewhere in the empire did not survive, so this one is rare.

The finest walls use no mortar at all; each block was ground to fit its neighbours so closely that a knife blade cannot enter the joints. In an earthquake the loose-fitted blocks jostle and bounce, then settle back into their exact places when the shaking stops, so Andean guides say the stones dance. A mortared wall would simply crack.

The greatest work is the part no visitor sees. The engineer Kenneth Wright found that about 60 per cent of the building effort went into foundations and drainage buried underground: deep stonework and a hidden bed of crushed rock that lets the torrential rain soak straight through the site. Without that drainage, Wright judged, the terraces would long ago have washed off the ridge.

madagascar-the-isolated-ark.context_blurb:
Madagascar is a giant island in the Indian Ocean, off the southeast coast of Africa and bigger than France. It has drifted alone for so long that its forests, its rocks and its living things look like nowhere else on Earth. People reached it only about two thousand years ago, very recently for an island.

Near Morondava, on the west coast, a dirt road runs between towering bottle-shaped trees almost 30 metres tall. They are baobabs, Grandidier's baobabs, the largest of their kind, and the road is called the Avenue of the Baobabs. Six of the world's nine baobab species grow only on Madagascar.

A baobab survives the long dry season by storing rainwater in its soft, spongy wood, so its trunk visibly fattens after the rains and grows thinner as the drought uses the water up.

The giants of the Avenue stand alone in bare fields, but they were never planted in a row. The land was once thick forest, and when people cleared it for rice and pasture they left the huge baobabs standing, the last survivors of the woods around them. The Malagasy call the baobab renala, mother of the forest.

Western Madagascar also holds a forest made of stone. The Tsingy de Bemaraha is a maze of grey limestone blades so sharp that its Malagasy name warns that no one can walk there barefoot. Nobody carved it: over millions of years slightly acidic rainwater seeped into the cracks of a flat limestone plateau and dissolved it from within, leaving only thin needles standing. Geographers call such dissolved landscapes karst, and the Tsingy is one of the most extreme on Earth.

Why is Madagascar so strange? The island broke away from the other continents and has sailed alone across open ocean for tens of millions of years, so its plants and animals evolved on their own path. More than nine in ten of its species live nowhere else.

It came loose in two steps as the ancient supercontinent Gondwana broke up: first it split from Africa, about 180 million years ago, and then, some 90 million years ago, from India.

In the dry south grows a spiny forest of tall, leafless, thorny stems, the Didiereaceae, that look just like the cacti of American deserts. A piece of one grafted onto a cactus fuses and grows on as a single plant. That graft works because they are not mere look-alikes: they are true cousins of America's cacti, close kin living an ocean apart.

Because Madagascar holds whole families of plants found on no other land, ecologists nickname it the eighth continent, a world of its own.

Today the island bleeds. Since the 1950s, slash-and-burn farming, overgrazing and fire have stripped much of its forest. Rain washes the bare red soil, heavy with iron, off the land and into the rivers, which pour it out to sea in great blood-red plumes that astronauts can see from orbit. The Betsiboka River's red stain is the most famous.

maelstroms-the-seas-great-whirlpools.context_blurb:
A maelstrom is a great whirlpool, spun up where strong tides are forced through a narrow gap between islands. Norway's coast holds the most famous ones and Scotland's islands another, and sailors have feared them for centuries, though real ones, powerful as they are, do not swallow ships whole.

The original is the Moskstraumen, off Norway's Lofoten Islands. Edgar Allan Poe made it the heart of an English story in 1841, and Jules Verne later used it for the climax of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. The word comes from Dutch, malen, to grind, and stroom, stream, so a maelstrom is literally a grinding stream.

Near the town of Bodø lies Saltstraumen, a strait only 150 metres wide where every six hours as much as 400 million cubic metres of seawater force through, spinning whirlpools 10 metres across; it is often ranked among the most powerful tidal currents in the world.

Scotland's Gulf of Corryvreckan, between the islands of Jura and Scarba, roars as the flood tide races over an undersea pinnacle of rock. In August 1947 a boat's engine failed there, and its passengers were stranded on a rock until lobstermen rescued them. One of them was George Orwell, who was living on Jura to finish his novel Nineteen Eighty-Four. He completed the first draft about three months later.

manaus.context_blurb:
Manaus is a big modern city of more than two million people, with tower blocks and traffic, set right in the middle of the Brazilian rainforest. It grew where the dark Rio Negro joins the Amazon, about 1,600 kilometres inland, and a rubber boom in the late 1800s briefly made it one of the richest cities on Earth.

Just downstream the two rivers meet but do not blend. The coffee-black Negro and the sandy-tan Solimões flow side by side in two stripes for about 6 kilometres. Brazilians call the spot the Encontro das Águas, the Meeting of the Waters.

They stay apart because they differ in temperature, in speed and in the sediment they carry: the Negro is warm and slow, about 28 degrees, while the Solimões is cooler, about 22 degrees, faster and loaded with silt from the Andes. Those differences make the waters differ in density, and it takes some 60 kilometres more for them to mix completely.

No paved road reliably links Manaus to the rest of Brazil. Almost everyone and everything still arrives by riverboat or by small plane, just as in the days of the rubber traders.

In the 1890s the rubber barons hauled marble, chandeliers and iron from Europe to raise a grand opera house, the Teatro Amazonas, which opened on the last day of 1896. Its stage curtain, painted in Paris, shows the Meeting of the Waters, the rivers that paid for it all.

The theatre's dome is visible across the city. Its 36,000 painted tiles are laid out in green, yellow and blue, the colours of Brazil's national flag. Much else came from Europe: roof tiles from Alsace, steel from Glasgow, marble from Carrara and 198 chandeliers.

The river that names the city is a wonder of its own. The Rio Negro is the largest of the world's blackwater rivers, stained dark like strong tea by tannins from the plants of the sandy forest it drains, yet carrying almost no mud, and so acidic, around pH 4, that few mosquitoes breed in it. The silty Solimões is its opposite.

manila-intramuros.context_blurb:
The Philippine capital, Manila, rose at the mouth of the Pasig, where the river meets Manila Bay. For more than three centuries it was the seat of Spanish rule in Asia. In the middle of today's huge city survives its oldest core, a Spanish town of churches and plazas sealed inside stone ramparts and a moat.

That walled quarter is Intramuros, Latin for within the walls, founded by Miguel López de Legazpi in 1571.

The walls divided people. Spaniards, from governors to friars, lived inside; the islands' own people, and most of the Chinese, lived outside. Chinese merchants crowded their trading quarter, the Parian, right up against the outside of the walls. The old city shows both faces of colonial rule plainly: Spain fenced the Filipinos out, and Spain also left the churches, plazas and streets that still give Manila its face.

At the river mouth stands Fort Santiago, a stone citadel begun in 1571 on the site of Rajah Matanda's earlier fort. Santiago is the Spanish name for Saint James, patron of Spain and of its soldiers, and his image is carved above the gate.

The oldest of the seven bastions, the Baluarte de San Diego of 1587, was said to be shaped like an ace of spades, a stone playing card jutting toward the moat.

Early in 1945 a month of fighting, the Battle of Manila, reduced Intramuros to rubble and killed more than 100,000 civilians. Of the seven stone churches inside the walls, only San Agustin Church, finished in 1607 and the oldest stone church in the Philippines, was left standing. It is now a World Heritage Site.

Beyond the walls spreads Manila Bay, some 2,000 square kilometres of calm, shallow water. What Manileños love most about it are its sunsets, which blaze gold and crimson across the water and are counted among the most beautiful on Earth.

mariachi-jalisco-mexico.context_blurb:
Mariachi is the sound much of the world hears as the voice of Mexico: violins singing, trumpets blazing and guitars driving the beat, played by musicians dressed like the old Mexican horseman. It took shape on the cattle ranches of the Mexican west during the nineteenth century, and in 2011 UNESCO listed it as part of the living heritage of humanity.

Mariachi is the musical emblem of Jalisco, in western Mexico, and its big-city home is the state capital, Guadalajara. From there the serenading bands spread across Mexico and around the world.

The small Jalisco town of Cocula calls itself the World Cradle of Mariachi, the place where the son jalisciense, the folk style at the music's heart, first took shape.

The musicians wear the traje de charro, the suit of the charro, the Mexican horseman: a broad sombrero, a short embroidered jacket and close-fitting trousers studded down each leg with silver buttons.

The rhythm and the bass come from two round-backed guitars rarely seen outside Mexico: the small, high five-string vihuela, strummed fast for the beat, and the huge, deep-bellied guitarrón, hugged like a barrel to boom out the low notes.

The trumpet that now cuts through every mariachi tune is a newcomer. For most of the music's history the bands had none. In the 1930s commercial radio pushed the bands to add it, because broadcasters wanted a brighter, more piercing sound that would carry over the air.

Guides like to say the word comes from the French mariage, wedding, coined when French soldiers hired local bands to play at their weddings. The story is a myth: the French army did not arrive until 1864. The word already appears in an 1833 civil record from Nayarit, three decades earlier, and again in an 1852 letter from a priest to the archbishop of Guadalajara. Scholars now trace it to Coca, a lost native language once spoken around Cocula.

marrakech.context_blurb:
Marrakech is an old royal city of Morocco, spread over a hot, dry plain at the foot of the snow-capped High Atlas. Inside its walls the medina is a maze of lanes, markets and gardens, and for centuries it was the capital of Berber dynasties whose empires reached deep into Africa and across the sea into Spain.

At sunset the whole city glows the same warm red, which is why it is called the Red City. That colour is not paint: the walls, gates and houses are built of pisé, red earth rich in iron that is rammed hard between boards and left to dry in the sun. The great ramparts were raised around 1122 by the sultan Ali ibn Yusuf.

West of the city lies the Menara, a walled garden around a great pool dug in the 1100s to store water. On still days the pool becomes a mirror for the snowy peaks of the Atlas Mountains on the horizon, whose meltwater it was built to collect.

Every evening the great square of Jemaa el-Fnaa becomes an open-air theatre of snake charmers, drummers, acrobats, smoky food stalls and storytellers who keep old tales alive by voice alone. In 2001 UNESCO honoured the square for that living tradition of the spoken word, not for its stones.

Above the rooftops rises the Koutoubia Mosque, whose minaret, 77 metres tall, the Almohads finished in the 1100s. Its name comes from kutubiyyin, the booksellers, because a market of book and manuscript sellers once crowded the streets at its foot. It became the model for two sister towers, the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower of Rabat.

The city was founded around 1070 by the Almoravids, Sanhaja Berber nomads who rode up out of the Sahara, and from this caravan capital they went on to rule from West Africa to Muslim Spain.

The plain has no river, yet the city's gardens bloomed for nine centuries. Its builders dug the khettara, long, gently sloping tunnels that run back under the plain to the Atlas foothills and carry cool groundwater and snowmelt to the city by gravity alone. Kept in shade underground, almost none of the water evaporates on its long journey. The khettara is the North African form of the Persian qanat.

mecca-and-the-valley-of-the-hijaz.context_blurb:
Mecca, in the dry Hijaz region of western Saudi Arabia, is the holiest city of Islam. The Prophet Muhammad was born there in the 500s, and at its heart stands the Kaaba, the shrine toward which Muslims everywhere turn to pray. Each year millions of pilgrims come for the Hajj, the journey every Muslim who is able is expected to make once in a lifetime.

Most great holy cities grew beside a river or a spring. Mecca has neither. The old city lies tucked in a narrow mountain valley about 277 metres above sea level, some 70 kilometres inland from the Red Sea port of Jeddah, ringed by bare peaks, so that it is nicknamed the Hollow of Mecca.

The Kaaba is a plain stone building about 15 metres tall, and its Arabic name, ka'ba, simply means a cube. Its sides measure roughly 12 by 10.5 metres, not a perfect cube, but close enough to earn the name.

The direction that faces the Kaaba is called the qibla, and all mosques everywhere are aligned with it, so that prayers from Tokyo to Cairo all point to one building.

Each year, during the Hajj, the Kaaba is draped in a fresh kiswa, a vast cloth of black silk embroidered with verses of the Quran in gold.

Around the Kaaba spread the courtyards of the Sacred Mosque, the Masjid al-Haram, biggest of all mosques, which covers some 356,000 square metres and can hold about 3 million worshippers at once.

Near the city rises a mountain with a double summit, and pilgrims climb some 1,750 steps to a small cave just below its crest, the Cave of Hira. The mountain is Jabal al-Nour, which means the Mountain of Light.

The Black Stone, worn smooth by the touch of countless pilgrims, is set into one corner of the Kaaba. Many people repeat that it is a meteorite. In fact no scientist has ever examined it, so that claim remains untested. London's Natural History Museum has suggested it may be an ordinary earthly rock, and the belief that it fell from heaven is a tradition, not a measured fact.

The prayer direction has not always pointed here. In Islam's first years Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem, and only around 623 did Muhammad's community turn south to face Mecca, in the middle of a prayer. The mosque in Medina where that happened is still called the Mosque of the Two Qiblas.

The single most essential moment of the Hajj comes on the Plain of Arafat, about 20 kilometres east of the city, where the whole multitude of pilgrims stands from midday until the sun goes down on one day of the year. That standing, the wuquf, is among the largest gatherings of people on Earth.

mediterranean-climate-the-scattered-five.context_blurb:
A Mediterranean climate means long, hot, dry summers and mild, showery winters. It is named for the lands around the Mediterranean Sea, but it turns up in just five places on Earth: the Mediterranean Basin itself, the coast of California, the middle of Chile, southwest Australia and the Cape of South Africa. Each grew its own fire-loving shrubland, and all five are now famous wine country.

In most of the world the heaviest rain comes in the warm season, when hot air rises and storms build. The Mediterranean runs the year backward, with rainy winters, parched summers and months of cloudless, rainless heat, so the olive tree and the grapevine are built to wait out the summer drought.

The sun-baked hills of southern California are covered in chaparral, an oily evergreen tangle of chamise, manzanita and scrub oak, named from the Spanish chaparro, scrub oak. When the hot Santa Ana winds blow in autumn, whole slopes can go up in flames.

Central Chile, squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific, has its own silvery scrubland, the matorral. Walled in by the Atacama Desert to the north, the Andes to the east and the ocean to the west, it is so isolated that about 95 per cent of its plants grow nowhere else, among them the towering Chilean wine palm.

Fire is part of the cycle here, and the plants are built for it. Many chaparral shrubs store energy in a burl, a woody swelling at the root crown that fire cannot kill, so when the branches burn away the burl, safe underground, sends up new shoots within days.

Mark the five on a globe and a pattern leaps out. Each one hugs the western edge of its continent, between about 30 and 40 degrees from the equator, in the mid-latitudes. There, cold ocean currents chill the coast, and in summer a belt of high pressure drifts toward the pole and pushes the rain-bearing storms away; only in winter, when it slips back, can the storms get through.

At Africa's southern tip, near the Cape, grows fynbos, Afrikaans for fine bush, a low shrubland that packs about 9,000 plant species, two-thirds of them found nowhere else, into the smallest of Earth's six plant kingdoms. It holds more than 600 kinds of heath alone.

In Australia's southwestern corner, the sandy heath called kwongan bursts into one of the world's greatest wildflower shows each spring, with banksias, kangaroo paws and orchids. The region has over 8,000 kinds of native plants, and half of them grow on no other continent.

Many of these plants seal their seeds inside woody pods with resin for years, and only the fierce heat of a wildfire melts the seal, dropping the seeds onto fresh ash where nothing competes with them. In Australia's banksias, a tiny winged separator inside each pod then releases the seeds a few at a time.

Together the five regions cover only about 2 per cent of Earth's land, yet they hold close to a fifth of all the plant species known to science. Biologists link that richness to the long summer drought and the regular fires, which split the land into countless small habitats where new species arise.

megathrust-the-deepest-trenches-and-the-.context_blurb:
Where one of Earth's great plates dives beneath another, the long, sloping fault between them is called a megathrust. These are the largest faults on the planet. Along them lie the deepest trenches in the oceans, and from them come the most powerful earthquakes and the most far-reaching tsunamis ever recorded.

The deepest of all is the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, southwest of Guam. At its bottom, the Challenger Deep, the floor lies about 11 km down, close to 10,935 metres, lower than any other spot on the planet's solid crust. It is named for HMS Challenger, whose crew first sounded those depths in 1875.

Mount Everest stands about 8,849 metres high, so if it were sunk whole into the Challenger Deep, its summit would still be roughly 2 km under the surface.

The first people to reach the Deep, in 1960, went as a pair, but in 2012 the film director James Cameron made the dive in a one-man submarine, the first person ever to reach the deepest place on Earth all alone.

Why is the Mariana Trench so deep? The Pacific plate sinking there is up to about 170 million years old, some of the oldest, coldest and densest ocean crust on the planet, so it plunges steeply and drags the trench down with it.

At the bottom, the weight of all that water presses with about 1,099 atmospheres, more than a thousand times the air pressure at sea level, enough to crush an unprotected human instantly.

These diving plates also make the biggest earthquakes. Friction locks the plates together while they keep pushing, so strain builds up for centuries, until the fault suddenly lurches and slips all at once over hundreds of kilometres. Every quake of magnitude 9 or above ever measured has been such a megathrust rupture.

The strongest of all hit southern Chile near Valdivia in 1960, along the line where the Nazca plate slides under South America: at about magnitude 9.5, it ruptured some 800 kilometres of fault and sent a tsunami across the whole Pacific.

Megathrusts move the land itself. In the great Alaska earthquake of Good Friday 1964, Montague Island was heaved up about 13 m, lifting old beaches into the air, while other stretches of coast sank. At about magnitude 9.2, it was the second-strongest quake ever measured.

Japan's Tohoku quake of March 2011 shoved Honshu about 2.4 metres east and shifted so much mass that Earth spun a little faster, making each day about 1.8 microseconds shorter, the way a skater spins faster by pulling in her arms.

The Sumatra quake of 26 December 2004 tore the seafloor along about 1,300 km, roughly the distance from London to Rome, the longest rupture ever observed. It set the whole planet ringing like a bell.

Off Washington and Oregon lies the Cascadia fault, which last broke around 1700, before anyone on that coast kept written records. Scientists found the date in Japan, where villages logged a mysterious tsunami on 27 and 28 January 1700 with no earthquake to explain it, and traced that orphan wave back across the Pacific to a Cascadia rupture at about 9 in the evening of 26 January.

The coast kept its own record. Along Washington's shore stand ghost forests of grey, long-dead red cedars. When the fault slipped, the land suddenly dropped, salt water poured in over the forest and the trees drowned where they stood. Their last growth rings date to 1699, the final summer before the flood.

meissen-how-europe-cracked-chinas-porcel.context_blurb:
For centuries Europe's kings paid fortunes for porcelain shipped from China: hard, white, glassy ware that no European could make. Then, in Meissen, a small Saxon town on the Elbe near Dresden, the alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger cracked the secret, and Meissen became home to the first true porcelain works outside Asia.

The recipe had to be hidden. In 1710 Augustus the Strong, the ruler of Saxony, set his new porcelain factory inside the Albrechtsburg, a 15th-century castle on a bluff above the river, where walls and guards could keep the secret in.

The first ware to make Meissen's name was not white at all. Böttger's dark-red stoneware, later called Böttger ware, was so hard and dense that the finest pieces could be cut, faceted and polished as if they were gemstones.

A much-loved Meissen legend tells how Böttger found his white clay. It was being dug near Aue by the ironmaster Johann Schnorr and sold cheaply as a powder to whiten wigs. Böttger, the story goes, noticed that the powder on his own wig felt oddly heavy, had it tested, and found it was the very clay he had been hunting. The tale cannot be proved, but it is told with relish.

True porcelain came from so few corners of the world that one fine cup was worth a fortune, and kings and queens locked their pieces in cabinets like jewels. Porcelain was so precious that Europeans nicknamed it white gold.

Böttger and the scientist Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus knew that Chinese potters blended some particular white earth into their clay. The missing key was kaolin, a soft, snow-white china clay, which fired at more than 1,300 degrees turns white, glassy and translucent and rings like a bell when struck. Meissen moved its clay in sealed barrels under sworn secrecy, but the secret leaked, and rival works soon rose in Vienna, at Sèvres and in England.

Meissen fought the copycats with a mark. From about 1720 its painters added a small pair of crossed swords in blue under the glaze, borrowed from the arms of Saxony, and it is one of the oldest trademarks still in use anywhere. The painter Johann Gregor Höroldt then gave the ware brilliant colours, and the sculptor Johann Joachim Kändler modelled the figurines every rival rushed to copy.

melbourne.context_blurb:
Melbourne is a big city on Australia's south coast, spread around Port Phillip Bay where the Yarra River meets the sea. A gold rush in the 1850s made it rich almost overnight, and for a time it was even the nation's capital. Today it is known for grand Victorian streets, clanking trams and weather that changes its mind.

Its liveliest corners are its laneways, narrow service alleys behind the grand streets that are now crammed with little bars, cafés and murals. In Hosier Lane, an official street-art gallery since 1998, the walls are painted over again and again, often overnight.

When other cities tore out their tramlines for buses and cars, Melbourne kept its own. Its tram network is now the largest in the world, with about 250 kilometres of double track, some 24 routes and about 500 trams.

Trams rule the road here. Traffic in Australia keeps to the left, so turning right normally starts from the right-hand lane. At some tram-crossed junctions in the city centre, though, a driver makes a hook turn: he turns right from the far-left lane, pausing mid-junction until the way is clear, so his car never blocks a tram.

Gold was struck in Victoria in 1851. The great goldfields were at Ballarat and Bendigo, just inland, and in 1856 alone Victoria's fields yielded about 95 tonnes of gold. Melbourne's population leapt from about 29,000 to 123,000 in three years, and a British journalist named the rich new city Marvellous Melbourne.

Melbourne's weather is famous for four seasons in one day. The city sits where cold fronts off the Southern Ocean crash into hot air from the interior. When the cold southerly air arrives, the locals call it a cool change, and it can drop the temperature by about 15 degrees in less than an hour.

Australia is a quiet continent, with few active volcanoes. Yet the plains of dark basalt west and north of the city hold about 400 eruption points, one of the largest young volcanic fields in the world.

mesa-verde.context_blurb:
Mesa Verde, Spanish for green table, is a high, flat, wooded plateau in southwestern Colorado, slashed by deep canyons. For some seven centuries the Ancestral Puebloans farmed it, and around 1200 they built stone villages that are among the most spectacular ruins in North America.

They did not put those villages on the flat top. They built them inside natural alcoves that wind and water had hollowed out of the sandstone cliffs, tucked under the overhangs of the canyon walls, which is why they are called cliff dwellings.

Most of the 600 or so dwellings are tiny; about three in four have only one to five rooms. The giant is Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling in North America, with about 150 rooms and 23 round ceremonial chambers, once home to roughly 100 people.

Those round, sunken ceremonial chambers are called kivas, and the only way in was down a ladder from an opening in the roof, beside a central fire pit.

The builders chose their alcoves with care. Nearly every one faces south or southwest. In winter the low sun shone deep inside and warmed the stone walls, while in summer the high sun was blocked by the overhang, so the rooms stayed shaded and cool.

Around 1300 the people left Mesa Verde and migrated south, leaving the cliff villages empty. For about six hundred years the reason stayed a mystery. Then scientists read the growth rings in the builders' own roof beams, each ring a single year, and found a long drought, the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299, when the streams ran dry. Dating wood by its rings is called dendrochronology.

Legend says the cliff dwellers vanished, but they did not. Their living descendants are the Pueblo peoples of the Southwest, among them the Hopi, the Zuni and the pueblos of the Rio Grande. The old name Anasazi is a Navajo word meaning roughly ancient enemies, which is why scholars now say Ancestral Puebloans.

mexico-city-tenochtitlan.context_blurb:
Mexico City spreads across a high valley ringed by mountains and volcanoes, more than 2,000 metres up. Beneath its streets lie the ruins of Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Aztecs, which Hernán Cortés and his Spanish and Tlaxcalan allies conquered in 1521. The lake that once surrounded the city is gone, and the city is still paying for its loss.

Aztec legend says the god Huitzilopochtli told his wandering people to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus, devouring a snake, and they found the sign on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco in 1325. That eagle and snake sit at the centre of Mexico's flag.

The island had little dry land to farm, so the Aztecs made their own. They built chinampas, garden plots raised from rich lake-bottom mud and anchored with the roots of willow trees, productive enough to help feed a city of 200,000. In the canals of Xochimilco, farmers still tend them.

When Cortés arrived in 1519, Tenochtitlan's 200,000 people made it about five times the size of Henry VIII's London, one of the largest cities on Earth. Cortés wrote to his king that it rivalled the great cities of Spain.

Fresh water came in by aqueduct from the springs of Chapultepec, because the lake was too salty to drink. The Aztecs built it as two channels side by side, so that one could be shut and scrubbed clean while water kept flowing through the other.

Chapultepec, grasshopper hill, is now a park of about 686 hectares, more than twice the size of New York's Central Park.

After the conquest, the Spanish drained Lake Texcoco to fight floods and build out onto the lakebed, and as the old clay dries it shrinks, so the city sinks, in places nearly half a metre a year. The Angel of Independence opened in 1910 with nine steps; fourteen more have been added as the ground fell away.

In 1978, workers digging a trench downtown struck a huge carved stone disk of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui, and it led archaeologists to the Templo Mayor, the great twin-shrined temple at the heart of the Aztec city.

The Metropolitan Cathedral, begun in 1573, began to tilt as the soft ground sank unevenly. In the 1990s engineers drilled shafts and carefully dug soil out from under its higher side, so the great church settled back toward level.

The valley has always flooded. It is a closed basin, ringed by mountains, and no river runs out of it to the sea, so water can leave only by evaporating or through drains that people dig. On clear days two snowy giants watch over it. They are the volcanoes Popocatépetl, the smoking mountain, still active, and Iztaccíhuatl, the white woman, whose ridge looks like a sleeping princess. In the Aztec legend a warrior knelt beside his dead princess until both turned to stone.

The lost lake also makes earthquakes deadly. In 1985 and 2017, quakes centred hundreds of kilometres away flattened buildings in the capital. The city sits on a soft, waterlogged bed of old lake clay, which traps earthquake waves and magnifies them 5 to 50 times, so the ground rolls like jelly.

The fight to drain the valley began with a channel dug by hand in 1607. In 2019 workers finished the Túnel Emisor Oriente, a bored tunnel some 62 kilometres long and up to 200 metres deep, to carry stormwater and sewage out of the sinking basin.

miyajima-the-floating-torii.context_blurb:
Miyajima is a small forested island in Japan's Seto Inland Sea, near Hiroshima, long counted among the three most beautiful views in Japan. Its name means shrine island, and for many centuries it has been revered as an island of the gods. Deer roam its paths, and off its shore a giant vermilion gate rises out of the sea.

That gate is a torii, the traditional Shinto gateway that marks the line between the everyday world and sacred ground. The great O-torii stands about 16.5 metres tall, some 160 metres out in the bay.

It seems to float because of the tide: twice a day the sea rises around its posts, and when the water climbs to about 250 centimetres it hides the base completely. At low tide the same gate stands on sand that visitors can walk across.

The island was held so holy that ordinary people were forbidden to set foot on its soil. So the halls of the Itsukushima Shrine were built on wooden piers over the tidal flats, never touching the sacred ground, and pilgrims arrived by boat through the torii. Old taboos even forbade births, deaths and burials on the island, and to this day it has no cemetery.

mohenjo-daro-and-the-indus-cities.context_blurb:
Mohenjo-daro was built on the banks of the Indus in Pakistan around 2500 BCE, more than two thousand years before Greece or Rome. It belonged to the Indus Valley Civilization, one of the world's three earliest city-building cultures, with Egypt and Mesopotamia, which archaeologists uncovered in the 1920s. Its builders planned cities with a care the world would not match again for ages.

Seen from above, the city's streets run in a deliberate grid that meets at right angles, a fully planned layout covering some 300 hectares for perhaps 40,000 people.

Every brick was baked to the same proportions, 1 by 2 by 4, and the very same brick turns up in Indus cities hundreds of kilometres apart, proof that the whole civilization shared a single system of measurement.

Almost every house, not just the rich ones, had its own bathing floor and toilet, with wastewater running out through chutes in the walls. Covered brick drains carried that waste beneath the streets around 2500 BCE, about two thousand years before Rome began its famous sewer, the Cloaca Maxima.

At the city's heart lies the Great Bath, a sunken pool of fitted brick some 12 metres long, made watertight with a coat of natural tar. It is the oldest public water tank known anywhere, and perhaps the oldest ritual bathing pool, though no one knows what ceremonies took place in it.

The Indus people stamped writing onto more than 4,000 small objects, most of them carved seals, with between 400 and 600 different signs, yet the Indus script has never been deciphered. That silence hides even the city's own name, which is lost: Mohenjo-daro is a modern Sindhi name meaning Mound of the Dead Men, and what its builders called it is unknown.

In 1926 the archaeologist John Marshall lifted out a bronze figure only about 10 centimetres tall, a girl with one hand on her hip and bangles up her arm, nicknamed the Dancing Girl. Nothing proves she danced, but the 4,000-year-old figure looks astonishingly alive.

Egypt and Sumer shouted their rulers' power in pyramids, palaces and gilded tombs. Here archaeologists have found no tomb of a king, no obvious palace, no monument to any ruler. Many scholars cautiously conclude that it may have been a remarkably equal society, and a later study found that its houses actually grew more alike in size over time. Whether hidden rulers governed it is still argued.

At Lothal, an Indus city near the sea, the archaeologist S.R. Rao uncovered a great brick basin some 37 metres long, joined to a tidal river and once filled with seawater, widely seen as the oldest dock known in the world. Some scholars think it was instead a giant water tank.

Around 1900 BCE the Indus cities emptied. The leading theory today is that the region's climate dried out: the monsoon weakened and rivers that fed the cities shrank. It remains a theory, not settled fact, but the old idea of a violent conquest has largely been abandoned.

monasteries-in-impossible-places.context_blurb:
Monks of many faiths have chosen to build where it is hardest to reach: on rock pillars, on cliff faces, on a mountain peninsula with no road and in a desert valley. Greece's Meteora and Mount Athos, Bhutan's Tiger's Nest and St Catherine's in the Sinai are among the most astonishing, chosen for their distance from the world and the wonder of standing there.

In central Greece, giant towers of rock rise some 400 metres from the plain, and from the 1300s Orthodox monks built monasteries on their summits. The place is called Meteora, suspended in the air. For centuries there were no stairs, so monks and visitors alike were hauled up in a rope net, winched up from the top. Steps were finally cut in the 1920s.

The towers are made of rounded pebbles cemented into stone, and only rushing water rounds a pebble. About 60 million years ago a great river dumped its gravel here and built a delta, which hardened into rock that uplift and erosion later carved into towers.

In Bhutan, Paro Taktsang clings to a cliff 900 metres above its valley, and legend says Guru Padmasambhava, a Buddhist master of the 700s, flew there on the back of a tigress to meditate in its cave and tame the local demons. Its name means Tiger's Nest, and in 1692 a monastery was built around the cave, clinging to the granite like a gecko.

Mount Athos is a self-governing peninsula of monks in northern Greece, jutting 50 kilometres into the Aegean, with twenty monasteries. For about a thousand years it has kept the avaton, a rule upheld by Orthodox tradition and Greek law that forbids any woman or girl to set foot there, because the monks hold the mountain to be the garden of the Virgin Mary alone. Male pilgrims may come, but only a few each day.

No road links Athos to the mainland; the only door is the sea, by boat from Ouranoupoli. Even then a ticket is not enough: every visitor needs a written entry permit, the diamonitirion, which is checked as the boat lands.

St Catherine's Monastery lies in Egypt's Sinai desert, beneath the holy mountain, built around what tradition holds is the Burning Bush. Wars swept the region for centuries, yet no army ever destroyed it. The monks still guard the Ashtiname, a charter said to bear the handprint of the Prophet Muhammad and his promise to protect them, and ruler after ruler honoured it.

Through the 700s and 800s, Byzantine rulers had holy images smashed and burned across their lands, a campaign called iconoclasm. The Sinai lay beyond their reach. So St Catherine's kept its ancient icons, among them the oldest known image of Christ Pantocrator, Christ shown as ruler of all.

Its library is second only to the Vatican's for precious old books. In 1844 and again fifteen years later, the scholar Constantin von Tischendorf carried off pages of a handwritten Greek Bible from the 300s, now called the Codex Sinaiticus, one of the two oldest nearly complete Bibles in existence.

monte-alban.context_blurb:
Monte Albán is an ancient city on a mountaintop above the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico. For more than a thousand years, from about 500 BC, it was the capital of the Zapotec people, and its huge central plaza, lined with pyramids, palaces and tombs, still floats high above the valley floor.

Before they raised a single wall, the Zapotec levelled the top of the ridge entirely flat, creating a giant artificial platform in the sky some 1,940 metres above the sea. There they laid out a plaza about 300 by 150 metres, coated in white plaster, in a city that grew to some 17,200 people.

One early wall holds more than 300 carved slabs of naked men in twisted poses. Travellers in the 1800s called them the dancers, los Danzantes. Archaeologists now see wounds and mutilation on the bodies and read them as sacrificed war captives, set out in rows like a public gallery of the defeated.

In 1932 the archaeologist Alfonso Caso opened Tomb 7 and found the richest treasure ever discovered in ancient Mesoamerica, with about 121 pieces of worked gold. Its most famous piece is a human skull coated in a mosaic of turquoise, with polished shell set in its eye sockets. The hoard was in fact a later Mixtec burial placed in the old Zapotec tomb.

Every building on the plaza lines up with its grid except one, an arrowhead-shaped structure called Building J, deliberately set askew. Its steps point to where the star Capella rises at its first dawn appearance each year, which then fell within a day of the sun passing straight overhead.

Building J's walls also hold more than 40 slabs, each carved with the sign of a place above an upside-down human head, a Mesoamerican mark of a defeated enemy. Archaeologists read the gallery as a boast by Monte Albán's rulers that they had conquered all those towns, and for at least one region, Cuicatlán, digging confirms the conquest really happened.

The Danzantes and the conquest slabs carry more than pictures. Cut into them are dot-and-bar dates and signs that make them among the earliest examples of a written script anywhere in Mesoamerica.

monterey-bay-kelp-forests.context_blurb:
Monterey Bay curves along the central coast of California. A deep underwater canyon runs almost to its beaches, pulling cold, rich water up from the depths, and in that water grow forests that sway in the swell like trees in a wind, sheltering otters, seals, fish and sharks.

They are forests of giant kelp, the largest of all seaweeds, usually about 30 metres tall and sometimes over 50, the tallest underwater forests on Earth. The kelp grips bare rock with a claw-like holdfast rather than roots.

Each frond is buoyed up toward the sunlit canopy by its own tiny balloons, gas-filled floats called pneumatocysts, one at the base of every blade.

The forest survives only because the sea otter feeds on sea urchins, which would otherwise graze the kelp until nothing is left but rock, so biologists call the otter a keystone species. Where otters vanish, urchins swarm and leave an urchin barren.

Along some 1,000 kilometres of South Africa's Cape coast grows the Great African Sea Forest of giant bamboo kelp, and art and tools in the caves beside it suggest that people have lived along it for nearly 100,000 years.

The warm tropics have almost no kelp forests. Kelp needs cold, nutrient-rich water, below about 21 degrees, where cold currents bring nutrients up from the deep, which is why it rings cool coasts such as Tasmania, South Africa, Chile and California.

montreal.context_blurb:
Montreal stands on an island in the St. Lawrence River in the Canadian province of Quebec. The French founded it in 1642, and though Britain conquered it in 1760, it kept its French language and Catholic churches; today it is the largest mainly French-speaking city in the Americas. A green, wooded mountain rises in its middle.

In 1535 Jacques Cartier was led up that hill by people from the Iroquoian village of Hochelaga, and he named it Mount Royal, Mont Réal, for the king of France, which is where the city's own name comes from.

The park on its slopes, opened in 1876, was shaped by Frederick Law Olmsted, America's most famous park designer, who had already helped design New York's Central Park.

From afar Mount Royal has the rounded look of an old volcano, but it never was one. About 125 million years ago a mass of molten magma pushed up into softer rock and cooled hard while still trapped underground, never erupting; the softer rock around it wore away, and the tough core was left standing as the hill. It is one of a line of such hills called the Monteregian Hills.

Montreal's winters are brutal, so Montrealers moved part of their city below ground. The RÉSO, from the French word for network, links malls, metro stations, offices and hotels through some 32 kilometres of heated passages, the biggest network of underground walkways on Earth.

The explorer La Salle was sure a river route across the continent would lead to the riches of Asia, and he set out from his estate just upstream of the city. Years later he returned empty-handed. His mocking neighbours named his land and the rapids beside it La Chine, China, and the place is still called Lachine. Those rapids were too wild for boats, so every fur trader had to stop and carry his canoe around them, which made Montreal the hinge of the fur trade.

moraines-the-ridges-of-dumped-rubble.context_blurb:
A moraine is a ridge or mound of rubble, boulders, gravel, sand and clay all jumbled together, that a glacier carried along and then dropped. Glaciers work like bulldozers and conveyor belts at once, and their moraines record exactly where the ice once stood, from the valleys of Switzerland to the islands off New England.

At the end of the last ice age, the great ice sheet over North America reached its southern edge along the coast of New England and New York and left its rubble there. Cape Cod, Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard, Block Island and Long Island are pieces of that one line of terminal moraine, known together as the Outer Lands.

High on an alpine valley's flank, a lateral moraine marks the glacier's side: frost-shattered rock fell from the cliffs onto the edge of the ice, and when the ice shrank the ridge was left stranded high, like a bathtub ring.

Where two ice streams merge, their inner side ridges join into one dark band down the middle of the glacier, a medial moraine. The Aletsch Glacier, the largest in the Alps, carries two such stripes all the way from Konkordiaplatz, where its feeder streams meet, to its snout 23 kilometres below.

Lake Garda, Italy's largest lake, is held in by a dam of glacial rubble: the ancient Garda glacier dumped curved ridges of it across the open end of its valley, a great horseshoe of moraine called the morainic amphitheatre.

Some valleys hold a whole series of low ridges, one behind another. These are recessional moraines, and each one marks a spot where the melting glacier's front stalled for a time during its slow retreat before shrinking farther back. Read in order, they map the ice's retreat like bookmarks.

moscow.context_blurb:
Moscow, Russia's capital for most of the last five centuries, grew up around a fortress on a bluff above the Moskva River. At its heart stand the red walls of the Kremlin and, beside them, Red Square and the swirling domes of St Basil's. Beneath the streets runs a metro whose stations are among the grandest halls built underground.

Red Square's Russian name, Krasnaya Ploshchad, has nothing to do with communism or red brick: in old Russian krasnaya meant beautiful, and only later did it come to mean red.

The Kremlin's red-brick walls, more than 2 kilometres around and studded with 20 towers, were raised in the 1480s and 1490s by master-builders brought from Italy. The fortress still houses Russia's government.

Between 1555 and 1561 Ivan the Terrible raised a cathedral beside the Kremlin to celebrate his capture of Kazan. From outside it looks like one wild building, but it is really nine separate chapels, eight smaller churches around a taller central one, fused into a single whole.

Its famous rainbow came later: when first finished it was mostly plain red brick with white stone trim, and the candy-coloured swirls were painted on between the 17th and early 18th centuries.

Its everyday name comes from Basil the Blessed, a barefoot holy fool who wandered Moscow and was deeply revered, buried in a chapel added in 1588. So a church built to glorify a fearsome tsar is remembered by the name of a penniless saint.

A legend says Ivan had the architect blinded so he could never build anything so lovely again. Historians call that a myth, because records show the builder, Postnik Yakovlev, went on to work on other cathedrals afterward.

Across the square stretches GUM, the Main Universal Store, built in the 1890s. Its stone front runs 242 metres, and under a light roof of iron and glass it is a huge shopping arcade, with indoor streets that once held some 1,200 shops.

Down in the metro, riders at Ploshchad Revolyutsii pass 76 bronze statues. One is a border guard with his dog, and for luck before exams people rub the dog's nose until it shines like gold.

At Komsomolskaya, a golden ceiling on white marble columns holds eight mosaics by Pavel Korin of Russia's victorious war heroes, from Alexander Nevsky and Kutuzov to Soviet soldiers raising the flag over the Reichstag.

Park Pobedy, Victory Park, the deepest station at about 84 metres down, has two huge mosaics by Zurab Tsereteli facing each other: Russia driving out Napoleon's France in 1812, and the defeat of Nazi Germany in the Second World War. An escalator of about 740 steps carries riders down.

Many stations lie far deeper than a railway needs because Soviet planners dug them to double as bomb shelters. In the Second World War, trains ran by day, and by night the platforms filled with cots where thousands of Muscovites slept safe from air raids.

mount-everest.context_blurb:
Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and Tibet, is the highest point on Earth's surface, about 8,849 metres above the sea. Its summit lies in air too thin to keep a human alive for long. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first stood on top in 1953; thousands have followed, and hundreds have died trying.

The top of the world was once the bottom of the sea. The grey limestone of the summit was laid down about 450 million years ago on the floor of a warm, shallow sea, and it is studded with fossil trilobites and sea lilies.

Tibetans call the mountain Chomolungma, Goddess Mother of the World, and in Nepal it is Sagarmatha, Brow of the Sky. Both peoples honoured it long before outsiders renamed it. British surveyors first listed it simply as Peak XV, and in 1852 the Indian mathematician Radhanath Sikdar worked out that it was the highest mountain on Earth. In 1856 it was named for Sir George Everest, the former Surveyor General of India, who objected to the honour and never once laid eyes on the peak.

Above about 8,000 metres lies what climbers bluntly call the death zone, where so little oxygen reaches the blood that the body cannot adjust and steadily breaks down. Only fourteen mountains on Earth rise above that line, the eight-thousanders, ten in the Himalaya and four in the Karakoram.

The second highest, K2, on the border of China and Pakistan, is lower than Everest but far deadlier, so steep and storm-lashed that climbers call it the Savage Mountain.

On Everest's standard route from Nepal, danger starts just above Base Camp. The Khumbu Icefall is a jumbled river of glacier ice that slides some metre or so every day, slashed by cracks deeper than a hundred metres, and its collapsing towers of ice can kill without warning. In 2014 one avalanche there killed 16 Nepali guides, so teams cross before dawn, while the cold holds the ice firm.

Just below the summit stood the Hillary Step, a rock cliff of some 12 metres, almost sheer, the last great test of the climb, named for Edmund Hillary. It seems to have collapsed in a Nepal earthquake in 2015, leaving a snow slope.

In May 2019 the climber Nirmal Purja photographed some 300 climbers waiting in one long single-file line along the summit ridge, deep in the death zone. Eleven people died that season, and the picture started a bitter debate about crowding.

How did seabed rock reach the sky? About 50 million years ago the Indian plate crashed into Asia, crumpling the old sea floor upward into the Himalaya, and that collision is still pushing the mountains higher.

Everest's summit is the highest point above the sea, but it is not the tallest mountain from foot to top. Hawaii's Mauna Kea rises more than 10,200 metres from its base on the Pacific floor, though most of it lies hidden beneath the waves.

Through most months the jet stream howls across the summit at more than 300 kilometres an hour. Only in late May, when the summer monsoon sweeps over South Asia and shoves the jet stream north, does a short calm window open for a summit push.

Everest is still growing, about 2 millimetres a year. A 2024 study found an extra lift: some 89,000 years ago a nearby river captured the Arun and carved a deep gorge, stripping away billions of tonnes of rock. Earth's crust floats on the denser mantle below, so when that weight was removed the lightened crust rose like an unloaded boat, lifting Everest higher.

mount-fuji.context_blurb:
Mount Fuji rises west of Tokyo on Honshu, Japan's main island. At 3,776 metres it is the country's highest mountain, a snow-capped cone so even that it looks drawn with a compass. For well over ten centuries pilgrims have climbed it and artists have painted it, and it is still a living volcano.

Fuji is a stratovolcano, a steep cone built up in layer upon layer of hardened lava and ash from many eruptions, which gives it that tall, symmetrical shape.

Fuji is dormant, not dead. Its last eruption, in December 1707, poured out no lava, but it hurled out about 800 million cubic metres in ash, which fell for weeks on Edo, the shogun's capital, now Tokyo, about 100 kilometres away.

The summit is no point but a crater about 780 metres wide. Pilgrims who reached the top traditionally walked all the way around its rim, a circuit called ohachi-meguri, going around the bowl.

The cone we see, New Fuji, took shape only about 10,000 years ago, and it sits on two older volcanoes buried beneath it, Old Fuji and the ancient Komitake.

The most famous Japanese print in the world, Katsushika Hokusai's Great Wave off Kanagawa, shows a giant claw of water about to crash over fishing boats, with Fuji small and calm in the distance. It belongs to his series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, first published around 1831.

In 2013 UNESCO added Fuji to its World Heritage List not for its geology but as a cultural site, a sacred place and a source of artistic inspiration.

Fuji's own spirit is a goddess, Konohanasakuya-hime, the Flower-Blossom Princess, honoured in more than 1,300 shrines across Japan. Yet for centuries women were barred from the holy summit, judged ritually impure, until Japan lifted the ban in 1872.

Why did such a huge volcano grow on this exact spot? Fuji stands above a rare triple junction, a meeting point where three of Earth's plates come together: the Amurian, the Okhotsk and the Philippine Sea plates.

mount-kailash.context_blurb:
Mount Kailash is a lone, snow-capped pyramid of rock, 6,638 metres high, in the far west of Tibet. It is sacred to several faiths at once, and every year pilgrims come not to climb it but to walk around it, on a hard, high circuit around its base. Its summit is left alone.

Teams climb far taller Himalayan peaks every season, but no human has ever stood on top of Kailash, because China forbids any climb out of respect for the faithful. In the 1980s the great mountaineer Reinhold Messner turned down a permit to climb it, warning that to conquer Kailash would be to conquer something in people's souls.

Tibetans call it Gang Rinpoche, which means Precious Jewel of Snow.

Four religions hold Kailash sacred: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Bön, Tibet's ancient faith from before Buddhism arrived. Each faith tells its own story of who or what the mountain is, and pilgrims of all four walk around it, the Bön anticlockwise and the others clockwise.

To Hindus the mountain is the home of the god Shiva, who sits in endless meditation on its frozen peak beside his consort Parvati. Many Buddhists and Hindus also identify Kailash with Mount Meru, the great mountain they believe stands at the centre of the universe, the axis around which creation turns.

The walk around the mountain is the kora, a sacred circling of about 52 kilometres that takes three hard days. Its highest point is the Drölma La, a pass 5,650 metres up, swept by bitter wind, where pilgrims tie prayer flags and leave behind locks of their hair.

Buddhist pilgrims say one circuit washes away a lifetime of sins. Some keep walking for months, because 108 circuits, a sacred number, are said to free a pilgrim from the cycle of rebirth.

The land around the mountain is one of the great watersheds of Asia. Within about 60 kilometres of it rise the Brahmaputra, the Indus and the Sutlej. The fourth great river, the Karnali, is a major feeder of the Ganges.

At the mountain's foot lie two lakes side by side. One is holy Manasarovar, round and fresh, about 4,590 metres up. Its neighbour is Rakshastal, the lake of the demon, salty and shunned as unlucky, even though Manasarovar overflows into it through a natural channel.

A long vertical gash scars the south face. Tibetan Buddhists tell of a contest of miracles between the yogi Milarepa and Naro Bönchung, a priest of the Bön faith, to reach the summit first at dawn. Milarepa rode up on the first beams of dawn, and his startled rival tumbled from his flying drum, which gouged the scar as it slid down the mountain. It is told as a legend.

mount-roraima.context_blurb:
Mount Roraima rises from the rainforest of northern South America, in the Guiana Highlands. It is a vast block of ancient sandstone with sheer cliffs hundreds of metres high and a flat, rocky top. Walled off from the forest below, its summit is a world of its own, an island in the sky.

The Pemon people call such a flat-topped, cliff-walled table mountain a tepui, a word that means roughly house of the gods.

Three countries share its summit plateau: Venezuela holds most of it, with smaller slices belonging to Guyana and Brazil. At 2,810 metres it is also the highest point in Guyana.

For centuries hardly anyone glimpsed the top, because a cap of cloud wraps it almost every day of the year. Up there it is about 10 degrees by day and near freezing at night, while the jungle below swelters.

Its pale sandstone is nearly two billion years old, formed at a time when no animals or plants existed anywhere and the land was bare rock. Dinosaurs came less than 250 million years ago.

Life on the summit has been isolated from the lowlands for ages, so many of its creatures and plants evolved on their own and live nowhere else in the world. The tiny black pebble toad, for example, lives only on Roraima and one neighbouring tepui.

Rain falls on the summit almost daily and pours over the rim in silver ribbons, feeding streams that run to the Amazon, the Essequibo and the Orinoco, so local people call Roraima the Mother of Waters.

The summit itself looks like another planet, with black rock towers, sinkholes and rain-scoured pools. In one hollow, called the Crystal Valley, the ground glitters because it is strewn with clear crystals of quartz weathered out of the old rock.

The unreachable plateau fired the imagination of Arthur Conan Doyle, who in 1912 set his adventure novel The Lost World on a tepui like it, where Professor Challenger's explorers find dinosaurs still alive.

mount-st-helens-1980-the-sideways-blast.context_blurb:
Mount St. Helens is a volcano in the Cascade Range of Washington State, in the Pacific Northwest of the United States. On 18 May 1980 its north side gave way, and the eruption that followed killed 57 people, flattened whole forests and became one of the most closely studied eruptions ever.

For years Mount St. Helens had seemed a quiet, snowy cone, but its 1980 eruption was the deadliest and most destructive in the history of the United States.

That spring, magma forced its way up into the mountain and its north face began to swell. The bulge pushed out by about 5 feet, roughly a metre and a half, every single day, until by mid-May the slope had moved more than 400 feet.

At 8:32 that morning, a sudden earthquake of magnitude 5.1 struck about a mile under the north slope and shook the overloaded bulge loose.

The whole north face slid away at up to 150 miles an hour, about 2.8 cubic kilometres of mountain, the largest landslide ever recorded. Bigger and deadlier eruptions have happened, but no landslide in history matches it.

With its side stripped off, the magma inside was uncorked and exploded sideways, a lateral blast that tore across the land at over 300 miles an hour and flattened some 600 square kilometres of forest.

David Johnston, a young geologist of the US Geological Survey watching from a post about 6 miles north, had time only to radio his base in Vancouver, Washington, calling the city's name twice and crying that this was it, before the blast swept over him. His body was never found, and the ridge is now named Johnston Ridge.

Harry Truman, who was 83 and had kept the Spirit Lake lodge for 52 years, refused to leave, and he was buried with his sixteen cats under about 150 feet of debris.

Within 15 minutes the ash column stood 80,000 feet high, and winds carried the cloud east across the continent and all the way around the Earth in about 15 days. In Spokane, midday turned dark.

In minutes the summit lost about 1,300 feet, and where the cone had stood there now gaped a crater a mile wide, shaped like a great horseshoe open to the north. A new lava dome has been slowly growing inside it.

The avalanche crashed into Spirit Lake, lifting its surface nearly 200 feet and sweeping thousands of blasted trees into the water. More than 40 years later a huge raft of those floating logs still floats on the lake, pushed from shore to shore by the wind.

murano-venices-island-of-glass.context_blurb:
Murano is a little cluster of islands in the lagoon of Venice, less than two kilometres north of the city. For more than seven centuries it has been the home of Venetian glass, and its masters led Europe in the craft while their rulers guarded the secrets of the furnace as jealously as gold.

Venice was a crowded city built largely of wood. Its glassmakers' roaring furnaces kept starting fires, so a decree of November 1291 banished every furnace to Murano, where the flames could do less harm. The island was close enough to watch and far enough to keep both the fire and, later, the trade secrets contained.

Murano's makers packed some of their glass with tiny repeating bursts of colour and called it millefiori, from mille, a thousand, and fiori, flowers: a thousand flowers.

A master's skill counted as a treasure of the Venetian state, and he could not leave without permission. A master who slipped abroad to teach a rival city faced execution as a traitor, or the loss of everything he owned. If a runaway could not be reached, Venice jailed his own family to force him home, and by some accounts it might even send an assassin after him.

The same masters were honoured like few craftsmen anywhere. A decree of 1376 let a glass master's daughter marry into the Venetian nobility without losing rank, and her children still counted as nobles. Masters could even carry swords.

Early in the seventeenth century one of Murano's workshops made a brown glass glittering with tiny copper sparks and named it aventurine, from the Italian a ventura, meaning by chance, because it was said to have been found partly by accident. The English word adventure grew from the same root, but the phrase itself means chance.

Ordinary glass of the Middle Ages had an ugly greenish tint from the iron in its sand. In the 1400s Angelo Barovier cancelled out that tint by adding manganese, nicknamed glassmaker's soap, and created cristallo, a glass as clear as spring water.

Barovier also made lattimo, from latte, milk, an opaque milk-white glass designed to imitate Chinese porcelain, the costly luxury that rich Europeans prized above almost anything.

The most magical trick hides a flower inside solid glass. The maker gathers rods of coloured glass so that their ends form a flower, melts the bundle into a single thick cane, then heats and stretches it long and thin so the picture shrinks without smearing. Then he slices the cane crosswise into thin discs, and every slice shows the same tiny flower, like cutting through a stick of seaside rock. The slices are called murrine.

Women were shut out of the glass trade, which fathers handed down to sons. Yet Angelo's daughter Marietta Barovier ran the family workshop, and in 1487 Venice granted her the right to her own glass furnace, a rare privilege for any woman of the time. She is credited with inventing the striped chevron bead.

mycenae-the-lion-gate-and-the-cyclopean-.context_blurb:
Mycenae is a ruined citadel on a rocky hill in southern mainland Greece. Some 3,300 years ago it was the seat of warrior kings of a Bronze Age civilization that spoke an early form of Greek, and in legend it was the home of Agamemnon, who led the Greeks against Troy. Its walls and gate are among the oldest great monuments in Europe.

The road into the citadel passes through the Lion Gate, where two great carved lionesses rear on their hind legs on either side of a central column. Built around 1250 BC, it is the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe still standing where it was first set. The lionesses' heads, carved separately, were lost long ago.

The walls are built of limestone blocks so enormous, some weighing nearly a hundred tonnes, that Greeks of later ages thought no ordinary men could have lifted them. They said the one-eyed giants called Cyclopes must have piled them, and so this style of huge-block building is still called Cyclopean.

The citadel could hold out against a siege. A hidden stair of about 99 steps runs down through the rock inside the wall to an underground cistern fed by a spring piped in from outside, so the people never ran out of water.

In 1876 the excavator Heinrich Schliemann found a gold mask over a dead man's face in a royal grave and announced that he had looked on the face of Agamemnon. The mask is real Bronze Age gold, but it is far older than Agamemnon could have been, dating to around 1550 BC, about three centuries before the time of the Trojan War.

Outside the gates lies the Treasury of Atreus, a tomb shaped like a beehive and built around 1300 BC. Its stone dome spans some fourteen and a half metres, every course of stone stepped a little farther inward than the course beneath. For well over a thousand years it was the widest dome on Earth, until the Romans built the Pantheon in Rome, whose dome spans about 43 metres.

The single slab laid across its doorway weighs about 120 tonnes, some 8 metres long, the heaviest stone the Greeks ever raised. How Bronze Age crews lifted it is still debated.

Back at the Lion Gate, a single great beam of stone, the lintel, spans the doorposts, and above it the builders left a hollow triangle in the wall. That relieving triangle steers the crushing weight of the wall out to the sides, around the lintel, so the beam never has to carry it and cannot snap. The lion slab is only a light panel filling the gap.

The column between the lionesses is strange: it grows wider toward the top, the reverse of any later Greek column. It is a sacred symbol the Mycenaeans borrowed from the Minoans of Crete, an older island civilization whose art and palaces they deeply admired.

nan-madol.context_blurb:
Nan Madol is a ruined stone city on the edge of Pohnpei, a green volcanic island in Micronesia, in the western Pacific. Starting around 1200, the Saudeleur lords raised nearly a hundred artificial islets out of the shallow sea and walled them with dark stone, and how they managed it still puzzles archaeologists.

Its roughly 92 islets are laced with tidal canals that visitors cross by canoe, so early travellers called it the Venice of the Pacific. Its own name, in the Pohnpeian language, means the space between things, a nod to those channels weaving among the islets.

Most ancient builders looked for solid high ground, but these builders stacked their city on a coral reef just under the tide, and it is the only ancient city known to stand on one. It became a World Heritage Site in 2016.

The walls are made of what look like giant black logs. They are natural columns of basalt, formed when thick lava cooled and cracked into prisms that are mostly six-sided, hexagonal, like those of Ireland's Giant's Causeway. The builders stacked them crisscross and packed coral rubble into the gaps.

All the columns came from one volcanic plug on the far side of Pohnpei, on the opposite coast from the reef, and had to be moved all the way around to the city. Some weigh 5 tonnes and a few as much as 50. No one has proved how they were moved, but the leading guess is that the builders floated them around the coast on rafts of logs, riding the high tide.

Scholars estimate that the builders shifted about 750,000 tonnes of basalt and coral in all, without the wheel, the pulley or tools of metal. That is a rough estimate, not a measurement.

The greatest of the islets, Nandauwas, stands behind double walls of stacked basalt up to about 25 feet high, held together by weight alone, and at its heart lies the tomb of the first king of the Saudeleur line.

The Saudeleur priest-kings were the first rulers ever to unite all of Pohnpei under one rule, some 25,000 people, and they governed from Nan Madol until about 1628. Oral tradition says the warrior Isokelekel then overthrew the last of them.

The city was planned in two halves. Madol Powe was the sacred half, for the dead and the priests who tended their tombs, and Madol Pah was the half for the living rulers and their government.
