naples-and-the-bay-of-fire.context_blurb:
Naples spreads around a sweeping bay on Italy's southern coast, in the shadow of Mount Vesuvius, the volcano that buried Pompeii in AD 79. West of the city lie the Campi Flegrei, the burning fields, where the ground steams, heaves and sinks. Few great cities live so close to so much fire.

Pliny the Younger, then a teenager, watched the AD 79 eruption from across the bay and later described it in letters to the historian Tacitus. He wrote that the ash cloud rose on a tall trunk and spread out at the top like the umbrella pine, the flat-crowned stone pine of the Italian hills. His account was so exact that scientists named the most violent kind of eruption, with a towering column of ash, a Plinian eruption, after him.

The ash set hard around the people of Pompeii, and their bodies rotted away inside it, leaving hollows. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into those hollows and chipped away the ash, revealing the people as they were frozen at the moment they died.

Vesuvius is not finished. Its most recent eruption came in 1944, during the Second World War. Its falling ash and cinders wrecked about 80 American bomber planes, B-25s parked at an airfield nearby.

In the Campi Flegrei lies the Solfatara crater, where vents hiss out sulphur gas and more than 150 pools of boiling mud blister and bubble. The Romans thought it was a gate to the underworld.

The Campi Flegrei is a supervolcano. Some 39,000 years ago it produced the Campanian Ignimbrite, far bigger than anything Vesuvius has done. Its grey ash settled as far away as Eastern Europe, where geologists still find the layer.

In 1538 the earth near Pozzuoli tore open and erupted for a week and a day, and when it fell quiet a brand-new mountain stood there, Monte Nuovo, one of the youngest mountains in Europe.

At Pozzuoli the ground itself rises and falls. Over months and years it rises by several metres and then sinks back, a slow movement called bradyseism, from the Greek for slow earthquake, driven by magma and gas far below. In the 1980s the town rose so much that its harbour stopped working.

The proof stands in Pozzuoli's old Roman market, where three marble columns bear a band of small holes bored by sea molluscs, date mussels that can only drill while underwater, so the columns must once have stood in the sea before rising again.

Under Naples runs a maze of tunnels cut into soft volcanic tuff, first quarried by Greeks for building stone some 2,500 years ago and later turned by Romans into cisterns. When the Second World War brought bombing raids, the people of Naples crowded into those old caverns, using them as air-raid shelters.

nara-the-first-capital-and-its-great-bud.context_blurb:
Nara, in central Japan, became the country's first permanent capital in 710. For a few brilliant decades it borrowed Chinese ideas of government and Buddhist building, and then the court moved on, leaving a quiet city of great temples. Today more than a thousand tame sika deer roam its parks and streets.

Before Nara, the capital moved after nearly every emperor's death, because a place where someone had died was believed to be spiritually polluted. Empress Genmei ended that costly habit by founding a fixed capital at Nara, laid out on a grid copied from China's capital, Chang'an.

Visitors buy deer crackers, shika senbei, and many of the deer have learned to beg for them by dipping their heads in a bow.

Since ancient times the deer have been protected as sacred messengers of the Shinto god of Kasuga Shrine, and killing one was punished by death, with the last execution in 1637. Legend says the thunder god Takemikazuchi first rode into Nara on a white deer.

Researchers at Nara Women's University showed that the bow is learned, not instinct: when the COVID lockdown emptied the park of tourists, the deer bowed far less often. Deer at other parks never learned it at all.

At the temple of Tōdai-ji sits the Daibutsu, a seated bronze Buddha about 15 metres high. In 752, before ten thousand monks and thousands of dancers, an Indian priest named Bodhisena completed it by painting in the pupils of the statue's eyes, a rite called the eye-opening.

The hall around it, the Daibutsuden, was the biggest wooden building in the world until 1998, even though the hall rebuilt in 1709 is about a third smaller than the first, cut from eleven bays to seven when the money ran out.

Inside stands a wooden pillar pierced at its foot by a hole as big, people say, as one of the Buddha's nostrils, and temple lore says any child who squeezes all the way through is granted good fortune or enlightenment. The hole is real; the reward is folklore.

nazca-lines.context_blurb:
On a desert plain in the south of Peru, the Nazca people drew pictures so big that only the sky sees them whole: straight lines running for kilometres, and animals bigger than a football field, scraped into the desert floor some 2,000 years ago. A giant picture made on the ground like this is called a geoglyph.

On foot, a line looks like nothing more than a scratch in the dirt, and the great shapes only appear when seen from the air, best from about 500 metres up.

The Nazca made them by lifting away the dark, rust-coated pebbles that cover the plain, laying bare the paler ground beneath, so that each line is only a shallow trough.

Such shallow marks should have blown away long ago. They survive because the Nazca plain is one of the driest deserts on Earth, where almost no rain falls to wash them away.

The best-loved figure is the hummingbird, about 93 metres long with a needle beak and outstretched wings, the emblem of the whole site on postcards and stamps. There are more than 70 animal figures in all.

In 2020, workers building a new viewing platform on a hillside spotted a faded cat about 37 metres long, lounging with its long tail, made around 200 BCE and older than the famous figures.

One hillside figure, about 35 metres tall with a raised hand, was nicknamed the Astronaut. In 1968 the Swiss writer Erich von Däniken claimed the lines were landing strips for alien ships and this figure a spaceman. Archaeologists credit the Nazca with their own art and read the figure instead as an owl-headed shaman, a figure from Nazca belief. The investigator Joe Nickell later laid out a giant figure himself with only wooden stakes and cord.

In 2024 researchers from Japan's Yamagata University used AI trained to pick out faint figures in aerial photographs, and in six months found 303 new geoglyphs, nearly doubling the number known.

For four decades the German mathematician Maria Reiche lived beside the desert, measuring and sweeping the lines, and she spent her life arguing that they formed a giant calendar of the sun and the stars. The idea began in 1941, when the historian Paul Kosok watched the midwinter sun set along one line. Many scholars now favour other ideas, such as water rituals or sacred paths walked in ceremony, so the purpose is still debated.

new-orleans.context_blurb:
New Orleans grew up in southern Louisiana, close to where the Mississippi meets the Gulf, founded by the French in 1718. It has been French, Spanish, French again and American. Much of it now lies in a shallow bowl below the level of the sea, guarded by walls of earth against the river, the lake and the Gulf of Mexico.

About two-thirds of the city lies at or below sea level, while the river at high water stands some 14 feet above it, so from the top of a levee you see the Mississippi flowing higher than the streets of the town.

The first settlers knew where to build. In a flat delta the highest ground is the bank of the river itself, because every flood dropped its heaviest silt right at the water's edge, building a natural levee, and on that ridge Bienville's settlers laid out the French Quarter in 1718. That is why the old quarter stayed mostly dry during Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

Beside the old quarter the Mississippi sweeps around the city in a great curving bend, which gave New Orleans its nickname, the Crescent City.

The ground is so wet that, locals say, a hard rain once floated coffins up out of their graves. So New Orleans buries many of its dead above the ground in stone tombs, laid out in rows like little streets in its Cities of the Dead. The oldest, St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, opened in 1789.

At Congo Square, where enslaved Africans were allowed to gather on their free Sundays under a French colonial law, hundreds gathered to drum and dance, and over generations the rhythms they kept alive grew into jazz.

In 1913 the engineer A. Baldwin Wood built giant screw pumps, the most powerful in the world, to drain the swamps for new neighbourhoods. But once the water was gone, the spongy swamp soil dried out, rotted and packed down, so the land itself sank. More than half the city now lies below sea level.

The river wants to leave. Over the ages the Mississippi has jumped from one channel to another across its delta. Today it is straining to abandon its long route past the city for a quicker, steeper way to the sea down the Atchafalaya River. Since 1963 the giant floodgates of the Old River Control Structure have held it back, and in the flood of 1973 the river nearly broke through.

Coastal Louisiana is drowning: since the 1930s its marshes have shrunk by an area about the size of Delaware. Scientists blame mainly the levees and dams upstream, which trap the river's mud and stop it spilling out to rebuild the marshes, so the land sinks and washes away.

new-york-city.context_blurb:
New York City sits on the Atlantic coast of the United States around one of the finest natural harbours in the world. Its five boroughs, Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island, hold more than eight million people, and its towers, bridges and parks are among the most famous human-made landscapes on Earth.

The Statue of Liberty once shone reddish-brown like a fresh coin, but her skin is copper only about 2.4 millimetres thick, and air and water slowly corroded it into the pale green coat called verdigris. That green layer now protects the metal beneath.

Central Park looks like wild country, but Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux designed it from scratch in the 1850s, and nearly every hill, pond and tree in it was put there on purpose. Clearing the rocky site took so much blasting that the workers used more gunpowder than the armies burned in the whole Battle of Gettysburg.

When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, its main span over the East River, almost 1,600 feet long, made it the longest suspension bridge on Earth, and it joined Manhattan and Brooklyn for the first time. The men who dug its foundations worked in pressurized chambers under the river, and many came up crippled or dying from what we now call the bends. Washington Roebling, the chief engineer, was paralysed by it and ran the work from his bedroom with a telescope, while his wife Emily oversaw the site.

Manhattan's streets follow a rigid grid of blocks planned in 1811, but Broadway, an older road, slants across the whole island, carving out triangular plazas such as Times Square.

Grand Central Terminal's great hall is roofed with a blue-green sky of gold zodiac stars. Within two months of its opening in 1913, a commuter noticed that the whole sky was painted backward, east swapped with west, probably because the painter flipped the star chart. When restorers cleaned the ceiling in the 1990s, they left one dark patch near Cancer on purpose, to show how thickly decades of tobacco smoke had blackened it.

The Hudson beside Manhattan is not truly a river but a tidal estuary, an arm of the sea whose current reverses with the tides as far as Troy, about 150 miles inland. The Lenape called it the river that flows both ways.

The tallest towers cluster in Midtown and the Financial District because there the hard old bedrock, Manhattan schist, lies close to the surface, strong enough to carry them.

On the Empire State Building, the tallest tower on Earth in 1931, the spire was meant to be a mooring mast where zeppelins would dock and let their passengers off, but the high winds around the tower made that impossible.

The city drinks more than a billion gallons of water a day, carried from reservoirs in the Catskill Mountains and the Delaware watershed, up to 125 miles north. Nearly all of it flows downhill the entire way, by gravity alone, without a single pump. The Delaware Aqueduct, about 85 miles long, is the longest continuous tunnel in the world.

new-zealand-and-zealandia-the-drowned-co.context_blurb:
New Zealand rises out of the South Pacific as two long, mountainous islands. Geologists now see them as the high ground of something far bigger, a continent almost entirely drowned beneath the sea. New Zealand is also one of the last large lands people ever reached: Polynesian voyagers arrived only about 800 years ago.

Charts of the seabed reveal that New Zealand stands on a great slab of continental crust called Zealandia, about 94 per cent of it under water, and in 2017 geologists formally argued that it counts as a true continent.

Only two large pieces of Zealandia break the surface: New Zealand toward its southern end and the tropical islands of New Caledonia far to the north. Everything between them is drowned continental shelf.

The continent's highest point is Aoraki, Mount Cook, a peak of snow and ice 3,724 metres high in the Southern Alps of the South Island.

New Zealand split from the other continents about 80 million years ago and drifted alone for so long that most land animals never reached it. It has almost no native mammals, only two tiny kinds of bat that flew across the sea, so birds and insects filled the empty places, and with nothing hunting them on the ground, several birds gave up flying altogether.

The South Island is being torn and lifted. Running almost ruler-straight for about 600 kilometres down its length is the Alpine Fault, the seam where the Australian plate and the Pacific plate slide past each other, heaving the Southern Alps upward. Its last great earthquake struck around 1717.

In the wild southwest of the South Island, Ice Age glaciers carved deep valleys that the sea later flooded, and the whole region is called Fiordland after those drowned valleys, the fiords. Best known of them is Milford Sound, with Mitre Peak soaring straight out of the water, and more than 6 metres of rain falls in a year; Rudyard Kipling called it the eighth wonder of the world.

Lake Taupō, in the heart of the North Island, fills the crater of a supervolcano. About 25,600 years ago it blew out some 1,170 cubic kilometres of rock and ash in the Oruanui eruption. Of all the super-eruptions known, that blast is the most recent; no volcano anywhere has erupted on that scale since.

newgrange-and-bru-na-boinne-the-solstice.context_blurb:
In the green farmland of the Boyne Valley in eastern Ireland rises Newgrange, a vast round mound of earth and stone heaped over a passage tomb. Farmers of the Neolithic, the New Stone Age, built it over five thousand years ago, with no writing and no metal tools, and they aimed the whole monument at one sunrise of the year.

Newgrange went up around 3200 BC, roughly five centuries before Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza.

The mound is about 85 metres across and some 12 metres high, an estimated 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth, every load of it gathered and piled by hand.

Its front gleams with a wall of white quartz that the builders carried from the Wicklow Mountains, set with dark granite cobbles from farther north. The shining wall you see today was rebuilt from quartz found scattered at the foot of the mound.

Across the entrance lies a huge kerbstone carved with a bold triple spiral, a triskele, cut with nothing but stone tools. Another triskele hides deep inside the chamber.

For a few mornings around the winter solstice, the shortest days of the year, the rising sun shoots a beam down the long passage and lights the pitch-dark inner chamber for about 17 minutes.

The beam enters through a small opening above the doorway, which the archaeologist Michael J. O'Kelly named the roof-box after he stood alone in the chamber on 21 December 1967 and saw the beam arrive, the first modern witness.

The inner chamber is roofed by stacked flat stones, each jutting a little farther in than the one below, rising almost 6 metres with no mortar. Fifty centuries later it is still dry, partly because the builders carved grooves into the roof-stones to carry rainwater outward, away from the chamber.

Newgrange is not alone. It stands in Brú na Bóinne, a bend of the River Boyne holding at least 90 Stone Age monuments, a World Heritage Site since 1993. Its two great sister passage-tombs are Knowth and Dowth, grassy mounds with carved kerbstones and dark chambers of their own. Knowth alone holds more than a third of all the megalithic art in Western Europe.

niagara-falls.context_blurb:
Niagara Falls thunders on the Niagara River, where the United States meets Canada, at the point where the water of the upper Great Lakes pours out of Lake Erie toward Lake Ontario. It is neither the tallest nor the widest waterfall on Earth, but few carry such a weight of water over the edge.

At the brink, Goat Island stands in the middle of the river and splits the waterfall in two: the Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side and the American Falls on the American side. A tiny scrap of rock, Luna Island, then cuts the slim Bridal Veil Falls off the American Falls, which is why Niagara counts three falls in all.

The giant curve of the Horseshoe takes almost the whole river, about nine-tenths of the flow, leaving only a tenth for the other two together. Its crest curves some 670 metres across.

The falls are not fixed in place. They are creeping upstream, eroding backward toward Lake Erie, and in some 12,000 years they have moved about 11 kilometres from where they began, leaving the long gorge behind as their trail.

The cliff is a sandwich: tough Lockport dolostone on top, soft Rochester shale beneath. The plunging water cannot easily cut the tough cap, so it scoops out the weak shale beneath it until the overhanging ledge, left without support, breaks off.

Niagara was born at the end of the last ice age, when the ice sheets melted back about 12,500 years ago. The meltwater filled the Great Lakes, and their overflow began spilling over the edge of a long ridge, the Niagara Escarpment near Queenston, which was the first plunge of the falls.

A few kilometres downstream, the river swings around a sharp bend into the spinning Niagara Whirlpool, where some fifty-five centuries ago the retreating falls broke into an old river gorge that glaciers had long ago packed with debris.

On the morning of 29 March 1848 the falls went almost silent. A warm spell had cracked the winter ice on Lake Erie, and easterly winds shoved the floes into the river's mouth, where they jammed into a dam of ice that choked off nearly all the water for about a day and a half. People walked out on the dry riverbed, and by many accounts they dug up old muskets, bayonets and tomahawks from the War of 1812, which had been fought along this river.

In June 1969 engineers switched the American Falls off on purpose, piling some 28,000 tons of rock into a dam that sent the whole river over the Horseshoe. They left the American Falls dry for about five months so that geologists could examine its crumbling rock close at hand. At its foot lay a great heap of boulders from rockfalls in 1931 and 1954. Everyone expected the heap to be cleared away, but the study showed the boulders were bracing the fragile cliff and holding it up, so in 1975 the experts left them in place.

norse-runes-and-the-jelling-stones.context_blurb:
Runes are the sharp, angular letters that the Vikings and their Germanic ancestors cut into wood, bone and stone for more than a thousand years. At Jelling in Denmark stand two great royal runestones raised in the 900s, and across Scandinavia thousands more still stand in fields and churchyards.

The Vikings had no paper and no ink. Their letters were made to be carved: a writer cut each rune into wood or stone with a knife, which is why every letter is built of short, straight strokes.

Carvers avoided flat horizontal strokes because, cut into a plank, such a line runs along the grain of the wood, blurs, and can split the plank apart. Curves were dropped too, since they are hard to slice cleanly.

The runic alphabet is called the futhark, after the sounds of its first six runes, f, u, th, a, r and k, run together into one word. It is the same trick that made our word alphabet out of the Greek alpha and beta.

Around 965 King Harald Bluetooth raised the greater Jelling stone. Its runes boast that he won all Denmark and Norway for himself. It also boasts that he made the Danes Christian, which is why the stone is nicknamed Denmark's baptismal certificate. It is, of course, a king's own boast carved in stone.

One face of the stone shows Christ with his arms spread, tangled in ribbon-like branches, and it is the oldest known image of Christ in all of Scandinavia. Scholars think the carver posed him as if hanging in a tree on purpose, to echo the god Odin, who in Norse myth hung for nine nights on the world-tree Yggdrasil.

Today the granite is bare and grey, but traces of pigment caught in its grooves show that it was first painted in vivid, bright colours. Denmark's National Museum has used those specks to reconstruct its original look.

In 1997 engineers named their new wireless technology Bluetooth after Harald, because he united quarrelling Danes as the technology unites gadgets. The popular story says its little logo is his two initials, the runes for H and B, joined into a single bind-rune. That story is widely repeated but not documented. His own nickname probably came from a dark, dead tooth.

In Sweden stands the Rök stone, raised around 800 by a father named Varinn for his dead son, and its roughly 760 runes, carved across all five faces, make up the longest runic inscription known. It is also full of riddles and secret cipher runes.

ocean-gyres-the-garbage-patch-and-the-sh.context_blurb:
Across every ocean, the winds and the spin of the Earth bend the surface currents into vast, slow wheels of water. In their calm centres, whatever floats tends to gather: rafts of golden seaweed in the Atlantic, a haze of plastic in the Pacific, and in one place the cradle of every Atlantic eel.

There are five of these ocean-wide wheels, called gyres, a pair each in the Pacific and the Atlantic and a fifth in the Indian Ocean, each turning clockwise north of the equator and anticlockwise south of it.

The biggest is the North Pacific Gyre, about 20 million square kilometres of turning sea walled by four great currents, and any one drop of water needs some 54 months to travel once around it.

In its calm heart, halfway between California and Hawaii, floats the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, which the yacht captain Charles Moore sailed into by accident in 1997. It spreads across a stretch of ocean roughly double the area of Texas.

Yet no satellite can photograph it, because it is not a solid raft at all: about 94 per cent of its estimated 1.8 trillion pieces are microplastics smaller than a fingernail, scattered thinly like pepper in soup.

When The Ocean Cleanup weighed the patch's plastic, almost half the weight, about 46 per cent, turned out to be abandoned fishing nets and other lost gear. These ghost nets keep snaring sea life for years.

In the North Atlantic lies the strangest sea of all. The Sargasso Sea has no shore anywhere: it is the only sea on Earth with no land coast, bounded instead by four ocean currents, among them the Gulf Stream. It is named for the golden sargassum weed that drifts across it in great rafts.

Sargassum is called holopelagic because it spends its whole life drifting on the open sea, growing and breeding there, without ever being anchored to the bottom.

When Columbus's ships pushed into the weed in 1492, his sailors feared that it would snag their ships and hold them trapped for ever. Their fear seeded centuries of legends, although the weed has never actually stopped a ship.

Around 30 degrees north, the winds around the Sargasso can die for weeks, and the story goes that becalmed crews threw their dying horses overboard to save drinking water, which gave the zone its name, the horse latitudes.

For more than two thousand years, from Aristotle onward, no one knew where eels were born. In 1920 the Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt followed smaller and smaller eel larvae across the ocean until the tiniest led him to the Sargasso Sea, the birthplace of every freshwater eel of Europe and North America.

old-sanaa.context_blurb:
Sanaa, high in the mountains of Yemen at the southwest corner of Arabia, is one of the oldest cities on Earth still lived in. Its walled Old City is a forest of tall, slim tower houses, brown below and iced with white patterns above, and some of them have stood for centuries.

People have lived here without a break for some 2,500 years, and Yemeni legend reaches back further still, crediting Shem, a son of Noah, with founding the city after the Flood beneath Mount Nuqum, the peak that overlooks it. No historian can confirm a founder; it is a legend.

Its more than 6,000 tower houses climb five to nine storeys, yet only their lowest floors are stone: above that they are built of rammed earth and bricks of fired mud, which is why old Sanaa is called a city of ancient skyscrapers.

The white gypsum trim that ices every floor is more than decoration: Sanaa gets real rain, and the gypsum acts as a waterproof skin, shedding the water that would otherwise wash the mud walls away.

High in the upper rooms, half-round fanlights of coloured glass set in carved white gypsum sit above the windows, and they are called qamariya, from qamar, the Arabic word for moon. In the afternoon they wash the walls in coloured light.

For over ten centuries, travellers have entered the Old City through its great fortified gate, Bab al-Yemen, the Gate of Yemen, which still pierces the high clay walls.

In 1972, workers mending the roof of Sanaa's Great Mosque, one of the oldest mosques in the world, found sacks of ancient parchment hidden in its attic. One page held a secret: long ago its first writing had been scraped off and written over, making it a palimpsest. Under ultraviolet light, scholars read the faint lower layer and found a copy of the Quran even older than the one written on top, on parchment dated to roughly 578 to 669. It is among the oldest Quranic manuscripts known.

palenque.context_blurb:
Palenque is a Maya city in the forested hills of Chiapas in southern Mexico, its pale limestone temples rising out of the jungle. It flourished from about 300 to 800, and its greatest king, Pakal, was laid to rest in one of the most astonishing tombs ever found in the Americas.

Its grandest building is the Temple of the Inscriptions, a stepped pyramid named for the stone tablets in its summit temple, carved with 617 Maya glyphs that tell the life of the king buried inside.

In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed that one floor slab in the temple had holes for lifting. Beneath it a hidden stairway, packed with rubble, ran down into the pyramid. His team took four seasons to clear it. In 1952, some 25 metres down inside the pyramid, they opened a walled-up doorway into a king's tomb, the first ever found inside a Maya pyramid. In the room before it lay the skeletons of six young attendants.

The king, Pakal, wore a death mask of about 200 pieces of jade, the green stone the Maya prized above gold, with eyes of shell and obsidian.

The lid of his stone coffin, about five tons of carved limestone, shows Pakal tipping backward at the moment of death. In 1968 Erich von Däniken claimed it showed the king piloting a rocket. Maya scholars reject that: the carving shows Pakal falling down the World Tree, the great cross-shaped tree at the centre of the Maya universe, whose roots reach the underworld and whose branches hold up the sky. The glyphs carved around him name the scene plainly.

Along the hidden stair runs a hollow stone tube shaped like a serpent, from the tomb up to the temple floor, which the Maya are thought to have built as a road for the dead king's spirit. Ruz called it the psychoduct.

Rising from the royal palace is a square tower of four storeys, unlike anything at any other Maya city, whose walls carry glyphs of the planet Venus and from which priests apparently studied the sky.

Beneath the plaza, the Maya roofed over a stream inside a stone channel nearly 300 metres long. In one stretch, the Piedras Bolas aqueduct, they narrowed the channel so sharply that the water was forced under pressure and could spurt upward, the first pressurized water known anywhere in the ancient Americas.

palmyra.context_blurb:
Palmyra is an ancient city of golden stone at an oasis in the Syrian desert, halfway between the old empires of Rome and Persia. Two thousand years ago it grew rich from the caravans crossing the sand, and its people raised a skyline of columns, arches and tombs that blended Greek, Roman and Persian styles.

A city could rise here only because of the Efqa spring, the only reliable water on a long desert crossing, so every caravan crossing the desert had to stop at it. Twenty kinds of date palm grew around it.

Palmyra grew rich by charging a toll on the goods that passed through, and it carved its customs rules, the Palmyrene Tariff, onto a great stone slab listing the tax on every kind of cargo.

Down the heart of the city runs the Great Colonnade, a ceremonial street about 1.1 kilometres long, once lined with hundreds of columns nearly 10 metres high. Its beauty earned Palmyra the name Bride of the Desert.

Outside the city, in the Valley of the Tombs, the richest families buried their dead in great stone towers up to four storeys high, sealing each relative into a niche, floor above floor.

The city's most famous ruler was Queen Zenobia, who rebelled against Rome and for a few years ruled an empire of her own. Around 272 the emperor Aurelian crushed her revolt and took her prisoner. By many accounts he then led her through the streets of Rome bound in chains of gold in his triumph, and afterward let her live out her life in a villa near the city. The ancient sources disagree, so her end is part legend.

In 2015 ISIS militants deliberately dynamited Palmyra's greatest monuments, among them its great temple and its triumphal arch. Days earlier they had killed the city's 83-year-old antiquities chief, Khaled al-Asaad, for refusing to reveal where its treasures were hidden. Yet the monuments can be pieced back together, because before the war researchers had made detailed 3-D scans of them, and digital models built from those scans now guide the work. Rebuilding of the Arch of Triumph began in 2022.

pamukkale-and-hierapolis.context_blurb:
At Pamukkale, in the southwest of Turkey, an entire hillside glows white, stepped with shallow pools of warm turquoise water. Hot springs built it, and on the plateau above stand the ruins of Hierapolis, a Greco-Roman spa town where people came to bathe in the same waters two thousand years ago.

The soft, heaped look of the white rock reminded people of piles of cotton, so they named it Pamukkale: pamuk means cotton and kale means castle, the cotton castle.

The white rock is travertine: hot spring water carries dissolved lime, and as it cools in the open air the lime hardens out as another thin layer of stone, the same recipe that grows stalactites in caves.

The terraces are still alive, because as long as the hot springs keep flowing, fresh white rock goes on forming on them, year after year. The white cliff is already about 2,700 metres long and 160 metres high.

On top of the cliff stands Hierapolis, the holy city, an entire Roman spa town with a theatre for some 15,000 people, colonnaded streets, temples and a vast city of tombs. In 1988 the terraces and the ruins were listed together as one World Heritage Site.

Long ago an earthquake toppled the marble columns of a portico into a hot spring, and today bathers swim in that 36-degree pool, nicknamed Cleopatra's Pool, right among the fallen ancient columns. The tale that Cleopatra once swam there is only a legend.

At Hierapolis, priests led bulls and birds to the mouth of one cave, where the animals dropped dead, and the Greeks and Romans called it the Gate of Pluto, a doorway to the underworld of the god of the dead. The geographer Strabo wrote that sparrows he threw in died at once. Long thought a myth, the cave was rediscovered in 2013.

The priests themselves walked away unharmed every time, which looked like a miracle. The real reason was simple: the cave breathes out carbon dioxide, which is heavier than air, so the deadly gas lay along the ground in a low, invisible layer, deep enough to kill a small animal but far below a tall priest's head. A 2018 study found the gas layer about 40 centimetres deep and deadliest at dawn.

pangaeas-ghost-how-we-know-the-map-moves.context_blurb:
A world map looks fixed, but it is not. The continents ride on great plates of rock that drift a few centimetres a year, and over hundreds of millions of years they have crowded together into supercontinents such as Pangaea and torn apart again. In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener argued that the continents move, and for decades he was mocked.

The first clue is on any map: the bulge of West Africa and eastern South America fit together like two torn halves of one shape, a match that the map-maker Abraham Ortelius noticed as early as 1596. Wegener argued that the coasts truly had been torn apart.

Mountain belts match too: the worn-down Appalachians of North America line up with the Scottish Highlands across the Atlantic, the severed other half of one ancient range. Wegener was a meteorologist and polar explorer, not a geologist, and his critics held that against him.

Fossils clinched it. Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile that could never have swum a salt ocean, turns up in the rocks of both Brazil and South Africa. The simplest explanation was that the two coasts had once been a single joined land. Still, geologists resisted for decades, because Wegener could not name a force strong enough to move a continent.

In 1970 a research ship, the Glomar Challenger, drilled long cores from deep under the Mediterranean seabed, and Kenneth Hsü and William Ryan read a startling story in them. Some five and a half million years ago, when the Strait of Gibraltar closed, the whole Mediterranean dried up into vast salt flats, leaving buried salt more than 2 kilometres thick. Later the Atlantic burst back through and refilled it in one of the greatest floods in Earth's history.

The geologist J. Tuzo Wilson showed that oceans repeatedly open and shut along the same zones of the globe, a rhythm now called the Wilson cycle. Where the Atlantic lies today, an earlier ocean, the Iapetus Ocean, had already widened and then vanished long before the Atlantic was born.

Today we can watch the drift happen. GPS stations on either side of the Atlantic show them creeping apart by about 2.5 centimetres a year, measured to the millimetre. Wegener's mocked idea is now something we measure directly.

paris-the-city-above-and-below.context_blurb:
Paris, on the River Seine in northern France, has been the capital of France for more than a thousand years. Above ground it is a city of grand boulevards, glowing chapels and an iron tower; below ground runs a second city of old quarries, tunnels and bones.

The city was built from its own underworld. For centuries workers dug tunnels beneath Paris to quarry the building stone that the city above was made from, leaving the ground honeycombed with empty galleries. That pale, creamy stone is Lutetian limestone, named after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris, and laid down in a warm, shallow sea some 45 million years ago. The Louvre and the Arc de Triomphe are both built of it.

For centuries the city's dead went into packed churchyards such as the Cimetière des Innocents, where the ground rose higher than a man's head. One spring, in 1780, the gas and pressure of the rotting dead burst through a wall into a neighbouring cellar. The city closed the cemetery, and from 1785 workers moved the bones by torchlight into the empty quarries.

Those bone-lined tunnels are the Catacombs, where the skulls and thighbones of perhaps six million Parisians are stacked into walls and arches. Over the way in, a carved slab orders every visitor to halt, for here begins the empire of Death: Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la Mort.

The old quarries run for some 300 kilometres, mostly closed to the public, and illegal explorers called cataphiles roam them. In August 2004 police training in the tunnels stumbled on a secret cave running on stolen electricity, where the explorers had built a fully equipped cinema, complete with a bar, seats cut from the rock and taped dog barks to scare off intruders.

On the island at the centre of the city stands the Sainte-Chapelle, whose upper chapel is almost all glass: fifteen stained-glass windows, each about 15 metres tall, holding more than a thousand Bible scenes. King Louis IX raised it in the 1240s as a giant jewelled case for one sacred treasure, the Crown of Thorns. He paid about 135,000 livres for the relic, more than three times the roughly 40,000 livres that the whole chapel cost.

For the new Metro of 1900, Hector Guimard gave the entrances railings of green cast iron that curl like plant stems and lamps like flower buds, and they became symbols of Art Nouveau, the new art. About 86 of his entrances survive.

The Eiffel Tower stands 300 metres high, bare wrought iron built for the World's Fair of 1889. It was licensed to stand for only 20 years, but it was saved because its great height made a superb antenna for radio and wireless telegraph. On a hot sunny day the iron on its sunlit side warms and lengthens, so the top leans away from the sun by as much as 15 centimetres.

perito-moreno-glacier-patagonia.context_blurb:
The Perito Moreno Glacier pours off the great ice fields of the southern Andes in Argentine Patagonia. It ends in a towering wall of ice standing in the waters of Lago Argentino, and walkways let visitors stand facing it, close enough to hear the ice crack and groan.

The wall is about 5 kilometres wide and some 70 metres high. Every so often a tall slab splits away from its face and crashes into the lake with a boom like a cannon, an event that scientists call calving.

The oldest ice has been squeezed so hard that almost all its air is gone, so it soaks up the red part of sunlight and gives back only deep blue.

For decades, while most glaciers on Earth shrank back, Perito Moreno was famous for staying put. It crept forward about 2 metres a day, almost exactly replacing the ice that broke off its front, so it stayed in balance instead of shrinking, earning the name the balanced glacier. That era has ended: since 2019 it has thinned fast and pulled back hundreds of metres.

Every few years the advancing ice reaches the far shore of the lake and seals off one arm of it, the Brazo Rico. With no way out, the trapped water rises as much as about 30 metres above the main lake.

The pressure slowly bores a tunnel under the ice dam, hollowing out a great arch that thins until it falls. Then the pent-up water roars through in the famous rupture, which crowds wait for, sometimes for days. It keeps no schedule, happening about every four or five years on average.

Perito Moreno is one of about 48 glaciers flowing from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, often called the third-largest store of fresh water on Earth, after the ice of Antarctica and Greenland.

permafrost-and-siberias-frozen-ground.context_blurb:
Permafrost is earth that never thaws, through summer and winter alike, for two years running or more, and some of it has been frozen for tens of thousands of years. It lies beneath vast stretches of Siberia, Canada and Alaska, and it keeps the bodies of ice-age animals as if in a freezer.

It lies under roughly a quarter of the exposed land of the Northern Hemisphere, some 23 million square kilometres.

In 2007 a reindeer herder in Siberia found a baby mammoth, later named Lyuba, who had lain for more than 40,000 years in the permanently frozen ground, which kept her skin, her organs and even her last meal intact.

As the frozen ground thaws, it can collapse. In Russia's Sakha Republic the Batagaika crater, a tadpole-shaped scar about a kilometre long, keeps growing as its frozen walls slump, and the locals' nickname calls it a gateway to the underworld. Its walls expose frozen layers up to about 650,000 years old.

Yakutsk, perhaps the coldest city on Earth, is built on deep permafrost, and a heated building would thaw the ground beneath it and sink. So its apartment blocks stand on stilts driven deep into the frozen soil, lifting their warm floors clear of the ground so the permafrost stays frozen.

On the Yamal Peninsula, round craters 60 to 80 metres across have burst open in the tundra since 2014, and they are gas-blowout craters, blasted out when methane building up in thawing ground explodes, not meteorite impacts.

Snow matters too. A thick, fluffy layer of snow acts like a blanket, trapping the ground's heat and letting the permafrost warm, so at Pleistocene Park on the Kolyma River, Sergey and Nikita Zimov drive horses, bison and muskoxen to trample the snow flat and let the deep cold reach the soil. Their herds have cut winter ground temperatures by about 7 degrees.

persepolis.context_blurb:
Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire, raised on a vast stone terrace beneath the mountains of southern Iran by Darius the Great from around 515 BC. Here the King of Kings received the gifts of his whole empire. Alexander the Great took the city in 330 BC, and fire brought its halls down.

The terrace is reached by a double stairway of 111 steps, each only about 10 centimetres high and the flights nearly 7 metres wide. A popular tradition says the steps were made so low and broad that riders could take their horses straight up onto the terrace. Modern scholars doubt it, thinking the low steps were meant for a slow, stately climb on foot.

At the Gate of All Nations stand two colossal guardians, lamassu: bulls with great wings and the bearded heads of men, set there to ward off evil. Unlike older Assyrian ones, which had five legs, these have their natural four.

The great audience hall, the Apadana, had a roof of cedar beams resting on 72 columns. Each rose about 20 metres, far taller and far slimmer than any Greek column, like a stone reed. Only about 14 still stand. At the top of each, where it met the beams, the sculptors carved the front halves of two animals, bulls, lions or griffins, set back to back so that their backs cradled the roof.

Along the Apadana stairway marches a carved stone procession of 23 delegations, the subject peoples of the empire, each in its own native dress and each bringing tribute to the king. Each gift is a clue to its homeland. The delegation from Elam, the hot lowland around Susa, brings a living gift that still startles: a lioness with her two cubs.

Why Alexander burned the city is still argued. The historian Arrian wrote that he did it as planned revenge for the Persian burning of Athens, while Diodorus, Plutarch and Curtius told of a drunken feast at which the Athenian Thais urged him on. The ancient writers never agreed.

The fire also saved something. In the record rooms lay vast numbers of soft clay tablets, the empire's daily paperwork of wages, rations and travel passes. The blaze baked them hard as pottery, so more than 30,000 survived to be read, mostly in the Elamite language.

persian-carpets-irans-woven-gardens.context_blurb:
For more than two thousand years, weavers in what is now Iran have knotted carpets of wool and silk. Persian carpets are famous for their astonishingly fine knots and for designs that picture paradise as a watered garden seen from above, and the finest old ones fetch millions.

The soft surface of a knotted carpet, its pile, is nothing but the trimmed tops of millions of tiny tufts of wool, each knotted by hand around the threads stretched on the loom.

The Ardabil Carpet of the 1500s holds about 26 million knots, some 300 to 350 in every square inch, and every one of them was tied by a weaver's hand, knot by knot. No machine tied a single one.

Persian weavers wrap each knot around just one thread, while Turkish weavers loop theirs evenly over two, and that difference lets a Persian rug bend its design into curving flowers and vines that a Turkish knot draws only stiffly.

Old carpets almost never carry a name, but the Ardabil does. In one corner, above a line of verse by the poet Hafez, the weaver who made it worked in his own name, Maqsud of Kashan, a servant of the court. It also hides a secret: it was woven as one of a matching pair for the shrine at Ardabil. The larger one went to London's Victoria and Albert Museum in 1893; the smaller is now in Los Angeles.

Garden carpets are maps of real gardens. Many follow the chahar bagh, the four gardens, a plan that divides a walled garden into four equal beds separated by channels of flowing water. In Old Persian such a walled garden was a pairidaeza, a walled-around place, and Xenophon, a Greek who served in Persia, took the word home, from where it passed through the Bible into English as paradise.

Around 550, King Khosrow I spread a carpet called the Spring of Khosrow across his palace floor at Ctesiphon, a whole spring garden with paths of gold, streams of silver and flowers of real jewels, so he could walk among blossoms in winter. When Arab armies took Ctesiphon in 637, the Caliph Umar ordered the great carpet cut into pieces and shared out among his soldiers as loot. Not a scrap survives.

You will often hear that every Persian carpet hides one deliberate mistake. The story says a weaver adds the flaw because only God is perfect and no human work should claim to be. It is folklore; there is no real evidence that weavers did it.

The oldest knotted carpet on Earth, the Pazyryk carpet, about 2,500 years old, survived in a chieftain's burial mound in Siberia's Altai Mountains because water seeped into the tomb and froze, locking it in ice until 1949.

Iran's weaving cities each have a look of their own. A dealer knows a Tabriz rug by its Mahi, or fish, design, in which little curving leaves seem to swim around a central medallion.

petra.context_blurb:
Petra lies hidden in a maze of red sandstone canyons in southern Jordan. More than two thousand years ago it was a rich desert capital, and its people carved temples and tombs straight into the cliffs. For centuries the outside world forgot it, until a Swiss explorer slipped in, in disguise, in 1812.

Its builders were the Nabataeans, a wealthy Arab trading people who turned a dry gorge into a busy capital. Petra made almost nothing itself; it grew rich by taxing the long camel trains from southern Arabia, which carried frankincense and myrrh, fragrant resins burned in temples across the ancient world.

It is called the Rose City because its sandstone is banded pink, red and orange, coloured right through by iron in the rock.

The way in is the Siq, a dark slot more than a kilometre long and in places only about 3 metres wide, and it is a natural crack where movements of the earth split the rock apart, later smoothed by running water. No one cut it by hand.

At its far end the Siq opens on Al-Khazneh, a towering facade of columns and statues blushing pink in the sun. The Nabataeans did not build it up from blocks; they carved it straight down into the living cliff, from the top downward, out of solid rock.

Its nickname, the Treasury, is a mistake: inside are only bare carved rooms, and it was almost certainly built as a royal tomb, probably for King Aretas IV. The name came from a Bedouin legend that an ancient pharaoh had sealed gold inside the great stone urn at the top, so local marksmen shot at it for generations, hoping to crack it open. The urn is solid rock.

The Treasury is not Petra's largest monument. That is the Monastery, Ad-Deir, about 47 metres tall and reached by some 800 rock-cut steps high above the valley floor. Its name comes from Christian crosses cut inside it much later.

The valley gets almost no rain and has no river, yet some twenty thousand people lived here. The Nabataeans caught the sudden flash floods with dams and rock-cut channels and stored the water in hundreds of hidden cisterns. They even sold the extra. They also piped spring water for miles through clay pipes whose tapered ends slotted together, which smoothed and controlled the flow.

In AD 363 a violent earthquake shattered the city and broke its water system, and Petra never truly recovered.

For centuries afterward local Bedouin let no stranger near. In 1812 Johann Burckhardt, a traveller from Switzerland, got in by a ruse: dressed as a Muslim pilgrim, he claimed he had vowed to sacrifice a goat at the tomb of Aaron above the valley, and a guide led him through.

pinatubo-1991-the-eruption-that-cooled-t.context_blurb:
In June 1991 a mountain in the Philippines woke from a sleep of about 500 years in one of the greatest eruptions of the 20th century. Scientists saw it coming in time to save thousands of lives, and the gas it threw into the sky cooled the whole planet for two years.

The mountain was Pinatubo, in the Zambales Mountains on the island of Luzon, so overgrown with jungle that hardly anyone knew it was a volcano.

Scientists of the Philippine volcano institute, PHIVOLCS, working with the US Geological Survey, read the earthquakes, the gas and the swelling dome and forecast the great blast about two days ahead, so officials could evacuate tens of thousands of people from its slopes. The warning is credited with saving thousands of lives.

On 15 June the ash column rose about 40 kilometres. Only one eruption of the 20th century was bigger: Novarupta, in Alaska, in 1912.

Pinatubo blasted roughly 17 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, the most of that gas ever measured by instruments. High above the weather it turned into a haze of tiny sulfate droplets. That haze worked like a mirror around the planet, bouncing part of the sunlight back into space before it could reach the ground. For about two years the world's average temperature fell by around half a degree.

The danger did not end with the eruption. For years, monsoon rains turned the loose ash on the mountain into rivers of volcanic mud. Such a flow is called a lahar, and in 1995 one buried the town of Bacolor, filling its 16th-century San Guillermo Church to half its height. Worshippers still enter through its old upper windows.

pingyao-the-frozen-ming-city.context_blurb:
Pingyao is a small walled town in Shanxi province in northern China, its grey lanes lined with courtyard houses and old shops. In the 1800s it was the money capital of China; then trade moved elsewhere, the town stood still, and by standing still it saved itself.

Almost every old Chinese city eventually tore down its walls, but Pingyao kept its city wall whole: about 6 kilometres of grey brick and rammed earth, 12 metres high, rebuilt in 1370. Some twenty thousand townsfolk still make their homes within it.

Along the top stand 72 watchtowers and more than 3,000 battlements, numbers said to honour the 72 gifted disciples and 3,000 students of Confucius. That is tradition, not documented fact.

Seen from above, the town is laid out as a tortoise, a Chinese symbol of long life: the south gate is its head, two wells are its eyes, the north gate is its tail and the side gates are its legs.

In 1823 a shop on West Street, Rishengchang, became China's first draft bank. Before then traders had to haul chests of silver along roads haunted by bandits. Now a merchant left his silver at one branch and carried only a redeemable paper draft, which he cashed for the same sum at a branch far away.

By the 1800s about 22 such banks, more than half of all in China, were packed inside Pingyao's walls, and the town became known as the Wall Street of old China.

pisa-the-tower-that-sank-as-it-rose.context_blurb:
Pisa, on the Arno River in central Italy, was once a rich sea-trading republic. Today most visitors come for one building: the white marble bell tower of its cathedral, which began to lean while it was still being built and has leaned ever since.

The lean began around 1178, when only about three storeys stood, because the tower sits on a shallow foundation over soft, waterlogged clay and sand that sank unevenly beneath it. It was a foundation problem, never a design choice.

Building took nearly two hundred years, with a long pause for wars. When work resumed, the masons made the upper columns taller on the sinking side to straighten the climb, and because each stage leaned a little differently, the tower is built in a subtle curve, like a banana.

By 1990 it leaned 5.5 degrees and was nearing collapse. Engineers led by an international committee slowly removed soil from beneath its north side, the high side that had sunk less, so that side settled and the tower eased back toward upright. It reopened in 2001, leaning about 3.97 degrees.

polynesian-wayfinding.context_blurb:
Polynesian wayfinding is the art by which the ancestors of Hawaiians, Māori, Samoans and Tahitians crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific with no compass, chart or metal tools, and found nearly every island in the largest ocean on Earth. They read the stars, the swells, the clouds and the birds.

Their world is the Polynesian Triangle, the vast stretch of ocean with Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island at its three corners, larger than any nation on the planet.

They sailed it in double-hulled voyaging canoes, two long hulls lashed side by side with a deck between for people, water, taro and piglets.

At night a navigator held his course by the star compass, a ring of 32 named houses around the horizon, memorising which house each guiding star rose out of and sank into.

The sea itself spoke. Lying flat in the hull with his eyes closed, a master could feel the long ocean swells that bend and wrap around an island and cross beneath the canoe, and know that land lay ahead, far beyond sight.

Birds pointed the way too. Terns and noddies sleep on land but fly far out to sea at dawn to fish. So at dawn a navigator sails against the flocks, but at dusk he follows the white terns home, and they lead him to the island.

Low coral atolls stay hidden below the horizon, but the shallow lagoon inside one throws a faint green glow onto the underside of the cloud above it, revealing the atoll long before its land appears.

Māori tradition says the long-tailed cuckoo, which vanished each spring from tropical islands such as Rarotonga toward the southwest, told the ancestors that some land no one had yet found lay to the southwest, and they followed it to New Zealand.

In 1769 the Raiatean navigator Tupaia sailed with Captain Cook and drew a chart naming 74 islands across some 2,000 miles of ocean, entirely from his own memory. His home island, Raiatea, is remembered as Hawaiki, the ancestral homeland, and on it stands Taputapuātea, the greatest marae, or open-air temple, of Polynesia, now a World Heritage Site.

For years sceptics insisted that Polynesians had simply drifted onto their islands. By the 1970s no Hawaiian still knew the old art. The last masters lived on Satawal, a tiny island in Micronesia, and one of them, Mau Piailug, agreed to teach it back. In 1976 he guided the new double canoe Hōkūleʻa about 2,500 miles from Hawaii to Tahiti by stars, swells and birds alone. When she sailed into Papeete harbour a month later, some 17,000 Tahitians crowded the shore to greet her.

pompeii-and-herculaneum-frozen-by-vesuvi.context_blurb:
In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius, above the Bay of Naples, erupted and buried two Roman towns at its foot, Pompeii and Herculaneum, under hot ash, pumice and searing flows of gas. The eruption sealed in everything, from loaves and graffiti to the shapes of the people themselves, and no other place shows Roman daily life so completely.

Pompeii vanished under metres of ash and stayed lost for about 1,700 years, until diggers uncovered an inscription bearing its name in 1763. The digging showed that both towns had been sealed just as they were, down to loaves on the shop counters and slogans on the walls.

In the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet, a floor mosaic shows a dog above the Latin words cave canem, beware of the dog.

The ash set like rock around the dead, and the bodies rotted away inside it, leaving hollows. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli, the director of the dig, poured liquid plaster into those hollows to cast the victims, then chipped away the ash to reveal them in their final poses. One famous cast shows a guard dog at the House of Orpheus, still chained by its collar, caught on its back with all four legs thrust into the air.

The walls are full of Roman voices. More than 1,500 painted election notices survive, and some are attack ads. One mocking endorsement claimed that a candidate was backed by all the town's late drinkers. The scrawl that guides quote most is a wall's own complaint: the writer marvels that the wall has not collapsed under the weight of so many people's boring scribbles, a protest against graffiti written as graffiti.

Herculaneum, closer to the volcano, was buried about 20 metres deep by flows near 500 degrees. That heat did not destroy its timber roofs, its beds, its doors or its food; it turned them to charcoal, a process called carbonization, and they survived almost whole. A round loaf found in 1930 still shows the deep cuts that divided it into eight wedges, and the stamp of its baker.

Down by the old shoreline, about 300 people crowded into stone boat sheds hoping for rescue by sea, and a blast of air heated to hundreds of degrees killed them almost at once.

A grand seaside house, the Villa of the Papyri, held some 1,800 scrolls of papyrus charred black, the only library to survive intact from the ancient world. The scrolls fall to dust at any attempt to unroll them, and for two and a half centuries they stayed unread.

In 2023 a contest called the Vesuvius Challenge set out to read them without opening them, scanning the rolled scrolls with high-energy X-rays inside a particle accelerator and training AI to spot the faint ink. That autumn Luke Farritor, an American computer-science student aged 21, read the first word: porphyras, the Greek word for purple.

potosi.context_blurb:
Potosí sits more than 4,000 metres up in the cold Bolivian Andes, beneath a reddish, cone-shaped peak called Cerro Rico, the Rich Mountain. For some two hundred years after the Spanish began mining it in the 1540s, that one mountain poured out much of the silver that flowed from the Americas around the world.

Silver was the only reason for the city, and around 1600 its mines had made Potosí one of the largest cities on Earth, with about 120,000 people living in the thin, icy air.

Geologists read in the rock how the silver got there: hot, mineral-rich water rose through cracks in the mountain, and as it cooled it left silver, tin, lead and zinc behind in veins.

Potosí's mint struck silver coins, the famous pieces of eight, which Spanish treasure fleets carried to Europe and the Manila galleons carried to Asia, until they became almost a world money.

So much wealth poured out that Spanish speakers still say a thing vale un Potosí, meaning it is worth a fortune, and Cervantes used the phrase in Don Quixote.

The cost fell on the miners. From 1574 Spain's colonial rulers made every Andean highland community send about one grown man in seven to work the mines under a labour draft called the mita, and mercury used to refine the ore slowly poisoned the workers. So many died below that Cerro Rico became known as a mountain that eats men. The death toll was never recorded and is still fiercely disputed.

Five centuries of digging have bored more than 100 kilometres of tunnels through the peak. Surveyors find that the mountain is slowly losing height and wearing down, its summit sinking a few centimetres every year. In 2014 UNESCO listed the city as a World Heritage Site in danger.

prague.context_blurb:
Prague, the capital of the Czech Republic, straddles the Vltava River in the heart of Europe. Spared heavy bombing in the Second World War, its old centre is a living gallery of Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, crowned by a vast castle on its hill and joined by a stone bridge lined with saints.

On the Old Town Square hangs the Astronomical Clock, the Orloj, first recorded in 1410. Older astronomical clocks were built elsewhere, but all of them have stopped, so Prague's is the oldest such clock still running today. It was made by the clockmaker Mikuláš of Kadaň with the astronomer Jan Šindel.

Every hour a crowd gathers. A carved skeleton, Death, rings his bell and turns his hourglass. Beside him stand three other carved figures, Vanity holding his looking-glass, Greed clutching his money and a Turk standing for worldly pleasure, and they shake their heads, as if not ready to follow him. Then two little windows open and the Twelve Apostles glide past, two at a time. Finally a golden rooster, added in the 1860s, flaps its wings and crows to end the show.

A beloved legend says the councillors had the clockmaker Master Hanuš blinded so he could never build a finer clock for another city. Historians say it never happened.

Charles Bridge spans the river on a long row of stone arches. Legend says its 14th-century builders strengthened their mortar with eggs, and that whole villages sent cartloads, one even boiling them first so they would not break on the road. Lab tests have only partly backed the tale.

In 1393 King Wenceslaus IV ordered John of Nepomuk, a priest, thrown from the bridge to drown, legend says for keeping the queen's confession secret. Five lights are said to have shone on the river where he died, so in art the saint wears a halo of five stars. His statue of 1683 is the oldest of the thirty on the bridge, and tradition says that whoever touches the bronze plaque beneath it will return to Prague someday.

Above the river, Prague Castle sprawls over some 70,000 square metres, and Guinness World Records calls it the largest ancient castle complex on Earth. It is still the Czech president's residence. Inside its walls is Golden Lane, a row of tiny cottages first built for the emperor's guards, later taken over by goldsmiths, whose craft gave the lane its name.

In St Vitus Cathedral the Bohemian Crown Jewels lie behind a door with seven locks, and the seven keys are held by seven different people, among them the president and the archbishop, who must all come together to open it.

In 1618 angry Protestant nobles burst into the castle and threw two royal officials and their secretary out of a window, a fall of some 21 metres. All three survived. Catholics said angels had caught them; the Protestants sneered that a soft pile of manure and rubbish in the moat had broken their fall. The quarrel helped spark the Thirty Years' War.

prambanan.context_blurb:
Prambanan is a cluster of soaring stone temples on the plain of central Java in Indonesia, raised around 850 by a Hindu dynasty. Java was once a great centre of Hindu and Buddhist civilization, and Prambanan is the largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia.

Its tallest tower, a spire 47 metres high in the middle of a row of three, belongs to Shiva, who destroys and renews the world, the dancer whose steps turn the universe. Two smaller temples beside it honour the other two great gods of the Hindu trinity, and the site's old name was Shivagrha, the House of Shiva.

Carved panel by panel along the inner walls runs the Ramayana, the tale of Prince Rama, whose wife Sita is carried off by the ten-headed demon-king Ravana, and of the war to win her back with Hanuman's monkey army. On full-moon nights it is still danced beneath the towers.

A few miles away on the same plain stands Prambanan's great Buddhist neighbour, Borobudur, a vast terraced mound crowned by ring upon ring of bell-shaped stupas.

Why are there so many shrines? In a Javanese legend, Princess Roro Jonggrang told the prince Bandung Bondowoso that she would wed him only if he could build a thousand temples between dusk and dawn. His spirit workers had raised 999 when the princess tricked them into fleeing by faking the dawn. The furious prince cursed her into stone, and a statue in the Shiva temple is still pointed out as the princess herself. It is folklore, not history.

quebec-city.context_blurb:
Quebec City, the capital of the Canadian province of Quebec, stands on a high cliff above the St. Lawrence River. Samuel de Champlain founded it in 1608, making it one of the oldest European-founded cities in North America, and its French-speaking old town still lies inside stone ramparts.

Its name comes from the Algonquin word kebec, meaning where the river narrows, because just below the city the wide St. Lawrence squeezes tight between the cliffs. Whoever held the heights commanded the water road into the continent.

When Jacques Cartier climbed the cliff, he found glittering stones and named the height Cap Diamant, Cape Diamond, but his diamonds were only crystals of plain quartz. The French even coined a saying: as false as a Canadian diamond.

Its walls, about 4.6 kilometres around, make Quebec the only town north of Mexico still ringed by its old fortifications, which you can walk on today. In the 1870s, after the British soldiers left, the town nearly tore them down for traffic, until the Governor General, Lord Dufferin, stepped in to save them.

On the cliff top stands the Citadelle, a star fort whose walls jut out into angled bastions, so that defenders could catch attackers at any stretch of wall in crossfire from two sides. It is still an army base, and a cannon fires from it every noon.

Above the old town rises the Château Frontenac, which looks like a castle but has always been a hotel, built by a transcontinental railway company, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and opened in 1893 to lure travellers onto its trains.

rain-shadow-deserts-the-dry-side-of-the-.context_blurb: A rain-shadow desert forms on the leeward side of a mountain range. Prevailing moist air is forced upward by the mountains, cools, and drops its rain on the windward slopes. By the time the air descends on the other side it is dry. Death Valley is dry because of the Sierra Nevada; the Patagonian desert because of the Andes; the Gobi because of the Himalayas; the Negev because of the mountains of the Levant. Rain shadows explain many of the world's biggest deserts.

reggae-ska-and-dub-kingston-jamaica.context_blurb: In the 1960s and 70s, the small island of Jamaica produced an outsized cluster of popular music genres that reshaped global pop. Ska came first, out of the sound-system DJ culture of Kingston, drawing on American jazz and rhythm-and-blues. Rocksteady slowed it down. Reggae — identified above all with Bob Marley and the Wailers — slowed it further and infused it with Rastafarian spirituality and social protest. Dub, pioneered by producers like King Tubby and Lee Perry, stripped reggae tracks down to their rhythmic bones and layered on heavy reverb and echo.

reykjavik.context_blurb: Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland, is the northernmost capital of an independent country in the world, sitting just a few degrees south of the Arctic Circle. Although it only became a proper town in the 18th century, its name — meaning 'smoky bay' — refers to the steam rising from geothermal hot springs that the first Viking settlers saw as they came ashore. Those same hot springs now heat virtually every house in the city. Iceland sits on top of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where two tectonic plates pull apart, which is also why the ground around Reykjavik is so volcanically restless.

rio-de-janeiro.context_blurb: Rio de Janeiro, on the Atlantic coast of Brazil, has one of the most spectacular natural settings of any big city on Earth: steep granite peaks (Sugar Loaf, Corcovado) rising straight out of a tropical blue bay, with long white beaches wrapped around the base. From the summit of Corcovado an enormous Art Deco statue of Christ the Redeemer looks down over the city. Rio was the capital of Brazil until 1960, when the government moved inland to the newly built Brasilia; it remains the heart of Brazilian carnival culture.

river-deltas-where-a-river-drops-its-loa.context_blurb: A delta is a landform built up where a river slows down as it meets the sea, lake, or other still body of water, and drops the sediment it has been carrying downstream. The classic triangular shape (which gave the Greek letter delta its name) was first noticed by Greek observers of the Nile. Deltas are usually extremely fertile and heavily populated — the Ganges, Mississippi, Nile, Mekong, Rhine-Meuse, and Yangtze deltas each support tens of millions of people, often at risk from storms, floods, and sea-level rise.

rome-the-eternal-citys-engineering.context_blurb: Rome, the capital of modern Italy, was for roughly five hundred years the capital of an empire that stretched from Scotland to Mesopotamia. The modern city is layered on top of that ancient one: a Renaissance church sits inside a Roman temple here, a medieval tower rises from the stump of a Roman theatre there. In the middle of Rome is Vatican City, the independent state that is the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church, with its own basilica, museums, and (though they rarely draw their swords) its own Swiss Guard.

rongorongo-the-lost-script-of-easter-isl.context_blurb: Rongorongo is a mysterious script found carved into wooden tablets by the people of Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in the remote southeastern Pacific. It is one of only a handful of writing systems that may have been invented independently in human history. By the time 19th-century missionaries noticed the tablets, the people who could read them were already dead — many killed by Peruvian slave raids and introduced disease — and only a few dozen tablets survive. Modern scholars have tried for over a century to decipher the script, mostly without success.

rotorua.context_blurb: Rotorua is a town in the North Island of New Zealand, famous for being built right on top of an active geothermal field. The whole place smells of sulphur. Hot pools bubble in people's back gardens, geysers go off a short walk from the town centre, and heated mud boils in roadside parks. It is also one of the heartlands of Maori culture — the local iwi have lived with and used these hot springs for centuries, and tourists come as much for traditional Maori hospitality as for the geology.

ryoan-ji-kyotos-garden-of-stone.context_blurb: Ryoan-ji is a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan, whose rock garden is one of the most famous works of art in the Japanese tradition. The garden is a rectangle of raked white gravel in which fifteen stones are placed, arranged in groups, with nothing else — no plants, no water. No matter where you stand to look at it, at least one of the fifteen stones is always hidden from view. It was laid out in the 15th century, and nobody is quite sure what, if anything, it is meant to represent.

salar-de-uyuni.context_blurb: The Salar de Uyuni, in the high Andes of Bolivia, is the world's largest salt flat — an almost perfectly flat expanse of white salt stretching to the horizon in every direction. It is the dry bed of a huge ancient lake. For a few months of the year a thin layer of water from the surrounding mountains covers it, turning the whole salar into a vast natural mirror reflecting the sky. The Salar also holds an enormous share of the world's known lithium reserves, locked up in brine beneath the salt crust.

samarkand-the-registan-and-timurs-blue-c.context_blurb: Samarkand, in modern Uzbekistan, was one of the glittering cities of the medieval Silk Road and the capital of the 14th-century conqueror Timur (Tamerlane). Timur deported the best craftsmen from the lands he sacked and set them to work beautifying his city. The result is one of the most dazzling pieces of Islamic architecture anywhere on Earth: a central square called the Registan ringed on three sides by huge madrasas whose facades are entirely covered in intricate turquoise and blue tile mosaics.

samba-and-bossa-nova-rio-de-janeiro.context_blurb: Samba is the national dance of Brazil, born in the early 20th century in the working-class and Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods of Rio de Janeiro from African, Portuguese, and Brazilian folk roots. It became the heart of Rio's famous Carnival parades. In the late 1950s a sophisticated, quieter cousin of samba, called bossa nova, was born in the beach-side apartments of Ipanema and Copacabana. Musicians like Antonio Carlos Jobim, Joao Gilberto, and the poet Vinicius de Moraes crossed samba's rhythms with cool jazz harmonies — the result was 'The Girl from Ipanema' and a whole quietly cosmopolitan Brazilian sound.

san-francisco.context_blurb: San Francisco sits on a hilly peninsula on the Pacific coast of California at the mouth of a vast bay. It leapt into existence as a boom town during the 1849 California Gold Rush and has repeatedly reinvented itself since: as the great Pacific port of its day, as the city flattened and rebuilt after the enormous 1906 earthquake, as the capital of the 1960s counterculture, and in our own era as the headquarters of Silicon Valley's internet companies. The Golden Gate Bridge spans the mouth of the bay in a dramatic sweep of orange steel.

santorini-the-caldera-behind-the-atlanti.context_blurb: The Greek island of Santorini, in the Aegean, is actually the ragged rim of a sunken volcanic crater. In roughly 1600 BCE the volcano exploded catastrophically, blowing out its own middle and leaving behind the horseshoe-shaped island cluster we see today. The eruption may have contributed to the decline of the Minoan civilization on nearby Crete and is often suggested as the historical kernel of Plato's story of Atlantis — the island civilization that supposedly disappeared beneath the sea in a day and a night.

seoul-palace-city-on-the-worlds-stranges.context_blurb: Seoul has been the capital of Korea for most of the last 600 years. In 1950 it changed hands four times during the Korean War, which left the Korean peninsula split in two by a cease-fire line only a short drive north of the city. Seoul rebuilt itself from the ruins and became one of the wealthiest, most technologically advanced cities in Asia. Its old royal palaces — courtyards and tiled roofs restored after years of Japanese demolition — sit in the shadow of glass skyscrapers.

sequoyah-and-the-cherokee-syllabary.context_blurb: Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith in the early 1800s who had never learned to read or write any language. He became fascinated with the idea that the words of the English-speaking white settlers around him could be captured on paper, and he set out to produce the same gift for his own people's language. Working alone over several years, he devised a 'syllabary' — a set of about 86 symbols, each standing for one Cherokee syllable — and the Cherokee Nation officially adopted it in 1825. Within a few years Cherokee literacy rates were higher than those of their white neighbours.

serabit-el-khadim-the-alphabet-born-in-a.context_blurb: At Serabit el-Khadim, a remote Egyptian turquoise mine on the Sinai Peninsula, archaeologists have found strange rock-cut inscriptions in a very early script, dating to roughly 1800 BCE. The signs look like simplified Egyptian hieroglyphs, but they are being used for a Semitic language — the ancestors of Hebrew, Aramaic, and Phoenician. Many scholars now think these 'Proto-Sinaitic' inscriptions represent the earliest known step toward the alphabet, probably invented by Semitic-speaking workers at the mines who had seen Egyptian writing and simplified it for their own tongue.

seville-the-inland-gate-to-the-americas.context_blurb: Seville, in southern Spain, is the capital of Andalusia and the fourth-largest city in the country. It sits on the Guadalquivir River, far enough inland that a sailing ship can only just reach it on the tide. In the 16th century, that geography put Seville in a monopoly position: for about two hundred years, every ship travelling between Spain and its new empire in the Americas had to pass through its port. The city grew spectacularly wealthy, which paid for its enormous Gothic cathedral and its elegant royal palace, the Alcazar.

shanghai-the-bund-facing-the-future.context_blurb: Shanghai sits on the Yangtze River delta on the east coast of China. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it was carved up into foreign-controlled 'concessions' and became a cosmopolitan port lined with grand European-style banks along the river — the famous 'Bund.' After 1949 it was austerely closed off; from the 1990s onwards it has exploded into one of the great global financial cities, with a forest of skyscrapers rising on what used to be marsh across the river from the Bund.

shibam.context_blurb: Shibam is a small walled town in the Hadramawt valley of Yemen, famous as 'the Manhattan of the desert.' Within its mud-brick walls stand several hundred tower-houses, some rising up to eight or eleven stories, all built packed tight together on a tight grid plan. It is widely considered the oldest skyscraper city in the world. Most of the current buildings are a few hundred years old, though they stand on much older foundations.

shwedagon-pagoda-yangon.context_blurb: The Shwedagon Pagoda, in the heart of Yangon in Myanmar, is the holiest Buddhist site in the country. It is a single enormous gilded stupa — a solid conical mountain of brickwork sheathed in real gold leaf — rising from a hilltop and ringed by smaller shrines. The structure has been renovated and re-gilded by successive Burmese kings over the centuries; its very topmost tip is set with a single large diamond. Devotees walk clockwise around the pagoda making offerings.

sigiriya.context_blurb: Sigiriya in central Sri Lanka is an isolated plug of volcanic rock rising abruptly about 180 metres above the surrounding plain. In the late 5th century CE, King Kashyapa fortified its summit and built himself a palace up there, approached by a staircase that passed between the paws of a colossal carved lion gatehouse. Partway up the cliff, under a sheltering overhang, are a series of frescoes of celestial maidens that are among the oldest surviving Sri Lankan paintings.

silk-chinas-two-thousand-year-secret.context_blurb: Silk is a shining, strong textile fibre spun by the caterpillars of certain moths. Chinese tradition says it was discovered around 2700 BCE by the empress Leizu, and for roughly two thousand years China kept the technique for making it a jealously guarded state secret. Caravans travelled westward from China all the way to Rome carrying bolts of the finished cloth — the famous Silk Road is named for this traffic — while the actual silkworms, their eggs, and the mulberry leaves they ate stayed inside China. The secret eventually leaked out via Korea, Japan, and India.
