singapore.context_blurb: Singapore is a small city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, sitting on one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world. It was founded as a British trading post by Stamford Raffles in 1819, became briefly independent in 1965 after being expelled from the Malaysian federation, and under the long rule of Lee Kuan Yew transformed itself from a scrappy port into one of the wealthiest and most tightly-managed cities in the world. Famously orderly, it is also one of the few islands of English Common Law in Southeast Asia.

skara-brae-and-neolithic-orkney.context_blurb: On a windswept beach of the Orkney Islands north of Scotland sits Skara Brae, the best-preserved Stone Age village in all of northern Europe. Built around 3100 BCE and buried by sand for most of the next five thousand years, its stone houses still have their original stone dressers, bed-frames, and hearths standing in place. A great storm in 1850 stripped the sand away and revealed it. The village is older than Stonehenge and older than the Egyptian pyramids.

st-petersburg.context_blurb: St Petersburg was founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703 on a boggy stretch of the Baltic coast in the far northwest of Russia, explicitly as a modern 'window on the West.' Peter forced his aristocrats to move there, build Italian- and French-style palaces, and reorient Russia's culture toward Europe. The city served as the capital of the Russian Empire for two centuries. During World War II it endured the brutal 872-day Siege of Leningrad, in which something like a million civilians died.

stockholm.context_blurb: Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, is built on fourteen islands at the point where Lake Malaren meets the Baltic Sea, giving it a strikingly watery, maritime character. Sweden has not fought a war in over two hundred years, which has let Stockholm's old town — the Gamla Stan — survive intact as one of the best-preserved medieval city centres in northern Europe. The city is also where the Nobel Prizes are awarded each December.

stone-town-zanzibar.context_blurb: Stone Town is the old quarter of Zanzibar City on the island of Zanzibar, off the Tanzanian coast. For centuries the island was a crossroads where African, Arab, Indian, and European cultures mixed: it was ruled by sultans of Oman, who grew rich on cloves and (less creditably) on the slave trade. Its tall coral-stone houses are famous for carved wooden doors, each a signature of the family that lived behind it. The singer Freddie Mercury of Queen was born here.

stonehenge-salisbury-plain.context_blurb: On the chalk downs of southern England stands Stonehenge: a ring of enormous standing stones, some topped with horizontal lintels locked in place like Lego. It was built in stages between roughly 3000 and 1500 BCE by Neolithic and early Bronze Age people whose names we will never know. The site is aligned to the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Where some of the stones came from, how they were moved tens or hundreds of kilometres, and what the whole thing was for are all still mysteries that archaeologists argue about.

summits-left-unclimbed-out-of-reverence.context_blurb: A handful of mountains around the world have been deliberately left unclimbed in modern times out of respect for the local people who hold them sacred. Mount Kailash in Tibet is one. The entire peak of Gangkhar Puensum in Bhutan — technically the highest unclimbed mountain on Earth — is off-limits by Bhutanese government decree. Mount Machapuchare in Nepal, Mount Kawagarbo in Yunnan, and others also carry no-climb policies. These are deliberate choices to preserve the religious meaning of a place.

svalbard-and-the-global-seed-vault.context_blurb: Svalbard is a cold Norwegian archipelago high in the Arctic Ocean, about halfway between mainland Norway and the North Pole. It is one of the northernmost places on Earth with permanent settlements. Buried in a mountainside on one of its islands sits the Global Seed Vault — a huge refrigerated backup library of over a million distinct crop varieties from every country on Earth, meant to safeguard the world's agricultural diversity against regional catastrophes. The vault is often called 'the doomsday vault.'

sydney.context_blurb: Sydney, on the southeastern coast of Australia, grew up around one of the great natural deep-water harbours of the world. It was founded as a British penal colony in 1788; today it is Australia's largest and most populous city. Its skyline is defined by two neighbouring icons on the harbour: a steel arch bridge from 1932 and a white-sailed opera house from 1973. The surrounding beaches, inlets, and sandstone cliffs make it one of the most spectacularly-sited cities in the Southern Hemisphere.

ta-prohm.context_blurb: Ta Prohm is one of the temples of the Angkor complex in Cambodia, built in the 12th century as a Buddhist monastery. When the French began restoring Angkor in the early 20th century, they decided to leave this one almost as they found it: half-swallowed by jungle, with enormous silk-cotton and strangler-fig trees growing on top of the stone galleries, roots prising apart the walls. It is the picture people usually have in mind when they imagine a jungle-eaten lost temple, and it was used as a setting for the first Tomb Raider film.

taj-mahal.context_blurb: The Taj Mahal, on the banks of the Yamuna River in Agra, India, is a vast white-marble mausoleum completed in 1653. It was ordered by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth. The whole structure is laid out as a huge symmetrical garden-tomb, with reflecting pools, calligraphy, and inlaid semi-precious stones; the marble subtly changes colour through the day. It is widely considered one of the most beautiful buildings ever built.

tallinn.context_blurb: Tallinn, on the Baltic Sea, is the capital of Estonia and once one of the northernmost outposts of the Hanseatic League of medieval trading cities. Its upper and lower towns, both protected by stone walls studded with round defensive towers, together make up one of the best-preserved medieval walled cities in all of northern Europe. Tallinn is unexpectedly famous in another dimension: in the two decades since Estonia regained independence from the Soviet Union, it has become one of Europe's most digitally advanced cities, home of Skype's original engineering team and a model for e-government.

tambora-and-the-year-without-a-summer.context_blurb: In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa exploded in what geologists call the largest volcanic eruption in recorded human history. Tens of thousands of people in the vicinity were killed outright. The volcano hurled vast amounts of sulphur into the stratosphere, and the following year — 1816 — summers across the Northern Hemisphere were brutally cold. New England and Europe got frost and snow in June and July. Crops failed, food prices rose, and a group of friends on a lakeside holiday in Switzerland, kept indoors by the weird weather, wrote the ghost stories that produced both Frankenstein and the first modern vampire tale.

tartan-and-the-kilt-highland-scotland.context_blurb: The patterned woollen cloth known as tartan has been woven in the Scottish Highlands for many centuries. Specific colour and stripe combinations — the 'setts' — were traditionally associated with particular regions and later with specific Highland clans. The pleated knee-length wool wrap known as the kilt is a somewhat later development that reached its modern form in the 18th century. Both tartan and the kilt were briefly banned in Scotland after the Jacobite uprising of 1745, as a tool for suppressing Highland identity. The ban was repealed, and tartan has flourished ever since.

temperate-rainforests-the-cool-wet-giant.context_blurb: The world has two very different kinds of rainforest. The famous tropical ones straddle the equator; the temperate ones hug the cool, foggy, mountainous west coasts of the mid-latitudes. The best-known temperate rainforests run along the Pacific coast of North America from northern California up into Alaska. Others grow in southern Chile, in Tasmania and New Zealand, and in a thin strip of coastal Norway. Their rain is so steady that the branches of the vast evergreens — redwoods, Sitka spruce, Douglas firs — are drooping with mosses and lichens.

tenochtitlan.context_blurb: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded around 1325 on islands in a shallow lake in the Valley of Mexico. By the early 16th century it was one of the biggest cities in the world, with grand pyramid-temples, canals, floating gardens, and causeways connecting it to the mainland. When Hernan Cortes and his small Spanish force arrived in 1519 they were astonished by what they saw. Within two years they had conquered the city, in alliance with Aztec rivals, and begun building modern Mexico City on top of its ruins.

teotihuacan.context_blurb: Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico north of modern Mexico City, was one of the biggest cities in the ancient world. At its height around 500 CE it had somewhere around 125,000 people, making it bigger than any city in Europe at the time. Its planned grid of streets is dominated by two massive pyramids — the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon — along the central 'Avenue of the Dead.' We do not know what the builders called themselves. The city was already a mysterious ruin to the later Aztecs, who gave it the name it still bears.

the-aksum-obelisks-stelae-of-axum.context_blurb: In the ancient Ethiopian city of Aksum stand some of the tallest single blocks of stone ever quarried and raised anywhere on Earth. Carved more than 1,700 years ago by the Christian kingdom of Aksum, they are tall granite pillars sculpted to look like multi-storey buildings, with rows of 'windows' and 'doors' incised into their faces. The largest one lies broken on the ground; it probably collapsed during the attempt to raise it. One of the others was carried off by Mussolini's troops in 1937 and only returned to Ethiopia in the 2000s.

the-alps.context_blurb: The Alps are the great mountain range of central Europe, arcing across parts of France, Italy, Switzerland, Germany, Austria, and Slovenia. They were pushed up by the slow collision of the African tectonic plate with Europe, and that collision is still going on. Their famous peaks — the Matterhorn, Mont Blanc, the Eiger — have been the training ground for mountaineering for two centuries. The Alps are also the water tower of Europe: four of the continent's main rivers (the Rhine, the Rhone, the Danube, and the Po) rise in them.

the-amazon.context_blurb: The Amazon, in South America, is the largest river in the world by volume: it carries about one-fifth of all the freshwater running into the oceans. By length it is a very close second to the Nile. Its drainage basin covers an area roughly the size of the continental United States and is dominated by the Amazon rainforest, home to a staggering fraction of all the species on Earth. The river rises in the Andes and runs more than 6,000 kilometres east across Brazil to the Atlantic Ocean.

the-andes.context_blurb: The Andes form the longest mountain range on dry land, running for roughly 7,000 kilometres down the entire western edge of South America from Venezuela to Patagonia. They were raised by the slow forcing of the Pacific plate down under the South American plate; both the subduction and the uplift are still active, which is why the range is studded with volcanoes and earthquakes. The Inca built their empire among the Andes, and today their towns and cities hold the highest capital, the highest navigable lake, and some of the highest permanently inhabited settlements in the world.

the-appalachians.context_blurb: The Appalachian Mountains run for about 2,400 kilometres down the eastern side of North America, from Canada to Alabama. In their youth, several hundred million years ago, they were as high as the Himalayas; today they are a long chain of wooded, rounded, deeply eroded ridges and valleys. They form a line that European settlers struggled to cross for the first century of American colonization. Geologically, parts of them line up with mountain ranges in Scotland and Morocco, which were all once part of the same single range before the Atlantic Ocean opened and split them apart.

the-aral-sea.context_blurb: The Aral Sea, straddling the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in Central Asia, was once the fourth-largest inland body of water in the world. In the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the two rivers that fed it to irrigate cotton fields across the surrounding desert. The lake shrank catastrophically. Today most of its old basin is dry salt desert; rusting fishing boats sit stranded in the sand kilometres from any water. It is widely considered one of the worst human-caused ecological disasters ever recorded. The northern remnant has been partially restored.

the-arctic-ocean-and-the-north-pole.context_blurb: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of Earth's oceans, surrounded on nearly all sides by the land of North America, Europe, and Asia. For most of history it has been covered by a layer of floating sea ice. The geographic North Pole sits in the middle of this ice — there is no land under it, only ocean — which is why reaching the pole has traditionally meant trekking across drifting ice floes. The Arctic sea ice has been visibly shrinking over recent decades as the climate warms.

the-atacama.context_blurb: The Atacama Desert runs for a thousand kilometres along the coast of northern Chile between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes. It is one of the driest places on Earth: parts of it have gone decades at a stretch without recording measurable rain. The combination of extreme dryness and high altitude also gives the Atacama some of the clearest night skies in the world, which is why many of the world's largest telescopes are built there.

the-atacama-the-driest-place-on-earth.context_blurb: The Atacama Desert of northern Chile is widely considered the driest desert on Earth. Some weather stations in it have never recorded rainfall. Its extraordinary dryness comes from a combination of three factors: it sits on the leeward side of the Andes in a rain shadow; it also sits on the warm leeward side of the coastal range along the Pacific; and offshore the cold Humboldt Current stabilizes the air and discourages storms. NASA uses it to simulate conditions on Mars.

the-bagpipes-contested-home.context_blurb: The bagpipes are one of the oldest wind-instrument families on Earth; variants on them are found from Scotland to Pakistan. The world most strongly associates them with the Scottish Highlands, where the Great Highland Bagpipe has been a battle instrument of Scottish regiments for centuries. But bagpipe-type instruments were played throughout the ancient Mediterranean and have been found at Hadrian's Wall; versions appear in Spanish Galicia, Bulgaria, Ireland, and across the Balkans. The question 'where were bagpipes invented?' turns out to be surprisingly hard to answer.

the-bay-of-fundy-highest-tides-on-earth.context_blurb: The Bay of Fundy, between the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has the highest tides anywhere on Earth. Twice a day the water level at its head rises and falls by over 15 metres — about the height of a four-storey building — in roughly six hours. The reason is a lucky accident of basin geometry: the natural slosh period of the bay happens to be about the same as the twice-daily tidal cycle, so each tide reinforces the next. At low tide, people walk out on sea floor that was underwater six hours earlier.

the-bering-land-bridge-beringia.context_blurb: During the last Ice Age so much of the Earth's water was locked up in continental ice sheets that global sea level stood more than a hundred metres below where it is today. In that time, Alaska and eastern Siberia were connected by a vast exposed plain of grassland rather than a narrow sea strait. Geneticists and archaeologists agree that this corridor, called Beringia, is how the ancestors of the Native American peoples first crossed from Asia into the Americas, probably in several waves between about 25,000 and 15,000 years ago.

the-blues-the-mississippi-delta.context_blurb: The blues was born in the Mississippi Delta region of the American Deep South, among African-American sharecroppers and labourers in the decades after the Civil War. Rooted in work songs, spirituals, and West African musical traditions, it developed a distinctive vocabulary of twelve-bar progressions, 'blue' flattened notes, and lyrics structured around repeated lines. From the Delta, singers like Robert Johnson, Charley Patton, and Son House carried the music up the Mississippi to Memphis and Chicago, where electrified versions evolved and eventually fed into rock and roll.

the-camino-de-santiago.context_blurb: The Camino de Santiago is the medieval Christian pilgrimage route that ends at the shrine of the apostle Saint James in the city of Santiago de Compostela, in Galicia in northwestern Spain. The best-known branch is the Camino Frances, a roughly 800-kilometre walking route that crosses the Pyrenees from France and traverses northern Spain. The pilgrimage dates to the 9th century, became one of the great devotions of medieval Europe, and has been massively revived in recent decades by both religious and secular walkers.

the-caspian-sea.context_blurb: The Caspian Sea, bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, and Azerbaijan, is the largest completely enclosed body of water on Earth — depending on how you draw the categories, it is either the biggest lake in the world or an inland sea in its own right. It is a leftover of the vast ancient ocean that once stretched across what is now central Eurasia. Its water is brackish, somewhere between fresh and sea water. Its basin holds enormous reserves of oil and natural gas and is the natural home of the beluga sturgeon, whose roe is the source of the most expensive caviar.

the-colosseum-romes-flavian-amphitheatre.context_blurb: The Colosseum, in the middle of modern Rome, is the largest amphitheatre ever built in the ancient Roman world. It was completed in AD 80 and could seat somewhere around 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights, mock sea-battles, and animal spectacles. Beneath its arena floor is a maze of chambers and lifts where gladiators and wild beasts waited to be hoisted up into view. Even half-ruined and stripped of its marble, it is still the biggest standing Roman building and the icon of Rome itself.

the-congo.context_blurb: The Congo River, in central Africa, is the second-longest river in Africa after the Nile and by volume second only to the Amazon anywhere in the world. It is unusual for crossing the equator twice on its long bending path through the rainforest. The Congo basin holds the second-largest tropical rainforest on Earth. Downstream of the modern cities of Kinshasa and Brazzaville, the river tumbles through the Livingstone Falls on its way to the Atlantic — a series of rapids so violent that the river is unnavigable by boat for its last few hundred kilometres.

the-coriolis-effect-why-the-storms-spin.context_blurb: Because the Earth is rotating, anything moving freely over its surface for a long time appears to curve, from the point of view of someone standing on the ground. This apparent curving is called the Coriolis effect. In the Northern Hemisphere it deflects moving air and water to the right of their path; in the Southern Hemisphere to the left. The result is that tropical storms in the Northern Hemisphere rotate counter-clockwise and those in the Southern Hemisphere rotate clockwise. It also helps drive the big trade-wind and ocean-current patterns of the globe.

the-darkest-skies-on-earth-where-the-mil.context_blurb: In the age of city lights, truly dark night skies have become one of the world's rarer sights. The darkest skies on Earth are in a handful of remote places — the Atacama Desert in Chile, the central Namibian desert, parts of the Australian Outback, and certain high mountain plateaus — where the air is clear, the altitude is high, and no large settlement sits within hundreds of kilometres. In these places the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a visible shadow on the ground.

the-dead-sea.context_blurb: The Dead Sea, between modern Israel, Jordan, and the Palestinian territories, is the lowest point of dry land anywhere on Earth, lying hundreds of metres below sea level. Its water is almost ten times saltier than the ocean. The salt makes it so dense that swimmers float on top of it as if lying on a sofa, and nothing larger than microbes can live in it. The lake is also shrinking fast as water is drawn out of the Jordan River upstream, leaving ominous sinkholes along its retreating shoreline.

the-didgeridoo-arnhem-land-australia.context_blurb: The didgeridoo is a long drone-pipe wind instrument invented by the Yolngu and other Aboriginal peoples of Arnhem Land, in Australia's Northern Territory. It is traditionally made from a eucalyptus tree branch that has been hollowed out by termites. Players buzz their lips into one end and use a technique called circular breathing — inhaling through the nose while continuing to push air out of the cheeks — to produce an uninterrupted drone for minutes on end. It may be one of the oldest wind instruments in continuous use anywhere.

the-door-to-hell-darvaza-gas-crater.context_blurb: The 'Door to Hell' is a crater in the middle of the Karakum Desert in Turkmenistan, roughly 70 metres across, that has been burning continuously for about half a century. The usual story is that Soviet geologists drilling for natural gas in 1971 accidentally punched into an underground gas cavern, the ground collapsed, and they set the escaping gas on fire expecting it to burn out in a few days. It never did. The flames are now one of the country's most famous landmarks.

the-east-african-rift-a-continent-tearin.context_blurb: The East African Rift is a long rift valley running north-south through eastern Africa, from the Afar region of Ethiopia down into Mozambique. It is the surface expression of a slow tearing of the African continent along a boundary where two plates are gradually pulling apart. The rift is studded with volcanoes, deep lakes (including Lake Tanganyika and Lake Malawi), and some of the richest fossil beds for early human ancestors on Earth. Many millions of years from now a new sea will probably run down this corridor.

the-everlasting-storm-catatumbo-lightnin.context_blurb: Over the far southern end of Lake Maracaibo in northwestern Venezuela, a very specific storm system develops almost every night for most of the year. Warm humid air from the lake rises, meets cold mountain air descending from the Andes, and produces continuous lightning for up to ten hours a night, around 300 nights a year. Local people have used it as a free natural lighthouse for centuries. The storm, called Catatumbo lightning, is thought to produce more lightning per square kilometre per year than anywhere else on Earth.

the-four-great-inventions-of-ancient-chi.context_blurb: Chinese tradition speaks of 'the Four Great Inventions' — technologies that Chinese civilization gave to the rest of the world and that reshaped life everywhere they spread. They are papermaking, printing, gunpowder, and the magnetic compass. Each one was invented in China centuries before it reached Europe. The British philosopher Francis Bacon, writing in 1620, observed that printing, gunpowder, and the compass had 'changed the whole face and state of things throughout the world' — without noticing that all three had come from China.

the-gamelan-java-and-bali.context_blurb: A gamelan is a traditional Indonesian ensemble made up almost entirely of tuned bronze percussion instruments: gongs, metallophones, drums, bamboo flutes, and occasionally a singer or stringed instrument. Gamelans are the heart of court and religious music on the islands of Java and Bali, where every village traditionally owned its own set of instruments. Each gamelan is tuned to its own unique pitches; the instruments of two different gamelans will not quite agree. The sound influenced Western composers like Debussy, Satie, and later Steve Reich.

the-ganges.context_blurb: The Ganges rises in a glacier in the Indian Himalayas and runs more than 2,500 kilometres across northern India into Bangladesh, where it joins the Brahmaputra and empties into the Bay of Bengal through the largest river delta on Earth. The river is the lifeblood of several hundred million people. For Hindus it is also a goddess, Ganga, and bathing in the river is believed to wash away sin. The lower Ganges plain is one of the most densely populated regions on the planet.

the-ganges-from-gaumukh-to-the-ghats-of-.context_blurb: The Ganges rises at a glacier called Gaumukh in the Indian Himalayas and flows for over 2,500 kilometres east across northern India, past the holy city of Varanasi, and on into Bangladesh. For Hindus, the river is the goddess Ganga, who came down from heaven to purify the world. All along its course it is lined with ghats — long stepped stone embankments where pilgrims come to bathe, pray, and (in the city of Varanasi) cremate their dead by the water's edge.

the-global-conveyor-belt-thermohaline-ci.context_blurb: Beneath the ocean's familiar surface currents runs a slower, deeper global flow called the thermohaline circulation. It is driven by small differences in water density caused by variations in temperature ('thermo') and salt ('haline'). Cold salty water near the poles sinks and begins a journey around the planet along the sea floor that can take over a thousand years before it rises again. This single enormous conveyor belt transports huge amounts of heat around the planet, which is one reason it matters for climate; climatologists worry that enough fresh glacier meltwater could slow it down.

the-gobi.context_blurb: The Gobi Desert sprawls across much of southern Mongolia and the northern Chinese region of Inner Mongolia. Unlike the Sahara, it is a cold desert: temperatures swing from well below freezing in winter to furnace heat in summer, because the Himalaya mountains block moist air from reaching this inland plateau. The Gobi is famous as the hunting ground where paleontologists first found the fossilized nests, eggs, and skeletons of dinosaurs like Velociraptor, Protoceratops, and Oviraptor in the 1920s.

the-grand-canyon.context_blurb: The Grand Canyon, in northern Arizona in the United States, is one of the most dramatic examples anywhere of what a river can do to a landscape. Over the last five million years or so, the Colorado River has carved a mile-deep gorge through the layers of the Colorado Plateau, exposing almost two billion years of geological history in cross-section. Standing on the rim, with the ribbon of river just visible at the bottom and vast coloured rock walls stepping down to it, is one of the great experiences of looking at the Earth.

the-great-aletsch-glacier-swiss-alps.context_blurb: The Great Aletsch Glacier in southern Switzerland is the largest glacier in the Alps. It is a river of ice over 20 kilometres long that flows down out of the high peaks of the Bernese Alps, with long dark 'medial moraine' stripes of rubble running down its middle where tributary glaciers merged into it. Over the past 150 years, like most alpine glaciers, Aletsch has been retreating fast. A chalet originally built right at the end of the ice is now a long walk from the current ice front.

the-great-barrier-reef.context_blurb: The Great Barrier Reef, running along the northeastern coast of Australia, is the largest coral reef system in the world and the only living structure visible from space. It stretches for over 2,300 kilometres and comprises nearly three thousand individual reefs. The reef has suffered serious mass bleaching events in recent decades as the ocean warms, and reef scientists are watching anxiously whether the reef as a whole will survive the next century intact.

the-great-blue-hole-belize.context_blurb: Off the coast of Belize in the Caribbean lies a nearly perfect circular hole in a shallow coral lagoon, about 300 metres across and 125 metres deep. The dark blue of the deep hole, surrounded by the pale turquoise of the shallow reef flat, is a striking sight from the air. The hole was a dry limestone cave during the last Ice Age; when the sea rose, the roof collapsed and the ocean flooded in. The French ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau made it famous in 1971.

the-great-caves-waters-underground-cathe.context_blurb: The world's biggest caves are mostly dissolved out of limestone by slightly acidic groundwater over millions of years. Hang Son Doong, in central Vietnam, is the largest cave passage known on Earth — big enough that a Boeing 747 could in theory fly along its interior. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system, with over 650 kilometres of mapped passages. Cave formations include stalactites hanging from the ceiling, stalagmites rising from the floor, and sometimes vast cathedral-sized chambers hundreds of metres below the surface.

the-great-ice-ages-and-their-orbital-pac.context_blurb: The Earth has gone in and out of ice ages many times over the last 2.6 million years, with great continental ice sheets growing across North America and Europe and then melting back. The pace of this cycle is governed by small periodic variations in Earth's orbit and axial tilt — the so-called Milankovitch cycles — which subtly change how sunlight is distributed over the planet across tens of thousands of years. The last time ice sheets covered Chicago, London, and Berlin was about 20,000 years ago.

the-great-mosque-of-djenn.context_blurb: The Great Mosque of Djenne, in the delta of the Niger River in Mali, is the largest building in the world made entirely of mud brick. Every spring, the people of Djenne gather for a festival in which they help re-plaster the mosque with fresh mud and rice-husk mortar before the next rainy season. Permanent wooden beams protrude from its walls to serve as scaffolding for this annual re-coating. The current building dates to 1907 but preserves the shape of a medieval original, in a city that was once a major stop on the trans-Saharan caravan trade.

the-great-pyramid-of-giza.context_blurb: The Great Pyramid on the Giza Plateau on the outskirts of modern Cairo is the only one of the ancient Seven Wonders of the World still standing. Built for Pharaoh Khufu in the 26th century BCE out of more than two million blocks of limestone, it remained the tallest man-made structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years. Its interior is a strange geometry of ascending corridors and sealed chambers. For centuries people assumed it must have been built by slaves; recent archaeology has instead uncovered the villages, bakeries, and tombs of the paid workforce that actually did the job.

the-great-sphinx-of-giza.context_blurb: Beside the pyramids of Giza crouches the Great Sphinx: a colossal recumbent figure with the body of a lion and the face of a pharaoh, carved from a single outcrop of limestone bedrock. It is one of the oldest and biggest sculptures on Earth, and the identity of the king whose face it wears is still argued over. Its nose is famously missing, and a persistent myth blames Napoleon's cannons for the damage, though the real culprit is someone else entirely.

the-great-wall-of-china.context_blurb: The 'Great Wall' is not really a single wall but a vast network of fortifications, towers, and ramparts raised over more than two thousand years by successive Chinese dynasties to guard their northern frontier against raiders from the steppe. The best-preserved sections, with their stone-and-brick battlements running along the ridges of the hills near Beijing, are the work of the Ming dynasty in the 15th and 16th centuries. In total, counting all branches and epochs, it stretches many thousands of kilometres across northern China.

the-greenland-ice-sheet.context_blurb: The Greenland Ice Sheet covers about 1.7 million square kilometres of the huge island of Greenland, piled up to several kilometres thick in the middle. It is one of only two true ice sheets on Earth, the other being Antarctica. If the entire Greenland ice sheet were to melt, global sea level would rise by about 7 metres. The ice has been building up for several hundred thousand years; drilling cores through it reveals a layer-by-layer record of ancient atmospheres, volcanic eruptions, and climate history.

the-gulf-stream-and-the-mild-edge-of-eur.context_blurb: The Gulf Stream is one of the great surface ocean currents of the Atlantic, carrying warm water from the Gulf of Mexico up along the eastern coast of North America and then east across the Atlantic toward Europe. The warm, moist air blown off that water keeps the climate of northwestern Europe much milder than it would otherwise be at those latitudes — Scotland and Norway are about as far north as Hudson Bay, but their winters are far gentler. The Gulf Stream is part of the global ocean conveyor belt.

the-ha-amonga-a-maui-trilithon.context_blurb: On the Pacific island of Tongatapu in the Kingdom of Tonga stands a strange prehistoric monument: three enormous blocks of coral limestone arranged as two uprights supporting a horizontal lintel, in the shape of the Greek letter pi. It was raised in about the 13th century and legend says it was lifted into place by the demigod Maui. The upper beam is cut to fit tight slots in the uprights, as if the stonemasons were trying to lock the whole thing together against earthquakes. Some researchers think it is a solar observatory for marking the solstices.

the-hadley-cell-and-the-30-degree-desert.context_blurb: The 'Hadley Cell' is a huge atmospheric circulation pattern that runs between the equator and about 30 degrees north and south latitude. Hot, moist air rises at the equator, dumps its rain in tropical storms, and spreads poleward at high altitude. By about 30 degrees it has cooled, dried out, and sunk back to the surface. The sinking dry air there creates most of the world's great deserts: the Sahara, the Arabian, the Thar, the Mojave, the Atacama, the Kalahari, and the Australian desert all sit at these latitudes.

the-highest-clouds-on-earth-noctilucent-.context_blurb: Most clouds form within a few kilometres of the ground. 'Noctilucent' clouds, by contrast, form about 80 kilometres up, at the edge of space, in a layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere. They are made of microscopic ice crystals that condense around tiny particles of meteor dust. They are so high that they continue to catch sunlight after the Sun has set at ground level, and they appear as faintly shining electric-blue wisps against a dark twilight sky, usually seen from high latitudes in summer.

the-himalayas.context_blurb: The Himalayas are the highest mountain range in the world, forming a long wall across Asia between the Indian subcontinent and the Tibetan Plateau. They include every one of the Earth's fourteen mountains over 8,000 metres. The range was pushed up — and is still being pushed up — by the collision of the Indian plate with Asia, which began about 50 million years ago and has not stopped. The glaciers of the Himalayas are the source of some of Asia's largest rivers, including the Ganges, the Indus, the Brahmaputra, the Yangtze, and the Mekong.

the-horn-the-arete-the-cirque-and-the-ta.context_blurb: When several glaciers eat into the sides of a mountain, they carve out dramatic distinctive shapes. The 'cirque' is the bowl-shaped amphitheatre where a glacier was born, with steep walls plucked out of the mountainside. The 'arete' is the knife-edge ridge left between two neighbouring cirques. The 'horn' is the sharp pyramidal peak sculpted when three or more cirques eat into a mountain from different sides — the Matterhorn in the Alps is the textbook example. A 'tarn' is the small lake that forms in a cirque after the ice is gone.

the-humboldt-current-upwelling-and-the-w.context_blurb: The Humboldt Current is a cold ocean current that flows north along the Pacific coast of South America. Its most important feature is upwelling: strong winds push surface water offshore, and cold nutrient-rich deep water rises to take its place. Those nutrients fuel an enormous bloom of plankton, which in turn supports one of the richest fisheries on Earth, mostly of Peruvian anchovies. The Humboldt is also why coastal Peru and Chile are so cool and dry despite sitting near the equator.

the-ice-age-painted-caves-lascaux-chauve.context_blurb: In the limestone caves of southwestern France and northern Spain are the oldest paintings any human has ever made that we can still see today. Lascaux, Chauvet, and Altamira were painted during the last Ice Age, between about 36,000 and 17,000 years ago, by hunter-gatherers using charcoal, ochre, and manganese. Their galleries of charging bulls, prancing horses, and stampeding rhinoceroses are so lifelike that the modern painter Picasso, visiting one of them, is said to have remarked that we had invented nothing in all the centuries since.

the-ice-crystal-sky-sun-dogs-and-the-22-.context_blurb: On days when a thin veil of high cirrus or cirrostratus cloud is drifting across the sky, sunlight (or moonlight) passing through the tiny hexagonal ice crystals in those clouds gets refracted in geometrically specific ways. The commonest result is a 22-degree halo — a pale ring around the Sun or Moon at exactly that angular distance. Sometimes a pair of bright spots called 'sun dogs' appears on each side of the Sun at the same radius. These phenomena were seen as omens in many cultures.

the-inca-quipu-an-empire-written-in-knot.context_blurb: The Inca Empire ran a well-organized state across thousands of kilometres of the Andes without any written language in the usual sense of the word. Instead, administrators used a 'quipu': a cluster of coloured, knotted strings tied in specific patterns to encode numbers and, probably, categories. The surviving quipus mostly record things like census and tribute data, but some researchers think more complex quipus may also have carried narrative or poetic content. Fewer than a thousand survive today.

the-indus-script-and-the-silent-seals-of.context_blurb: The Indus Valley Civilization — the Bronze Age cities of Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, and others — left behind thousands of small inscribed stone seals, bronze tablets, and pottery marks. The inscriptions use roughly 400 distinct signs, often alongside a picture of an animal, and they are tantalizingly short, averaging only about five characters. Nobody has decoded them. We do not even know for sure what language the Indus people spoke. The Indus script is the single most important undeciphered writing system in the world.

the-jet-stream-the-river-of-wind-that-st.context_blurb: The jet stream is a narrow ribbon of fast-moving air high in the atmosphere, flowing roughly west-to-east around the mid-latitudes of each hemisphere. It can reach speeds of several hundred kilometres per hour. Commercial airliners riding it eastbound can save hours of flight time. The jet stream also 'steers' the parade of mid-latitude storms moving around the world. When the jet buckles into big north-south meanders, it can lock weather patterns in place for weeks — bringing extreme cold snaps south or heat domes north.

the-kalahari.context_blurb: The Kalahari Desert covers much of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa. Technically it is a 'semi-desert' — it gets more rainfall than a true desert like the Sahara, enough to support thorny grasses, acacia trees, and a surprising density of wildlife. It is the ancestral home of the San people (sometimes called Bushmen), who have hunted and gathered its land for tens of thousands of years, and whose language of click consonants is one of the most unusual on Earth.

the-karakoram.context_blurb: The Karakoram is a mountain range running across the borders of Pakistan, India, and China. It is a continuation of the Himalayan system but geologically distinct and even more concentrated: four of the world's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks sit in its narrow 500-kilometre length, including K2. It also has the largest glaciers outside the polar regions. Many of its summits were first climbed only in the mid-20th century, and some of its subsidiary peaks are considered among the hardest technical climbs on Earth.

the-kathmandu-valley-city-of-a-thousand-.context_blurb: The Kathmandu Valley, in the foothills of the Himalayas in Nepal, is a bowl of green terraced farmland dotted with three old royal cities — Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur — each dense with pagoda-roofed Hindu and Buddhist temples. For centuries the valley was the end of the only trade route over the mountains between India and Tibet. The architecture is a hybrid of South Asian and Tibetan styles. A devastating earthquake in 2015 badly damaged many of its monuments, and painstaking restoration is ongoing.

the-lapita-pottery-trail.context_blurb: The Lapita are the vanished seafaring people whose ancestors were the first humans to reach most of the Pacific islands east of New Guinea. Archaeologists know them not by writing but by the distinctive pottery they carried with them — thin red clay stamped with intricate dotted geometric patterns — from about 1500 to 500 BCE. The same style of pot has been dug up from Papua New Guinea to Tonga, tracing the path of their outrigger canoes as they island-hopped across thousands of kilometres of open ocean.

the-last-green-blink-of-the-sun-the-gree.context_blurb: The 'green flash' is a brief optical phenomenon that can be seen for a second or two at the moment the Sun's upper edge disappears below a clear horizon — most reliably over the sea. The atmosphere refracts the different colours of sunlight by slightly different amounts; just as the last bit of the Sun is going down (or just as the first bit comes up), the blue and green wavelengths are bent most and briefly linger as a vivid green spot above where the Sun just was.

the-little-ice-age-written-on-the-land.context_blurb: 'The Little Ice Age' was a modest cold spell lasting roughly from the 14th to the 19th century, during which average temperatures in parts of Europe, North America, and Asia fell by only about one degree. That was enough to make glaciers grow, canals freeze over in Dutch paintings, winter 'frost fairs' spring up on the frozen River Thames in London, and Norse settlers abandon their colony in Greenland. The exact causes are still argued over — probably some combination of reduced solar activity, major volcanic eruptions, and ocean-circulation changes.

the-lut-desert-dasht-e-lut.context_blurb: The Dasht-e Lut, in eastern Iran, is one of the hottest places on Earth. Satellite measurements of the ground surface temperature there have recorded readings above 70 degrees Celsius — higher than any other land surface temperature ever measured. The desert is so hot and so dry that essentially nothing lives in its central hollow. Its wind-carved ridges of mud-stone — called yardangs — look so unearthly that the area is sometimes used as a stand-in for the surface of Mars.

the-maldives-and-coral-atolls-darwins-th.context_blurb: The Maldives are a nation of some 1,200 low-lying coral islands in the Indian Ocean, scattered across a chain of ring-shaped atolls southwest of India. No point in the country is more than a couple of metres above sea level. In the 1830s, Charles Darwin — while on his famous Beagle voyage — proposed that atolls form when a volcanic island gradually subsides, while a reef growing around it keeps pace by growing upward, so the volcano eventually sinks below the waves and leaves only the ring of reef. His theory has been largely confirmed by modern drilling.

the-mariana-trench-challenger-deep.context_blurb: The Mariana Trench, in the western Pacific east of the Philippines, is where the oldest, coldest, densest part of the Pacific plate is being forced down beneath the Philippine Sea Plate. Its deepest known point, Challenger Deep, is about 11 kilometres below the sea surface — deep enough that if Mount Everest were dropped into it, there would still be more than two kilometres of water above the summit. Only a tiny number of crewed vessels have ever reached the bottom.

the-matterhorn.context_blurb: The Matterhorn is the pointed pyramidal peak that straddles the border of Switzerland and Italy in the Pennine Alps. At 4,478 metres it is not an exceptionally tall mountain, but its symmetrical four-faced horn shape is so photogenic that it has become one of the icons of mountaineering. It was first climbed in 1865 by a party led by the Englishman Edward Whymper, in a successful ascent that turned into tragedy on the descent when four of the seven men fell to their deaths.

the-meander-and-the-oxbow-lake.context_blurb: A meander is a looping curve in the course of a river running across a flat landscape. Over time, the current erodes the outside of each bend and deposits sediment on the inside, so meanders slowly grow and migrate across the floodplain. Eventually a loop becomes so pronounced that the river cuts across its neck, leaving the old loop as an isolated, curved pond called an oxbow lake. The lower Mississippi, the Amazon, and many European rivers are strewn with oxbows and abandoned meander scars.

the-mekong.context_blurb: The Mekong is the great river of mainland Southeast Asia. It rises on the Tibetan Plateau and winds through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam, where it fans out into a vast fertile delta before reaching the South China Sea. For centuries it has been both a highway and a frontier. Its central Cambodian stretch forms the shoreline of Tonle Sap, a lake that reverses its flow with the seasons — an unusual hydrological trick found almost nowhere else.

the-mid-atlantic-ridge-where-the-seafloo.context_blurb: Running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean is a long submerged mountain chain called the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. It is where the North American plate meets the Eurasian plate and the South American plate meets the African plate — and where those plates are slowly pulling apart. New ocean floor is being created along the ridge all the time, oozing up as magma, cooling into basalt, and drifting slowly outward on both sides. In one place the ridge rises above the sea surface: the island of Iceland sits straddling it.

the-mississippi.context_blurb: The Mississippi River drains most of the central United States, flowing roughly 3,700 kilometres from Minnesota down to the Gulf of Mexico. Together with its tributaries — chiefly the Missouri and the Ohio — it forms one of the largest river systems in the world and historically opened up the whole American interior to steamboat trade. Mark Twain's novels made it the backdrop of American self-mythologizing. Where it meets the sea, it has built up a huge delta in Louisiana that is slowly subsiding into the Gulf.

the-monsoon-reversal-and-meghalayas-wett.context_blurb: The monsoon is a seasonal reversal in prevailing winds, driven by the big temperature difference between a huge landmass and the ocean beside it. The Indian subcontinent has the most famous and most reliable example. From about June to September, winds blow in off the Indian Ocean carrying moist air, which dumps enormous amounts of rain on the slopes of the Himalayas. In the Indian state of Meghalaya, two small towns — Mawsynram and Cherrapunji — are among the wettest inhabited places on Earth.

the-mystery-eruptions-reading-earths-ash.context_blurb: Beyond the famous eruptions of recorded history, volcanologists know that there have been even bigger blasts whose sources no one has definitely identified. By reading the layer-by-layer record of volcanic sulphur captured in Greenland and Antarctic ice cores, scientists can tell exactly when a major eruption occurred — but not necessarily which volcano caused it. A notorious example is the massive eruption of 1257 or 1258, which went unidentified in historical records for decades until the volcano Samalas on the Indonesian island of Lombok was pinpointed as the culprit.

the-named-winds-mistral-sirocco-harmatta.context_blurb: Many cultures have given names to their region's prevailing winds. The Mistral is a cold, dry wind that blows from the north over southern France. The Sirocco is a hot, dust-laden wind that blows north from the Sahara across the Mediterranean. The Harmattan carries red Saharan dust over West Africa. The Khamsin blows hot and sand-choked across Egypt. The Santa Ana rushes down the slopes of southern California. Each of these winds has shaped the landscape, farming, folklore, and sometimes even the architecture of the region it blows through.

the-namib.context_blurb: The Namib Desert runs along the Atlantic coast of Namibia, in southern Africa. It is probably the oldest desert on Earth; its basic climate has stayed arid for at least 55 million years. Its most famous feature is a line of towering red sand dunes near Sossusvlei, among the tallest dunes in the world. The desert is kept dry by a cold ocean current running past its shore, which steals moisture from the inland winds. The fogs that roll in off this cold current provide the only reliable water for the desert's bizarre specialist plants and animals.

the-nile.context_blurb: The Nile is the river that gave birth to Ancient Egyptian civilization and, for most of history, was considered the longest river on Earth. It flows north from sources in the lakes and highlands of equatorial Africa through thousands of kilometres of desert before fanning out into a vast green delta on the Mediterranean. For millennia its annual flood dropped a fresh layer of fertile silt across the surrounding fields each summer; the whole rhythm of life in Egypt was built around it until the Aswan High Dam ended the floods in the 1960s.

the-norwegian-maelstroms-saltstraumen-an.context_blurb: Off the northern coast of Norway, strong Atlantic tides are squeezed through narrow gaps between islands and whipped into some of the most powerful tidal maelstroms in the world. Saltstraumen, near the town of Bodo, is often called the strongest tidal current anywhere. Moskstraumen, off the Lofoten Islands further north, inspired writers from Edgar Allan Poe to Jules Verne to describe nightmare whirlpools. Modern tourists come to watch the water boil and swirl at the change of tides.

the-nubian-pyramids-of-mero.context_blurb: Most people have never heard that sub-Saharan Africa has more ancient pyramids than Egypt does. They stand in the Sudanese desert at Meroe, former capital of the kingdom of Kush, which ruled over much of the Nile valley south of Egypt for centuries. Built between about 300 BCE and 350 CE, the Nubian pyramids are smaller and steeper than their famous Egyptian cousins. In the 1830s an Italian treasure-hunter dynamited the tops off dozens of them looking for loot, which is why today they stand decapitated.

the-pacific-ocean-and-point-nemo.context_blurb: The Pacific is by far the largest ocean on Earth, covering more area than all the dry land on the planet combined. Somewhere in its empty southern reaches is Point Nemo — a point in the open ocean that is more distant from any dry land than anywhere else on the sea surface. The closest humans to this spot, when a crewed spacecraft is passing overhead, are the astronauts aboard the International Space Station. The region is used by spacefaring nations as a safe splashdown zone for retired satellites and spacecraft.

the-panama-hat-actually-from-ecuador.context_blurb: 'Panama hats' are not from Panama at all. They are hand-woven from the fibres of a palm-like plant that grows along the coast of Ecuador, where artisans in towns like Montecristi have been plaiting them for several centuries. The famous name is a historical accident: the hats were shipped from Ecuador through the Panamanian isthmus in the 19th century, and travellers crossing Panama on their way to the California gold rush bought them there. President Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the Panama Canal construction site, and the misleading name stuck.

the-pantheon-romes-unbeaten-concrete-dom.context_blurb: The Pantheon in the middle of Rome is one of the most impossible-looking buildings ever to survive from antiquity. Completed around AD 128 under the emperor Hadrian, its vast domed interior remained the largest concrete dome anywhere on Earth for the next 1,700 years, and it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built. In its ceiling is a single round hole, the oculus, open to the sky, which lets rain fall straight down into the middle of the floor. The whole thing is so geometrically perfect that a sphere exactly fills its interior.

the-pink-fire-on-the-mountains-alpenglow.context_blurb: After the Sun has set at ground level, high peaks can still catch its last reddish rays and briefly glow a warm pink-orange — a phenomenon called alpenglow. At the same time, looking in the opposite direction, you can see a soft pink band of sky just above the horizon, with the dark grey arc of Earth's own shadow rising below it. That pink band is called the Belt of Venus. Both phenomena are produced by the way sunlight is scattered through the long atmospheric path at low Sun angles.

the-pink-lakes-hillier-and-retba.context_blurb: Several lakes around the world are famously bright pink. Lake Hillier, on an island off the southern coast of Western Australia, and Lac Rose (Lake Retba) in Senegal, are two of the best-known. Their colour comes from a combination of salt-loving pink-and-red microbes and tiny crustaceans that thrive in extremely salty water. Lake Retba is salty enough to let swimmers float at the surface and salty enough to be commercially harvested for salt.

the-polar-lights-aurora-borealis-and-aus.context_blurb: The aurora borealis in the Northern Hemisphere and the aurora australis in the Southern are the same phenomenon: shimmering green, violet, and red curtains of light high in the atmosphere, visible mainly at high latitudes. They are caused by charged particles streaming out of the Sun, deflected by Earth's magnetic field toward the poles, and crashing into atoms in the upper atmosphere, which then re-emit the energy as coloured light. During particularly strong solar storms, auroras can occasionally be seen as far south as the Mediterranean.

the-red-sea-a-new-ocean-being-born.context_blurb: The Red Sea, between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, is a young ocean that is still being born. The African and Arabian tectonic plates began splitting apart about 30 million years ago, and the gap between them has slowly been widening ever since. Hot salty brines seep up from the sea floor along the central rift. In another twenty or thirty million years, geologists expect the Red Sea to have grown into a full-sized ocean basin as wide as the modern Atlantic.

the-ring-of-fire-a-rim-of-subduction-vol.context_blurb: The Pacific Ocean is almost completely ringed by a line of active volcanoes and major earthquake zones that geologists call the Ring of Fire. The ring stretches from New Zealand up through the islands of Southeast Asia, Japan, and Russia's Kamchatka, across the Aleutians, and down the entire western coast of the Americas to Chile. Along almost every part of this ring, oceanic tectonic plates are being forced down into the mantle beneath the surrounding plates, and the water carried down with them triggers melting and eruption on the way.

the-rub-al-khali-empty-quarter.context_blurb: The Rub' al Khali — Arabic for 'the Empty Quarter' — is the largest continuous expanse of sand on Earth, covering most of the southern Arabian Peninsula across parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen, and the UAE. It is almost completely uninhabited; even most Bedouin have historically skirted its edges rather than crossing it. In 2011, oil-exploration geologists working beneath it discovered the trace of a lost ancient trading city — perhaps the fabled Ubar — that may have been buried by the shifting sands.

the-sahara.context_blurb: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth, stretching roughly the width of the United States across North Africa. It separates the Mediterranean world from sub-Saharan Africa. Although it looks timelessly dry, the Sahara is not permanent: it has gone back and forth between desert and savannah over periods of thousands of years, driven by subtle wobbles in Earth's orbit. Six thousand years ago the Sahara was green, lakes stood in its middle, and hunters painted hippos and crocodiles on its rocks.

the-sargasso-sea-a-sea-with-no-shores.context_blurb: The Sargasso Sea, in the North Atlantic, is a strange region of calm, deep-blue water with no coastline — defined instead by the four strong currents that encircle it. Floating thickly on its surface are great mats of sargassum, a golden-brown seaweed that lives its whole life without ever touching the sea floor. The sargassum provides a floating ecosystem of its own, home to specialist crabs and fish. Mysteriously, European and American eels from vast stretches of both continents all migrate to the Sargasso Sea to spawn.

the-savanna-grassland-kept-open-by-fire.context_blurb: The African savanna is the great open grassland dotted with scattered acacia trees that stretches across much of sub-Saharan Africa; similar savannas occur in South America and Australia. It is one of the richest wildlife habitats on Earth, home to lions, elephants, zebras, giraffes, and the great seasonal migrations of wildebeest. Despite looking like a stable natural landscape, it is kept open and treeless by a combination of grazing animals, periodic drought, and above all regular fires. If fire is kept out, forests tend to creep back in.

the-sea-that-glows-blue-bioluminescent-b.context_blurb: In a handful of warm, sheltered coastal bays around the world — in Puerto Rico, Jamaica, the Maldives, parts of Southeast Asia, and off California — the water glows blue-green at night when disturbed. The glow comes from tiny single-celled plankton called dinoflagellates that produce flashes of bioluminescent light when stirred. Dipping a hand or a kayak paddle in the water sets off a spreading constellation of light. The best bioluminescent bays have populations of these plankton that are year-round and dense enough to produce clearly visible light.

the-sonoran-desert.context_blurb: The Sonoran Desert covers much of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, including Arizona and the Baja California peninsula. Unlike many deserts, it gets rain in two distinct seasons, which supports an unexpected profusion of plant life. Its icon is the saguaro cactus, a giant columnar cactus that can live for 150 years, grow up to 15 metres tall, and sprout its characteristic arms only after decades. The saguaro is also home to Gila woodpeckers that hollow out apartments in its trunk.

the-steel-pan-trinidad.context_blurb: The steel pan — the national instrument of Trinidad and Tobago — is one of the few genuinely new acoustic instruments invented in the 20th century. It was developed in Trinidad in the 1930s and 40s by poor young men who hammered discarded 55-gallon oil drums into tuned pitched surfaces, after the colonial British had banned traditional African drums and bamboo stamping-tubes. The steel pan became the sound of Trinidadian Carnival. Entire steel orchestras, with dozens of players, now give classical and pop concerts around the world.

the-sundarbans-mangrove-coast.context_blurb: The Sundarbans, straddling the border of India and Bangladesh at the mouth of the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, is the largest mangrove forest on Earth. Mangroves are salt-tolerant tropical trees that grow with their roots underwater, in tangled dense coastal forests that act as a nursery for fish and a natural buffer against storm surges. The Sundarbans is also the only mangrove region where tigers live; the Royal Bengal tigers that stalk its channels have earned a fearsome reputation among local fishers and honey-gatherers.

the-taiga-the-great-northern-forest.context_blurb: The taiga, or boreal forest, is the single largest forest biome on Earth. It wraps right around the top of the globe in a continuous belt of conifers across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia, and Siberia. Its trees — spruce, pine, fir, and larch — are built to stand brutal winters, with pointed shapes that shed snow and dark needles that soak up thin northern sunlight. The taiga stores enormous quantities of carbon, both in its trees and in the soggy, slow-rotting peat beneath them.

the-taklamakan.context_blurb: The Taklamakan Desert fills a huge basin in the far west of China, ringed on three sides by some of the highest mountains on Earth. Its name is often loosely translated as 'you can go in but you can't come out.' For most of history, Silk Road caravans skirted around its northern or southern edges, hopping from one oasis town to the next, rather than attempting to cross the sand. The ultra-dry conditions have preserved extraordinary mummies — some of them with reddish-blonde hair — in burial grounds along the desert's edges, from populations of mysterious origin.

the-tango-the-r-o-de-la-plata-buenos-air.context_blurb: The tango was born in the port-side neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo at the end of the 19th century. Both cities sit on opposite sides of the Rio de la Plata, the massive estuary between Argentina and Uruguay, and the music grew up in the dance halls and brothels frequented by waves of poor immigrants from Europe and Africa. It was initially considered scandalous. Taken up by Parisian high society around 1910, the tango became an international craze and later a national symbol of Argentina. Carlos Gardel became its first global superstar.

the-terracotta-army.context_blurb: Buried in the hills near the Chinese city of Xi'an is the tomb complex of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, who died in 210 BCE. Beside the still-unopened burial mound itself, farmers digging a well in 1974 discovered a colossal subterranean honour guard: thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, horses, and chariots arranged in battle formation, each soldier with his own individual face. The army is still being excavated. Many of the figures were originally brightly painted, though the colour mostly flakes off as the air hits it.

the-theremin-russias-untouchable-instrum.context_blurb: The theremin is an electronic musical instrument invented in 1920 by a Russian physicist named Lev Termen (Leon Theremin), who had been doing early research on radio-wave sensors. It is played without touching it: the performer waves their hands in the air near two antennas, one controlling pitch and one controlling volume. The instrument makes an eerie, swooping tone that was heavily used in science-fiction film soundtracks of the 1950s. Theremin himself was later kidnapped by Soviet agents and spent years as a prisoner designing bugging devices for the KGB.

the-three-ways-plates-meet-a-plate-bound.context_blurb: There are three fundamentally different ways that two tectonic plates can meet. At a 'divergent' boundary, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, two plates pull apart and new crust forms between them. At a 'convergent' boundary, like the Andes or the Himalayas, two plates push into each other, often with one being forced down beneath the other. At a 'transform' boundary, like California's San Andreas Fault, two plates grind past each other sideways without creating or destroying crust. All of Earth's biggest earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain belts can be sorted by boundary type.

the-tides-and-the-record-breaking-bay-of.context_blurb: Tides are the twice-daily rise and fall of sea level caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and (to a lesser extent) the Sun on Earth's oceans. In most of the world they move the water up and down by only a metre or two. In the Bay of Fundy, between the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the shape of the bay happens to resonate with the twice-daily tidal rhythm, so each incoming tide builds on itself and ends up moving the water surface by over 15 metres.

the-trade-winds-and-the-doldrums-the-hig.context_blurb: In the tropics on either side of the equator, steady winds blow from the east. In the Northern Hemisphere they are northeasterly; in the Southern they are southeasterly. These are the trade winds, which carried sailing ships across the oceans for centuries — Columbus rode them west to the Americas, and the Manila Galleon used them to cross the Pacific. Right at the equator the winds die to nothing in a hot, calm band of weather called the doldrums, where sailing ships could be becalmed for weeks.

the-wallace-line-an-invisible-border.context_blurb: In the island archipelago between Asia and Australia, there runs an invisible biological border that separates two completely different worlds of animal life. On one side you find Asian creatures: tigers, elephants, orangutans, monkeys. On the other side you find Australian ones: kangaroos, cockatoos, marsupials. The two faunas meet across a strait only a few dozen kilometres wide. The British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace noticed this in the 1850s during his years collecting specimens in the East Indies; the line is named after him, and it corresponds to a deep ocean trench that stayed submerged even during the lowest ice-age sea levels.

the-waltz-vienna.context_blurb: The waltz is a formal partner dance in triple metre that spread across European ballrooms in the late 18th and early 19th centuries from rural Austria and Bavaria. In Vienna it was taken up and transformed by composers like Josef Lanner and the Strauss family — Johann Strauss I and II — into fast, elegant pieces built on huge rolling melodies. The 'Vienna waltz' version is danced at speed. The dance was considered shockingly intimate when it first appeared in polite society, because partners held each other in a sustained close embrace.

the-worlds-great-rivers.context_blurb: The world's great rivers — the Nile, the Amazon, the Yangtze, the Mississippi, the Ganges, the Congo, the Volga — have been the arteries of civilization and the places most people have historically lived. Rankings of 'biggest' and 'longest' are surprisingly tricky: by volume the Amazon crushes every rival; by length the Nile and the Amazon run neck-and-neck, with the answer depending on exactly which upstream tributary you count. Each major river has its own hydrology, its own economy, and its own place in the imagination of the people who live along it.

the-yangtze.context_blurb: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia and the third-longest in the world, flowing nearly 6,400 kilometres across central China from Tibet to the East China Sea near Shanghai. It has been the main east-west transport artery of China for thousands of years. In the 1990s and 2000s China built the Three Gorges Dam across one of its most dramatic stretches, creating a reservoir over 600 kilometres long and the world's largest hydroelectric power station — at the cost of flooding dozens of towns and displacing more than a million people.

the-yellow-river-huang-he.context_blurb: The Yellow River — Huang He in Chinese — is the cradle of Chinese civilization. It flows across northern China from the Tibetan Plateau to the Bohai Sea, and its name comes from the enormous amount of yellowish silt (loess) it carries down from the loess plateau in its middle course. The river has repeatedly jumped its banks and shifted its route hundreds of kilometres, drowning entire regions; it has earned the nickname 'China's Sorrow' for the catastrophic floods it has unleashed over the centuries.

the-yucatan-cenotes-and-the-dinosaur-cra.context_blurb: The Yucatan Peninsula of southern Mexico is riddled with cenotes — natural water-filled sinkholes in the limestone, often connecting to vast underwater cave systems. The Maya considered them sacred, as gateways to the underworld. Modern aerial surveys revealed that a ring of cenotes marks the inner rim of an enormous buried crater — the Chicxulub crater — which was gouged out by the asteroid that is now believed to have killed the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.

throat-singing-tuva-and-mongolia.context_blurb: Throat singing, or overtone singing, is a technique in which a singer produces two or more distinct musical pitches at the same time, by shaping the vocal tract to amplify specific overtones of a sustained low drone. Several Central Asian cultures have independent traditions of it; the best known are from the small Russian republic of Tuva and from Mongolia, where it is called khoomei. Herders traditionally practised it on the open steppe. Done well, it can sound uncannily as if the single singer were a whole choir.

tidal-bores-rivers-that-run-backwards.context_blurb: A tidal bore is a wave that travels up a river from its mouth as the ocean tide comes in. On most rivers tides go in and out gradually, but in a few narrow, shallow, funnel-shaped estuaries, the rising sea piles up into a single steep wall of water that marches upstream, sometimes for kilometres. The largest tidal bore in the world races up China's Qiantang River each year during a particular lunar event; it draws big crowds, and surfers have learned to ride it.

tikal.context_blurb: Tikal, deep in the jungles of northern Guatemala, was one of the greatest cities of the Classic Maya between about 200 and 900 CE. Its central plaza is dominated by soaring limestone pyramid-temples that rise above the forest canopy. Howler monkeys roar at dawn through the ruins. Tikal was almost completely abandoned around the 10th century for reasons that archaeologists are still arguing about — probably some combination of drought, overpopulation, and warfare with its neighbours. The jungle swallowed it until Western explorers 'rediscovered' it in the 19th century.

timbuktu.context_blurb: Timbuktu is a dusty desert city on the southern edge of the Sahara in modern Mali. In the 14th through 16th centuries it was one of the wealthiest places on Earth, grown rich from the gold-and-salt trade across the Sahara, and home to a famous Islamic university that drew scholars from across the Muslim world. Its name became a European byword for 'the end of the Earth' because almost no European reached it and returned. Its old mud-brick libraries still hold tens of thousands of medieval manuscripts, which locals have hidden and smuggled from war and jihadists in recent years.

tiwanaku-and-pumapunku.context_blurb: Tiwanaku, high on the Bolivian plateau near Lake Titicaca, was the capital of a pre-Inca civilization that dominated the southern Andes between roughly 500 and 1000 CE. Its stonework is extraordinary: enormous blocks of andesite and sandstone, some weighing over a hundred tonnes, cut so precisely that their joins are nearly invisible. The nearby complex of Pumapunku is a strewn jumble of these cyclopean blocks that have been toppled, broken, or quarried away over the centuries. How a civilization without the wheel moved and worked these stones is still debated.

tokyo-the-endless-city.context_blurb: Tokyo, on the eastern coast of Honshu in Japan, is the largest metropolitan area on Earth, with somewhere around 37 million people living in its continuous sprawl. It was called Edo until 1868. Twice in the 20th century — once by earthquake in 1923 and once by firebombing in 1945 — most of it was flattened; each time it was rebuilt. Today it is a city that layers extreme modern pop culture over a quiet substrate of neighborhood shrines, back-alley bars, and old wooden houses tucked between glass towers.

tornado-alley-and-the-supercell.context_blurb: 'Tornado Alley' is a loosely defined region of the central United States, running from Texas up through Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska into South Dakota, that gets more tornadoes than anywhere else on Earth. The storms here feed on a specific collision of warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico, dry air off the Rockies, and cold air from Canada, all meeting in the central plains in spring and early summer. The parent of a tornado is usually a 'supercell' — a tall, rotating thunderstorm — and the biggest supercells can carry tornadoes that stay on the ground for over an hour.

tower-karst-stone-forests-and-drowned-dr.context_blurb: Tower karst is a dramatic variety of limestone landscape where erosion has reduced the rock to isolated steep-sided pinnacles, standing on a flat plain, their walls almost vertical. The most famous examples are in southern China around Guilin and Yangshuo along the Li River, whose landscape of mist-wrapped peaks is painted on classical Chinese scrolls and printed on the back of the 20 yuan note. Similar tower karst forms Ha Long Bay in Vietnam, Phang Nga Bay in Thailand, and the stone forest in Yunnan.

transform-faults-the-plates-that-grind-p.context_blurb: A transform fault is where two tectonic plates slide past each other horizontally, without colliding or pulling apart. The San Andreas Fault running through California is the most famous example; others include the North Anatolian Fault in Turkey and the Alpine Fault in New Zealand. Transform faults build little new ground and destroy little, but they produce the familiar sideways-slip earthquakes that have caused many of the deadliest modern disasters, including the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and the 1999 Izmit, Turkey earthquake.

troy-the-mound-of-hisarlik.context_blurb: Troy is the ancient city at the centre of Homer's Iliad, the great epic about the Trojan War, which generations of readers assumed was pure myth. In the 1870s a wealthy and showy German amateur archaeologist named Heinrich Schliemann started digging into a mound on the Turkish coast near the Dardanelles and uncovered one city built on top of another, layer after layer, nine in all. Not everyone agrees which of those cities corresponds to Homer's Troy, but the fact that there was a real place at all was a jolt that reshaped how classical scholars read ancient epics.

tsunamis-the-wave-that-empties-the-sea-f.context_blurb: A tsunami is not an ordinary wind-driven wave; it is a long-wavelength pulse of water that races across the open ocean after a sudden shift on the sea floor — usually an undersea earthquake, sometimes a volcanic eruption or landslide. In deep water a tsunami may be only a few centimetres high at the surface and can travel at jet-plane speeds. When it reaches shallow water near the coast it slows down and rears up into a towering wall. Just before it arrives, the sea often draws abnormally far back from the shore, exposing the sea floor.

tulum.context_blurb: Tulum is a small, late Maya city perched on cliffs above the turquoise Caribbean on the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico. Unlike most Maya cities, which were buried in jungle, Tulum has a wall around three sides and the sea along the fourth, making it one of the few walled Maya coastal towns. It was built around 1200 CE and was still occupied when the Spanish arrived in the early 1500s. From its clifftops its stone temples look out over the open ocean.

tundra-and-permafrost-the-frozen-ground.context_blurb: The tundra is the treeless cold-desert biome that rings the Arctic Ocean across northern Alaska, Canada, Scandinavia, and Siberia; a similar biome exists on high mountains above the tree line and around the fringes of Antarctica. The soil below the surface stays permanently frozen year-round, which is called permafrost. In the brief summer, only the top layer thaws, so plants are stunted and roots stay shallow. Enormous quantities of ancient carbon — in the form of long-dead plants — are locked up in the permafrost, which is one reason scientists watch it carefully.

u-shaped-valleys-and-hanging-valley-wate.context_blurb: A glacier carves a very different valley shape from a river. Rivers tend to cut V-shaped valleys with sharp bottoms. A glacier scrapes along more like a bulldozer, cutting a U-shaped valley with a flat floor and steep walls. When a small side-glacier joins a big main-trunk glacier, the two merge at the ice surface, but the smaller glacier's rocky base is cut less deeply. After the ice melts, that smaller side-valley is left 'hanging' high up on the main valley's wall, often with a waterfall at its mouth. The Yosemite Valley in California is full of them.

uluru-and-kata-tjuta.context_blurb: Uluru and Kata Tjuta are two striking rock formations near the exact centre of Australia — Uluru is a single massive rounded sandstone monolith, Kata Tjuta ('many heads') a cluster of neighbouring domes. Both are deeply sacred to the Anangu, the local Aboriginal people, whose dreaming stories identify specific features of each outcrop with the activities of ancestral beings. In 2019, after years of requests from the Anangu, climbing on Uluru itself was officially banned out of respect for their religious traditions.

uluru-and-the-red-centre.context_blurb: Uluru, in the arid centre of Australia, is a massive rounded sandstone monolith rising abruptly out of flat scrubland. It is held sacred by the local Anangu people, who have specific traditional law and story associated with features all over its surface. The rock catches sunlight so dramatically at dawn and dusk that it glows an intense red. Nearby stands Kata Tjuta ('the Olgas'), a cluster of equally spectacular dome-shaped formations. In 2019, out of respect for Anangu wishes, the Australian government officially banned the climbing of Uluru itself.

ushuaia.context_blurb: Ushuaia, on the island of Tierra del Fuego at the very southern tip of Argentina, calls itself the southernmost city in the world. It sits on the Beagle Channel — named for the ship on which the young Charles Darwin passed through — looking out at the mountains and glaciers of the subantarctic. For most of the 20th century its main employer was a prison for serious offenders of the Argentine state; today it is the main port of departure for cruise ships to Antarctica.

valparaiso.context_blurb: Valparaiso is a Pacific port city on the central Chilean coast. In the second half of the 19th century, before the Panama Canal opened in 1914, it was one of the great way-stations for sailing ships rounding Cape Horn between Europe and California, and sailors of many nationalities settled on its forty-two steep hills. Those hills are reached by rickety 19th-century funicular railways — the ascensores — and their walls are covered in bright murals, giving the whole city a slightly ramshackle, bohemian air.

varanasi-the-eternal-city-on-the-ganges.context_blurb: Varanasi, on the Ganges in northern India, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth. For Hindus it is the single holiest city of all: Shiva's city, where it is believed that dying releases the soul from the cycle of rebirth. Pilgrims come from across India to bathe in the river at dawn, and the dead are brought here to be cremated on the burning ghats by the water's edge. Writers from Mark Twain to Allen Ginsberg have tried, and mostly failed, to describe its intensity.

vatnajokull-iceland.context_blurb: Vatnajokull, in southeastern Iceland, is the largest glacier in Europe outside the Arctic.
