It covers nearly a tenth of Iceland and holds dozens of outlet glaciers, several active volcanoes buried under its ice, and a growing network of ice caves that are opened by seasonal meltwater. When one of its subglacial volcanoes erupts, it melts huge amounts of ice from below in a hurry, triggering sudden catastrophic floods — known in Icelandic as 'jokulhlaup' — that race across the surrounding plains.

venice-the-city-on-a-sunken-forest.context_blurb: Venice sits in a shallow lagoon on the Adriatic Sea, in northeastern Italy. Its early inhabitants, fleeing invasions on the mainland, found refuge on its scattered sand-islands and built the whole city on top of millions of wooden piles driven down into the mud. For centuries Venice ran one of the most important trading empires in the Mediterranean, growing rich on commerce with the Islamic world and the Byzantine East. Today it is slowly sinking as the lagoon itself is slowly rising, which is a problem no one has quite solved.

vesuvius-and-the-burial-of-pompeii.context_blurb: Mount Vesuvius, on the Bay of Naples in southern Italy, is the only active volcano on the European mainland. Its most famous eruption, in AD 79, buried the Roman cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum under metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The two cities lay buried and forgotten until the 18th century, when their excavation gave the modern world its single best window into daily Roman life. Vesuvius remains active today; a few million people live in its potential blast radius.

victoria-falls.context_blurb: Victoria Falls, on the Zambezi River on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, is one of the biggest waterfalls on Earth by width and height combined. The river suddenly plunges over a straight basalt cliff more than a kilometre wide into a narrow slot gorge on the other side, generating a column of spray that can be seen from fifty kilometres away. The local people called it Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders.' David Livingstone was the first European to see it, in 1855, and named it after Queen Victoria.

vienna.context_blurb: Vienna, in modern Austria on the Danube River, was for centuries the capital of the Habsburg Empire that ruled much of Central Europe. It twice withstood sieges by the Ottoman Turks (in 1529 and 1683), and in the 18th and 19th centuries it became the musical capital of the world — Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, and Mahler all worked here. In the early 20th century it was also the home of Sigmund Freud. The ring road around the old city traces the line of the old city walls that were pulled down in the 1860s.

volcanic-lightning-the-ash-clouds-dirty-.context_blurb: During some big volcanic eruptions, bright bolts of lightning crackle through the dark ash plume rising from the crater. This is 'volcanic lightning,' sometimes called a 'dirty thunderstorm.' It happens because particles of ash and ice colliding inside the fast-rising plume build up static charge, which eventually discharges in exactly the same way regular cloud-to-cloud lightning does. Photographers have made it a specialty, capturing the strange sight of forked bolts lacing through an orange-glowing ash column at night.

washington-d-c.context_blurb: Washington, D.C. is the capital of the United States, laid out from scratch in the 1790s on swampy ground on the Potomac River so that no existing state would host the federal government. The French-American architect Pierre L'Enfant designed its radiating diagonal avenues and open mall. In the city's exact centre stands the white dome of the Capitol, home of Congress; a long rectangle of lawn stretches west from it, lined with memorials and museums, past the Washington Monument obelisk and down to the Lincoln Memorial. During the War of 1812 the British briefly captured the city and burned the White House.

water-that-isnt-there-and-cities-in-the-.context_blurb: A mirage is an optical illusion produced when air of different temperatures bends light so sharply that distant objects or the sky itself appear mirrored or displaced. The familiar 'wet-looking patch' on a hot road is a mirage of the sky. A more dramatic kind, the Fata Morgana, happens when layered temperature inversions over cold water bend light into tall, distorted mirages of distant ships or coastlines — sailors have sworn for centuries that they saw whole floating cities and castles in the air far out at sea.

waterfalls-the-rivers-great-leaps.context_blurb: A waterfall forms wherever a river hits a sudden drop in its riverbed. Most of the time this happens because the rock in the bed changes from a hard layer upstream to a softer layer downstream; the river wears away the softer rock faster, carving a step. The highest waterfalls — Angel Falls in Venezuela, Tugela in South Africa — pour over the edges of flat-topped highlands. The biggest waterfalls by volume — Victoria and Iguazu — show up where huge rivers crash over a long cliff. Niagara and others are migrating upstream over the centuries as the lip of the fall erodes.

wave-rock.context_blurb: Wave Rock is a natural rock formation in Western Australia, standing in a wheat-growing area of the state's dry inland. It is a cliff of granite about 15 metres high that curves over at the top in a perfect, continuous arc — the shape of a cresting ocean wave about to break on the beach. It was formed by weathering at the base of the rock when it was still buried in the subsoil; after erosion stripped away the covering, the sheltered curved shape was exposed. The whole surface is streaked with vertical bands of mineral staining.

wellington.context_blurb: Wellington is the capital of New Zealand, perched on the southern tip of the North Island on a nearly land-locked harbour. The city sits across the Cook Strait from the South Island and right on top of an active fault line, so earthquakes are an ordinary fact of life. Its exposed location also means it is one of the windiest cities in the world. Despite being the capital, Wellington has only about half a million people and feels much more like a small town than its larger northern rival Auckland.

where-the-sun-forgets-to-set-midnight-su.context_blurb: At latitudes above about 66.5 degrees — the Arctic and Antarctic Circles — the geometry of Earth's tilt means that for part of the year the Sun does not set at all, and for part of the year it does not rise. The further you go toward the pole, the longer each of these periods lasts. At the pole itself the Sun is up for about six continuous months and down for the other six. The 'midnight sun' and 'polar night' make for strange daily rhythms in northern Scandinavia, Alaska, and the Antarctic research stations.

wieliczka-salt-mine.context_blurb: The Wieliczka Salt Mine, just outside Krakow in southern Poland, has been producing table salt continuously since the 13th century. Salt was once worth almost its weight in silver, and the mine was a key source of Polish royal wealth. Over seven centuries the miners dug a labyrinth of corridors and vast chambers more than three hundred metres deep — and along the way they carved whole chapels, altars, chandeliers, and bas-reliefs out of the rock-salt itself. It is one of the most unexpectedly beautiful sites anywhere underground.

xian-the-walled-city-at-the-end-of-the-s.context_blurb: Xi'an, in central China, is one of the oldest cities in the country, sitting at the eastern end of the overland Silk Road. Under its ancient name Chang'an it served as the capital of a long line of Chinese dynasties, most famously the Han and the Tang, when it was perhaps the biggest city in the world. Its Ming-dynasty city walls — massive, square, and still complete — enclose the old centre, and the terracotta army of the first emperor of unified China was buried just outside town.

yellowstone.context_blurb: Yellowstone, mostly in the state of Wyoming in the United States, is one of the oldest national parks in the world — set aside in 1872 — and it sits on top of one of the biggest active volcanic systems on Earth. Its surface is dotted with half the planet's geothermal features: boiling mud pots, hot springs in blazing colours produced by heat-loving microbes, and about half the world's active geysers. Yellowstone's underlying magma chamber is huge enough that if it ever had another full-scale eruption, the result would be a continent-scale catastrophe.

yogyakarta-borobudur-and-prambanan.context_blurb: Yogyakarta — called 'Jogja' — is a Javanese city in central Indonesia and still, uniquely in modern Indonesia, the seat of a reigning sultan whose palace sits in the middle of town. It is the launching point for visiting two of the greatest ancient temple complexes in Southeast Asia, the Buddhist Borobudur and the Hindu Prambanan, both nearby in the lush volcanic countryside. The city is also considered the cultural capital of Java — the home of batik cloth, Javanese shadow puppet theatre, and gamelan orchestral music.

zhangye-danxia-rainbow-mountains.context_blurb: In Gansu province in northwestern China, a stretch of sandstone hills called the Zhangye Danxia 'rainbow mountains' is striped in deep red, orange, yellow, green, and blue bands. The colours come from different mineral oxides in sediment layers that were laid down flat about 80 million years ago, then tilted up on their edges by tectonic forces, and finally exposed by erosion. The result looks almost painted on; it is probably the most photogenic patch of sandstone on Earth.
